item.title: What Isn’t Organised Crime?
item.dc:creator: Cristián Irarrázaval Zaldívar
item.category: Reflexive Globalisation and the Law: Expanding and Deepening its Understanding

item.content:encoded:
April 2026, Stammheim Prison in Stuttgart, Germany, where the militant group Red Army Faction (“RAF”) was tried in the 1970s. Five defendants without criminal records sit handcuffed behind bulletproof glass, separated from their lawyers, after more than eight months in pre-trial detention. In September 2025 they had broken into a plant of Elbit Systems Deutschland, a subsidiary of an Israeli military technology company, smashed equipment, sprayed “Baby Killers” on the walls and waited for the police. Among the charges: membership of a criminal association under paragraph 129 of the German Criminal Code.1)

Across the Atlantic, prosecutors in Fulton County in the US state of Georgia offered the rap line “I’m a general” as proof that the rapper and singer-songwriter Young Thug led a criminal army made up of associates of his record label. The 56-count indictment under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) yielded Georgia’s longest criminal trial and not a single murder conviction – murder being the main predicate offence.2)

In Arica, northern Chile, Joise Alvear Oropeza, a Venezuelan sex worker who paid a weekly extortion fee (vacuna) to members of the organisation Tren de Aragua, spent more than two years in a high-security prison awaiting the verdict in Chile’s first mega-trial against that organisation. The prosecution sought over one hundred years’ imprisonment, criminal association among the counts, largely on the strength of her intimate relationship with a co-defendant. She was acquitted on every count.3)

What do these cases have in common? In each, the offence that spearheads the fight against organised crime – criminal association or enterprise – turned property damage, cultural expression and sex work into something far graver. The mechanism is always the same: the undeniable danger posed by real criminal organisations justifies offences so elastic that they fit almost any group of people, and whose invocation unlocks consequences bearing no proportion to the conduct. By punishing mere membership, these statutes create what Gerard Lynch called the crime of being a criminal.4) The vagueness is not a drafting failure. It is by design, as the remaining sections will show. A liberal criminal law – understood as one committed to constraining the state’s power to punish – cannot leave that design unanswered. In this post, I argue that the solution lies in a restrictive reading of these offences, and that its key is identifying the wrongfulness specific to the offence: what separates a genuine criminal organisation from a group disliked by a transient majority is that its very existence threatens the state’s ability to fulfil its essential functions.

Palermo: A Definition That Excludes Almost Nothing

Article 2 of the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime (Palermo Convention) defines an “organized criminal group” as three or more persons, existing for “a period of time”, acting in concert to commit one (!) or more serious crimes – offences carrying a maximum penalty of at least four years – for a material benefit that may even be indirect. The same provision then lists what is not required: formal roles, continuity of membership, or a developed structure. This is the trademark of “suppression conventions”: maximum scope and minimum regard for those affected.5) The definition thus fits fishermen taking shellfish out of season far better than Tren de Aragua. Nothing in it asks what, if anything, the group threatens. And although the Palermo Convention was designed for “transnational offences”, several national legislatures have all but copied its provisions, with far-fetched prosecutions as the result.

The opening examples were not picked at random. Section 129 of the German Criminal Code is the paradigm of the European continental technique of punishing membership as such.6) Germany, however, has gone further than both the Convention and Framework Decision 2008/841/JHA of the European Union on the fight against organised crime, dropping the material-benefit element and lowering the predicate threshold to offences with a maximum penalty of at least two years – so that almost the entire criminal code, shoplifting included, qualifies.7) RICO, the main US federal instrument regulating organised crime since 1970, punishes a pattern of racketeering carried out through an “enterprise” whose requirements the Supreme Court has kept minimal.8) Chile, for its part, exemplifies the receiving end: uncritical reception, stripped of the constraints that (very incompletely) tame these offences in the Global North. The Chilean offence of criminal association (Articles 292 and 293 of the Criminal Code) is so wide that it has been used repeatedly against the sale of counterfeit sneakers and the illegal extraction of shellfish.9)

Not Just a Procedural Door-Opener

Association offences operate primarily as a door-opener whose real function is procedural. Convictions under section 129 of the German Criminal Code run between five and twenty a year; investigations run into the hundreds. The provision unlocks telecommunications and acoustic surveillance, online searches, undercover agents, dragnets, state trojans and IMSI catchers.10)

The disproportion between a threadbare suspicion and the measures it licenses is dangerous enough. Worse still is the selectivity with which association offences are applied: in Germany, against neo-Nazi music bands, cigarette smugglers, football hooligans, climate activists and leaflet printers; in Chile, under the related anti-terrorism statute, mainly against indigenous leaders, an application the Inter-American Court of Human Rights condemned.11) On the other hand, only rarely are these provisions applied to white-collar crime. Selectivity, admittedly, cuts across the whole of criminal law,12) but the fuzzier the offence, the more manipulable its interpretation and the more discretionary its application. The criterion I propose would help here too: a corporate network that captures regulators or courts through systematic bribery does threaten the state’s essential functions, and that is precisely when the offence should be invoked.

The Return Leg: Tough-on-Crime Norms Travelling North

Philipp Dann and Florian Jeßberger describe reflexive globalisation as a phase in which legal concepts are renegotiated in dialogue between South and North.13) In organised crime legislation, the southward flow is easy to observe: the North exports its suppression conventions (treaties obliging state parties to criminalise certain conduct, such as the Palermo Convention or the UN Convention against Corruption), the South over-implements. Sometimes the process descends into absurdity, as with the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act: pressed on US competitors through the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention, it was “switched off” in February 2025 by an executive order in the name of US competitiveness.14) The norm travelled; the discretion to suspend it stayed in the North.

A return leg, i.e. a northward flow, has nonetheless opened, and it carries norms, not only facts – most clearly in the law of terrorism, closely related to that of organised crime.15) As early as August 2015, the Salvadoran Constitutional Chamber held that the main criminal gangs (MS-13 and Barrio 18) were terrorist organisations, extending the label to members, collaborators, apologists and financiers of the groups.16) In February 2025 the US followed suit, designating Tren de Aragua, MS-13 and six cartels as “foreign terrorist organisations”. The label activates an offense of “material support”, which punishes any contribution to a designated group without proof of an enterprise – a threshold even lower than RICO’s – and months later supplied the vocabulary for lethal strikes against alleged “narco-terrorists” at sea.17) Ten years separate San Salvador from Washington. The innovation was not the concept. It was the scale. Nor did the US merely copy the technique; it rented the regime, paying several million dollars to hold 300 Venezuelan deportees in El Salvador’s CECOT mega-prison under a state of exception no US court had authorised.18)

Who Decides, and Who Can Object?

Those designations also answer the question of who decides. When a government determines whether a group is a criminal or terrorist organisation, the decision precedes any trial and, once it takes effect, the law may forbid a defendant from raising “any question concerning the validity of the issuance of such designation as a defence or an objection at any trial or hearing”.19)

In such cases, all that remains for the criminal process to determine is whether the defendant actually belongs to the group – and even that is increasingly settled by administrative fiat. The validation guide of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) scores indicators such as tattoos, worth four points on their own; anyone reaching eight is deemed a member of Tren de Aragua. CalGang, California’s gang database, shows where this leads: a 2016 audit found 42 people entered as under one year old – 28 of them for “admitting to being gang members”.20)

The mutual hardening of North and South, and the shrinking space left to courts for deciding what counts as a criminal organisation and who belongs to it, make a judicial answer – a restrictive reading of association offences – all the more pressing. Otherwise, due process and proportionality are as good as gone.

A Restrictive Reading: What Is the Wrongfulness of Criminal Association?

Constitutional review has proved difficult: the interests these statutes invoke, public order and public security, are what Roland Hefendehl calls Scheinrechtsgüter, placeholders lacking the contour a proportionality test needs to bite.21) Proportionality is far more powerful one level down, as a canon of construction: a source of narrow readings of the offence and even of unwritten elements. And the first question a proportionate reading must ask is what the wrongfulness of this offence actually is.

German case law shows a way forward, if a modest one. The Federal Court of Justice (BGH) requires that the association pose a significant threat to public security, a requirement found nowhere in the statute and without which three people who repeatedly steal chewing gum satisfy the wording.22) Obvious as this may seem, several legal orders apply the offence on the bare wording, with no such corrective. The BGH’s formula points in the right direction but leaves open what the target of the threat should be.

The criterion can be given more content still. Manuel Cancio Meliá locates the wrongfulness in the arrogation of the state’s monopoly of violence, so that only organisations that systematically use or threaten violence are covered – not climate activists or clothing vendors.23) I would go a step further: the wrongfulness lies in the existence of an organisation that calls into question the state’s ability to fulfil its essential functions. Football hooligans who arrange fights with rival supporters resort to violence, yet do not endanger the state’s functioning and therefore do not belong here. Conversely, an organisation set up not to kill police officers but to sabotage the computer systems of hospitals or ministries until they can no longer operate uses no violence yet strikes at precisely that ability. This criterion would confine the offence to a list of predicate crimes similar to, though narrower than, the one in section 5 of the German Criminal Code, which codifies the protective principle of jurisdiction: offences against the state’s vital interests, punishable wherever committed. None of this means that the conduct of the excluded groups goes unpunished: criminal damage, coercion, assault and trademark offences remain available.

The general part supplies further constraints, once one accepts that the association offence is an exception – to the rules on parties to a crime, on inchoate liability, on merger – and that exceptions should be read narrowly. Accessories should not be reached through the general rules on participation where the offence does not expressly cover their form of conduct; attempt should not give rise to liability unless the statute so provides (otherwise the result is pre-pre-inchoate liability);24) and offences committed in the context of the association should, as a rule, merge rather than accumulate. The doctrine of objective attribution (objektive Zurechnung) would dispose of most supporter cases: the printer who prints leaflets for an anarchist group at the market price performs a socially adequate act, and what he knew is beside the point.

Keeping the Label Honest

None of this denies that organised criminal activity can seriously threaten a state and its citizens. And although several authors doubt whether so vague a concept is of any analytical utility,25) I do not propose abandoning it. But if the label is to be used in criminal law, the genuinely dangerous social phenomenon must be kept as clearly apart as possible from its merely symbolic use. A group whose existence leaves the state able to fulfil its essential functions – even if it commits offences, so long as they are not of that kind – is not organised crime, however much a majority may dislike it. A restrictive reading of these offences is the only way to keep the “fight” against organised crime from sliding into authoritarianism. Liberal criminal law, in a world of Bukeles, Dutertes and Trumps, is admittedly an increasingly lonely and marginal commitment. But that is no reason to sacrifice justice and legitimacy to the fears of an anxious majority.

item.content:encoded:
In 1999, David Kennedy famously affirmed that “international law is different in different places”,1) a reality that practitioners and scholars around the world had already long experienced.2) From the Global South’s imperial critique and rejection of international law,3) to a religiously infused international law in the Arab World,4) or the recent acknowledgement of European international law as a regional law,5) one can argue that the “local” in international law is central to any inquiry on reflexivity.

These are indeed the premises. As the scholarship explains, any reflexive analysis of globalisation and international law must necessarily consider how historical narratives, inherited genealogies, and jurisdictional knowledge frameworks shape the legal order.6) Deeply embedded in Global North–Global South debates, Philipp Dann and Florian Jeßberger have recently proposed the idea of reflexive globalisation, arguing that globalisation has entered a new phase and should no longer be understood as a unidirectional process of “Westernisation”, but rather as a multidirectional renegotiation of concepts, vocabularies, and epistemic certainties.7) In the area of public international law, Global South practitioners and scholars of the Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL) have already for some time diagnosed “what is wrong” with international law and have devised responses to its systemic injustices. In this endeavour, adopting a “local” lens has proved instrumental.8)

Yet it is striking that, despite its own “history, historical genealogies and epistemic geography of international law”,9) marked by both participation in and, at times, resistance to the making of modern (liberal) international law, important exceptions notwithstanding,10) the Global East remains largely absent from this debate. Understood as a liminal space between North and South, between empire and transition, it has often been overlooked. It is therefore plausible to ask what reflexive globalisation might learn from the perspective of, and the engagement with the Global East.

Global East and Its Liminality

Following Martin Müller’s definition, the Global East here is understood as a liminal epistemic space in-between North and South, rather than a geographical delineation.11) Its roots lie in the 20th-century communist project,12) flourishing during the Cold War through the development of so-called socialist international law. The significance of this framework waned with the dissolution of the Soviet Union, as the world came to be viewed predominantly along the North–South divide. What remained was a shared condition of liminality among societies that could not be easily accommodated within this dominant paradigm, societies which, as Müller notes, “include both colonisers and colonies, aggressors and victims; some countries were both at the same time”.13)

The East is excluded from Global South debates and distanced from the Global North, which, through its civilisational mission, defined the East by its purported backwardness.14) From this perspective, the East shares what Dipesh Chakrabarty famously termed the postcolonial condition of being relegated to the “waiting room of history”.15) This dual exclusion, North and South, is central. The Global North excludes the East through a civilisational logic that frames it as permanently belated. As for the Global South, the Global East’s historical experiences do not fit the colonial/postcolonial framework, with many Eastern European states having been simultaneously colonisers and colonised, imperial powers and peripheral territories.16) This is not to suggest an equivalence between, for instance, Soviet and Western colonial projects, which operated through distinct ideological and legal vocabularies;17) rather, it is to highlight the structural ambiguity that results from being positioned on both sides of the imperial divide. The economic logic is similarly unsettled. The East is neither as impoverished as much of the Global South nor as prosperous as the Global North, yet parts of the South may, in reality, be considerably wealthier than parts of the East.18) Thus, the East remains caught in a structural ambiguity, a distinct epistemic position of liminality caught between competing hegemonic projects, imperial legacies and ideological inheritances (in-between) and absent from the dominant frameworks.19)

This condition of liminality explains not only the silence of the East and the ignorance of others about it, but also its current emancipation and return to knowledge production circuits. For international law, this does not entail the addition of yet another dividing line to the North–South binary. Rather, it calls for renewed attention to what the shared condition of liminality reveals about the Global East’s encounters with international law, and for giving voice to the Global East’s divisible college, i.e. practitioners, judges, and scholars whose engagements with international law rarely feature in the dominant Anglo-European or postcolonial canons,20) that speaks in registers shaped by particular history, geographical settings and by the everyday practice of navigating multiple, overlapping legal orders.

Global East, SWAIL and the Challenge of Reflexivity

The liminality of the Global East serves as a catalyst for advancing long-overdue inquiries into the encounters between liminal societies and international law. Recently, and especially after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, international legal scholarship has become increasingly interested in analysing and understanding Eastern Europe, and the Global East more broadly, and its encounters with international law. Knowledge production in this regard falls under the umbrella of Second World Approaches to International Law (SWAIL), which aims to engage with the double exclusion condition that characterises the Global East, and to bring different visions of international law into conversation, not with the aim of furthering fragmentation and division, but rather to better understand, and perhaps even complete, the puzzles of an international law predominantly seen in binary terms.21) As the editorial to a recent special issue notes, SWAIL can be understood as “a complex set of practices and ideas, as well as interpretations of those practices and ideas”.22) It is foregrounded in both mainstream views and critical approaches. In this sense, by problematising “concepts, methods, maps, histories, agendas, and even normative definitions of international law that have long been taken for granted as objects of inquiry”,23) SWAIL enters international law debates to give voice to the long-silenced and overlooked Global East, much as TWAIL has done for the Global South.

However, the story to be told is not necessarily centred around colonialism and colonial justice, but on the condition of liminality that created exclusion or a camouflaged inclusion. By camouflaged inclusion, I mean a semblance of belonging which might vanish or oscillate depending on the power projection. In this sense, what SWAIL may centre is the politics of positionality, how law’s meaning shifts depending on where one stands in relation to overlapping hierarchies of power. As such, the issue is not necessarily about who was wronged by colonialism and how this should be remedied, although this may be relevant in specific cases. The inquiry is rather about how liminal actors navigate international law when they are neither clear victims nor clear beneficiaries of the existing order; what strategies of engagement, appropriation, and reinterpretation emerge from this condition. The post-Soviet space exemplifies precisely this. It has undergone successive waves of legal transplantation, from socialist international law to post-1991 Westernisation, reflecting its historical reorientation between competing hegemonic projects. 24) These shifts, driven first by integration into the Soviet system and later by the West’s “mission civilisatrice”, ultimately shaped how international law is articulated across the region.25) This condition of “in-betweenness”, which shapes the current fragmented landscape, adds to the liminality and dual exclusion that SWAIL seeks to capture and exposes how international law’s binary framing fails to accommodate the region’s positional complexity. This in-betweenness also unveils that the region’s legal engagement is geopolitically positioned; states oscillate between West and Russia not necessarily from doctrinal conviction but in response to shifting power dynamics and security concerns. This reveals how law’s meaning is always situated, a key insight of reflexivity.26)

Moreover, legal language functions as an instrument with world-making effects,27) as seen in the post-Soviet space where states selectively incorporate international norms without fully absorbing them, reinterpreting them through distinct geopolitical and historical lenses. This adaptation and resistance challenge linear progress narratives, embodying reflexive globalisation’s core concern with how norms are remade through local practice rather than whether they are “correctly” applied.28)

What Reflexive Globalisation Might Learn from the Global East

This is where reflexive globalisation becomes analytically powerful. Rather than forcing the region into pre-existing binaries, North/South, West/East, coloniser/colonised, it invites us to consider what happens when we take the Global East’s liminality seriously as a source of insight rather than as a deficit. In doing so, reflexive globalisation may be approached both substantially and procedurally.29)

Procedurally, it can start by taking liminality as a resource for inclusivity. Rather than viewing liminality as a deficit, SWAIL treats it as a productive position from which to question settled categories. The Global East’s experience of being simultaneously inside and outside dominant legal frameworks can reveal what is obscured by binary oppositions. In this sense, international law becomes more inclusive, a “historically situated structure shaped by dominant discourses and their blind spots”.30)

Reflexive globalisation emphasises dialogue and iterative conversation as crucial to rethinking legal concepts.31) The SWAIL framework seeks precisely this: inclusion, dialogue, and the problematisation of dominant narratives. For the Global East, this dual imperative, self-reflexivity and reflexive globalisation, takes on a distinctive character. Self-reflexivity demands confronting layered and entangled legacies that resist binary North-South framings, while reflexive globalisation requires that these liminal experiences be fully integrated into the broader renegotiation of legal concepts, lest the dialogue remain incomplete.

Substantially, it is important to highlight that legal concepts are never simply transplanted; they are remade through translation, vernacularisation, and local practice. Reflexive globalisation must attend to these processes if it is to avoid reproducing the very hierarchies it seeks to unsettle, including, in its dynamics, not only North–South framings but also the East. The Global East’s experience of translation is distinctive in at least two respects. First, it has been a site of repeated transplantation, from socialist international law to Western liberal frameworks, and now to a fragmented landscape of competing hegemonic projects. This is not a single moment of translation but a continuous process of reorientation, where each layer of legal meaning remains sedimented beneath the next, available for reactivation when geopolitical conditions shift. Second, the Global East’s translations have often occurred under conditions of imposed inclusion through occupation, sphere-of-influence politics, and the coercive export of legal models. This means that the “local” in the Global East is not a pristine site of authentic meaning but itself a product of prior translations.

Reflexive globalisation, attentive to these dynamics, must therefore ask not only how norms are translated but also under what conditions of power translation occurs, and what residues previous translations leave behind. As Müller argues, “recovering the Global East means thinking from the interstices of the North and the South – not just for the East, but also for the North and the South”.32)

Conclusion

Reflexive globalisation offers a valuable framework for understanding the contemporary renegotiation of legal concepts in a multipolar world. It moves beyond the polarising choice between rejection and adaptation, recognising the entangled character of South-North relations. The Global East, with its history of liminality and dual exclusion, serves as an important testing ground for this framework. It allows us to think beyond binaries, whether North/South, West/East, or universal/particular.

The aim is to broaden the conversation and remind us that the predominant divide was never as stable as assumed. As SWAIL suggests, the most productive insights often come from those who fit nowhere because their positionality reveals what dominant frameworks cannot see.

Reflexive globalisation, in this sense, is not a neutral description of contemporary trends but a call to engage with the politics of legal knowledge. The Global East’s liminality reveals that international law is always practiced from somewhere,33) shaped by situated histories, geopolitical pressures, and strategic calculations. To take reflexive globalisation seriously is to ask, with SWAIL, not simply about who is included but also about whose experiences, whose vocabularies, and whose futures are rendered visible or invisible in international law’s ongoing transformations. And this is precisely what taking seriously the Global East’s liminality brings to reflexivity.

European governments have condemned the measure, but that is not enough. The Commission should promptly activate the Blocking Statute before the licence expires.

item.content:encoded:
After sanctioning the ICC Prosecutor, its Deputy Prosecutors and several judges, including its President, the US has now issued sanctions on the International Criminal Court itself. On 9 October 2026, the same day on which the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a former judge of the ICC, the US added the Court to its sanctions list. Moreover, the European banks, insurers and software providers that serve the Court now risk being designated in turn, and the licence that covers ordinary dealings with the Court expires on 7 April 2027. The EU has an instrument to respond, the Blocking Statute, but it has not extended it to the US sanctions on the Court. Extending it would expose any operator that cuts off the Court to having to justify that decision before a European court. European governments have condemned the measure, but that is not enough. The Commission should promptly activate the Blocking Statute before the licence expires.

From Judges to the Institution

On 9 October 2026, the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) added the International Criminal Court to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List, under Executive Order 14203 of 6 February 2025.

For twenty months, Washington had targeted individuals. It now targets the institution’s means of operating: its accounts, contracts and suppliers. The Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, announced that the United States would continue to dismantle the Court until Americans were no longer exposed to it.

The escalation began in February 2025, when the US sanctioned the ICC’s Prosecutor. Several judges followed. The French judge Nicolas Guillou was put on the sanction list on 20 August 2025, then the Deputy Prosecutors and, in August 2026, the President of the Court, Judge Tomoko Akane.

The legal basis is the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and EO 14203, implemented by the International Criminal Court-Related Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR part 528). All property and interests in property of the Court within US jurisdiction are blocked, and US persons, wherever located, may not deal with it without authorisation. Section 1(a)(ii) of the order further allows the designation of any foreign person who has materially assisted, sponsored or provided financial, material or technological support to a blocked person, or acted on its behalf.

The target of the sanctions is a treaty-based international organisation, but that is no obstacle under US law. The United States has never ratified the Rome Statute. Article 48 of the Statute and the headquarters agreement with the Netherlands bind only the States that consented to them.

OFAC has done this before. In April 2023, it designated the International Investment Bank, an intergovernmental institution founded in 1970 and then headquartered in Budapest. Within days Hungary announced its withdrawal and the bank left the European Union. The difference is one of scale: the Court has 125 States Parties, including all twenty-seven Member States of the Union, and sits on EU territory.

Four General Licences and a Six-Month Clock

The US has effectively put a six-month clock on the Court’s ordinary finances, thereby creating leverage over the Court and pressing the States Parties to address US concerns. It did so with four general licences (13, 14, 15 and 16), which create exceptions to the sanctions. The main one, General License 13, ends on 7 April 2027.

General License 13 concerns the Court’s finances. It allows ordinary dealings with the Court, such as contributions from States Parties, staff salaries, rent and supplier invoices, but only to keep the Court running or to wind it down, and only until 7 April 2027. It does not cover anyone who is separately sanctioned: a staff member can be paid, while a judge designated by name stays blocked.

The other three are narrower. General License 14 keeps telecommunications and business software available, with no end date. General License 15 allows pensions to be paid. General License 16 lets the custody of nine named detainees, among them Rodrigo Duterte, continue.

Unless OFAC renews General License 13, contracts with the Court will have to be unwound in spring 2027, and OFAC can amend or revoke any licence at any time. The State Department says the licences give States Parties time to show progress on US concerns. The deadline is leverage over the Court and over the States that fund it.

The Court had prepared, at least in part. According to William Schabas, it has moved part of its US software to European providers and ended its relationship with the insurer AXA, which operates in the United States.

Where European Operators Stand

Neither the United Nations nor the European Union has adopted any measure against the Court. In French law, the asset-freezing obligations in Articles L. 562-1 et seq. of the Monetary and Financial Code apply only to national, EU and UN measures, and the position is the same across Member States. The US designation creates, by itself, no obligation for an institution established in Europe.

Exposure arises first from a US nexus: dollar clearing, US persons among staff or in the decision chain, a US parent or branch, or US technology providers. A European bank that initiates a dollar payment cleared in the United States may be charged with causing a US person to violate the prohibitions, conduct that IEEPA and the order expressly cover. For those flows, every payment released will have to be traced to a licence and its conditions as they stood on the day of the transaction.

Flows with no US nexus fall outside the prohibitions but not outside the designation power. Under section 1(a)(ii)(B) of EO 14203, the Secretary of State may designate any foreign person who has provided financial, material or technological support, or goods or services, to a blocked person. The Court is now one. The bank holding its euro accounts, the insurer covering its staff and the provider hosting its data all fall within the terms of the provision. Section 1(a)(ii)(C), which targets anyone acting on behalf of a blocked person, reaches in law every member of the Court’s staff.

Secondary designation is discretionary and may come without notice. The 9 October licences lift the prohibitions binding US persons; they say nothing on whether a non-US operator acting within their scope is safe from designation, and no FAQ addressing the point accompanied the action. Once General License 13 expires, support for the Court’s ordinary functioning will lose even that indirect cover.

What European States Parties Already Owe the Court

Under Article 48(1) of the Rome Statute, the Court enjoys in the territory of each State Party the privileges and immunities necessary for the fulfilment of its purposes. The Agreement on the Privileges and Immunities of the Court gives that principle financial content. Article 6(3) exempts the Court’s property, funds and assets, to the extent necessary for its functions, from restrictions, regulations, controls or moratoria of any nature. Article 10 frees the Court from financial controls and moratoriums, and allows it to hold accounts in any currency and to transfer its funds freely.

These obligations bind the States that ratified the Agreement, not banks. A State Party commits no breach when a private bank closes the Court’s euro account on its own initiative. But the Agreement protects a result: the Court’s ability to hold and move funds in the territory of each State Party. When that ability is withdrawn under foreign coercion, a State that holds legal instruments to prevent it and declines to use them accepts an outcome the Agreement was drafted to exclude.

Under Articles 115 and 117 of the Statute, the Court is funded mainly by assessed contributions from States Parties. A payment from a European treasury to the Court’s euro account at a European bank requires no US nexus and no licence. It nonetheless exposes the receiving bank to the secondary designation power described above. Funding the Court therefore requires protecting the bank that receives the contributions.

The EU Instruments Left Unused

EU law already constrains spontaneous alignment with US lists. In Jenec (C-81/24, 11 June 2026), the Court of Justice held, on a reference from a Slovenian court, that listing by OFAC does not in itself justify refusing a consumer a basic payment account under Directive 2014/92: it is one factor in an individualised and documented assessment of money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk. The ruling is confined to consumers and basic accounts, but its reasoning travels: a foreign administrative listing does not replace the assessment that EU law requires.

Over-compliance is already documented. Testifying before a French parliamentary inquiry on 8 April 2026, Judge Guillou described insurers established in France that had stopped reimbursing medical care delivered in Europe, with no dollar and no US party involved. Extended to the institution, the same precaution can reach every one of its providers.

The Blocking Statute (Regulation 2271/96) has never been extended to the ICC sanctions. Doing so requires no new legislation: the Commission amends the annex by delegated act, as it did for the Iran sanctions with Delegated Regulation 2018/1100, adopted on 6 June 2018 and in force on 7 August. Once EO 14203 is listed, Article 5 prohibits EU operators from complying with it, unless authorised by the Commission, and Article 6 allows recovery of damages caused by its application.

The Court of Justice has given that prohibition practical effect. In Bank Melli Iran (C-124/20, 21 December 2021), the Grand Chamber held that Article 5 applies even in the absence of any order from US authorities. An operator may terminate a contract without giving reasons, but where the evidence suggests it did so to comply with a listed law, it bears the burden of proving otherwise. A bank that closed the Court’s account after an extension of the annex would have to justify that decision before a European court, which would weigh its exposure to US penalties under the principle of proportionality. The Blocking Statute cannot remove American leverage; it ends the assumption that complying with US sanctions is a legally risk-free choice.

Governments and parliamentarians have begun to point to the Blocking Statute. On 9 October, the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs condemned the designation and said France would use the Blocking Statute if necessary. In September, the Netherlands, as host State, asked the Commission to prepare it, while describing it as a last resort. On 9 October, Belgium’s Foreign Minister, Maxime Prévot, also called for its activation. On 13 October, 58 Members of the European Parliament, from the EPP, S&D, Renew Europe and the Greens/EFA, wrote to Ursula von der Leyen asking the Commission to activate it. On 22 October, the European Parliament awarded the Court its 2026 Sakharov Prize, and Ursula von der Leyen welcomed the award, saying that the Court “must be free to pursue its mission, independently, and without pressure or intimidation.” The Blocking Statute’s reach would be partial: designed to protect European operators, it would cover the Court’s providers and staff, not the international organisation itself.

The Anti-Coercion Instrument (Regulation 2023/2675) has not been triggered either, despite repeated calls, including a resolution of the French Conseil national des barreaux in April 2026. It would require the Council to find coercion by qualified majority before any response measure. Both instruments address the operators who are, in practice, the Court’s point of failure.

Until 7 April 2027, the Court will run on fallback providers and on a licence that OFAC may amend or revoke at any time, while its Trust Fund for Victims is already concerned about the payment of reparations. All twenty-seven Member States are parties to the Rome Statute and the Court sits on Union territory. The Union holds two instruments built against extraterritorial measures and has not turned either against these sanctions. If it does not do so, the compliance departments of banks, insurers and software vendors will settle the conflict one institution at a time, and they will settle it in favour of US law, as Judge Guillou’s insurers already have. A delegated act extending the Blocking Statute can and should be adopted and in force before the licence expires.

item.title: Race, Empire, and the Liberal International Order
item.dc:creator: Oumar Ba
item.category: Reflexive Globalisation and the Law: Expanding and Deepening its Understanding
item.description:
The complex set of international laws, rules, norms, and institutions that have shaped global governance since the end of World War II is now subject to an unprecedented set of challenges and reconfigurations. They all raise important questions about what the future may hold for this world order. Yet these debates miss a fundamental aspect about the foundations and predicates of the LIO.

item.content:encoded:
The liberal international order (LIO) is at a crossroads. The language of crisis is often evoked when discussing the current moment in International Relations (IR) scholarship.1) The complex set of international laws, rules, norms, and institutions that have shaped global governance since the end of World War II is now subject to an unprecedented set of challenges and reconfigurations. A belligerent and aggressive Russia, a more assertive China deploying both its hard and soft power, the Trump administration expanding its military attacks, straining the transatlantic partnership, and vowing to dismantle the International Criminal Court, all raise important questions about what the future may hold for this world order. Yet these debates miss a fundamental aspect about the foundations and predicates of the LIO.

Against Humanity

The RefLex fellowship provided me with time, space, resources, and intellectual community to revise my book manuscript titled Against Humanity: Race, Empire, and the Liberal International Order. Framed as a critique, it argues that the aftermath of World War II provided a set of institutional and normative frameworks that deployed liberal internationalism through the denial of humanity and a layered racial hierarchy upon which liberal imperial peace and international law were premised. Drawing insights from critical IR, postcolonial theory, and Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL), I develop these arguments via three main regimes of global governance which are all foundational to the postwar global order: human rights; (nuclear) security; and the crime of aggression in international law. My study focuses primarily on the drafting and adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), the United Nations (UN) Trusteeship Council’s governance of nuclear security, and the Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal’s adjudication of the crime of aggression.

I show how these foundational sites of the postwar order tell a broader story of racialised hierarchies of humanity. For instance, the adoption of the UDHR in Paris in 1948 was concomitant to the French campaign of “pacification” of Madagascar, which was the most brutal of French colonial wars at the time. The administration of the Marshall Islands by the United States under the supervision of the UN Trusteeship Council from 1947 until the 1980s was also a site of legislation of – and contestation to – nuclear imperialism in the Pacific, as colonial powers sought to provide a legal framework for a continued bombing of the Marshall Islands in pursuit of American nuclear supremacy. Finally, I trace a genealogy of the prosecution of crimes against peace at the Tokyo Tribunal convened between 1946 and 1948 and the enduring question of the crime of aggression that is still a sticking point in contemporary international law.

The book offers tools for approaching the study of international politics in a different light. It proposes different vantage points from which to bring together key moments of the postwar international order that had been otherwise kept discrete. The book uses a contrapuntal analysis framework, to read critically and from different perspectives, how texts, events, and places interacted in the postwar era. It brings to the fore the silences and erasures of crimes against and negation of humanity in the construction of the LIO. It offers also a new account of the history of the present by narrating a different genealogy of key moments, events, and places at the founding of the LIO.

Liberal Imperial Peace and Denial of Humanity

The forging of the post-World War II order is widely held as having ushered in a rules-based governance of global politics, which is said to be a culmination of a couple of centuries of liberalism built upon enlightenment, humanism, and the rule of law.2) Yet, humanity, as defined and proclaimed in the LIO, was not all-encompassing or universal. The humanity that was rooted in Enlightenment was primarily delimited along racial and imperial lines. Operating against the backdrop of colonialism, this humanity was at its core a denial of humanity. The LIO’s constitutive “other” is the racialised colonial subject,3) which has been deemed uncivilised and barbarian.4)

The order thus delineates the lesser or unhuman who are unworthy of protection within the framework of human rights, or by the laws of war, or from crimes against humanity.

The book shows that imperialism is constitutive of the LIO, which continues to operate through civilisational and racial logics of uplift, developmentalism, modernisation, and security. I propose the concept of liberal imperial peace, which I contend, better captures the system upon which liberal internationalism is projected.5) Liberal imperialism is thus the imprimatur of the LIO.

Empirically, the book reinscribes liberal imperial violence, and especially pacification, nuclear testing, and the crime of aggression in the liberal international project. Pacification aims to restore and impose liberal imperial peace. I use a contrapuntal reading of the pacification of Madagascar amidst the codification of the UDHR in 1948. In the postwar era as well, UN trusteeship governance, built upon the concept of standard of civilisation, provided a venue through which US nuclear tests blasted the humanity of the Marshallese. I argue that the Pacific Islanders were deemed disposable and dispensable through the two racial logics of arithmetic and geography. In the wake of the horrors of World War II, the codification of crimes against peace at the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals shows the mechanisms through which another core concept of the LIO reposed not on outlawing war but on criminalising a specific threat to the liberal imperial peace. Crimes against (liberal imperial) peace became later redefined as the crime of aggression.

The contrapuntal analysis framework – developed by Edward Said6)– allows to read critically and from different vantage points, how texts, events, and places interact. It highlights the sites of contention and construction of regimes of global governance, the boundaries around and hierarchies of humanity, but also how Global South actors deployed counter-discourses and alternatives to Western hegemony.7) Challenging the imbrication of the IR discipline with the racial and imperial logics of the LIO calls for a different methodological approach. This method – a critique – is openly and admittedly less anxious about the need to demarcate the observer from the observed.8) It acknowledges instead the researcher’s positionality as a social being from a specific socio-political background or inclination, with a singular intellectual and academic trajectory.9) This approach is also more attuned to historical approaches and genealogical contestation.

The critique that the book offers is ,however, not simply an evaluation of the LIO as a concept. The aim is also to understand its foundations, peeling the layers of their formation, and excavating and contesting the meanings and predicates of liberal internationalism. Doing so, I also engage the contemporaneous possibilities and alternatives to the prevailing accounts of the adoption of UDHR, of the global governance of nuclear testing, and of the concept of aggression in the aftermath of World War II. This approach turns the hegemonic and familiar into questions. It displaces meanings and allows us to reconsider the process by which hegemonic systems of truth materialised and delegitimised other ways of knowing.10) Ultimately, this critique is an exercise in problematising, interrogating, disrupting, unsettling, and denaturalising prevailing accounts of liberal internationalism. It is to (re)examine the subject of inquiry – the LIO – and expose its racial and imperial underpinnings.

As such, the book is a form of IR scholarship that “think[s] globally and politically.”11) It fuses together the ethical, epistemological, intellectual, and political. It reconstructs historical time not as linear, but rather multidimensional, multidirectional, and multi-sited. The overlapping temporalities and conceptual frames unsettle and disrupt conventional and stabilised narratives of the origins and deployment of the LIO.

The Liberal Imperial Logics of the Crime of Aggression

Aligned with the thematic areas and orientations of the RefLex community, the book shows that in the postwar order, the denial of humanity operated at the Tokyo Tribunal through exceptionalising Japan’s conduct regarding the crime of aggression, despite the broader colonial and imperial context in the Asia Pacific region. I provide an in-depth analysis of the monumental dissenting opinion by the Indian Judge Radhabinod Pal, which sought to acquit all the Japanese defendants of all the charges. Judge Pal’s dissent shows that imperialism still governed the world order and the system in which the victors of World War II sought to address the question of violence and breaches of international law. Pal’s critique dents the triumphant progress towards the development of a normative framework for international relations at the foundations of the LIO. Recasting the 1928 Kellogg-Briand Pact as a pact for imperial peace, I show that Pal’s work (at the Tokyo Tribunal and later at the UN International Law Commission) highlights the fissures within the liberal internationalist narratives, pointing out colonialism and imperialism as cornerstones of that world order.

More recently, wars of aggression have become once again a focal point in international affairs, while legal cases are pending before the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice, and the Council of Europe’s newly created Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine. I also show how Gaza and Ukraine speak to international law and international relations in ways that are reminiscent of the legal debates that animated the immediate post-World War II period. And here is perhaps why Judge Pal’s dissenting judgment, more than six decades later, can still help us make sense of our current moment.

item.title: The Purcell Principle
item.dc:creator: Kash Radocha
item.description:
There exists a doctrine in twenty-first-century Supreme Court decision-making called ‘the Purcell principle.’ The term refers to the concept that generally guides federal courts to leave in place the status quo of election processes when election day is near. Purcell’s intention is to prevent confusion among voters, but the principle has become an encompassing excuse for the justices to modify election conduct.

item.content:encoded:
As far-right candidates in Hungary, Brazil, and Serbia met their electoral demise in 2026, the world is seemingly holding its breath as the United States barrels towards its own trajectory-defining nationwide elections. The 2026 U.S. midterm elections see all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the nation’s 100 Senators on the ballot, meaning the composition and majority control of both chambers of U.S. Congress hangs in the balance of November 3rd’s results. Races across the country have been both contentious and contested, with Trump taking a heavy-handed approach in attempting to disrupt election processes and polls reporting swings in the likelihood of party-control over districts and states alike. Simply put, Trump and the Republicans are projected to lose their majority in the House – and perhaps even the Senate – and have initiated legal battles across the country with the potential to disenfranchise thousands if not millions of voters. The U.S. Supreme Court has responded in mystifying manners.

There exists a doctrine in twenty-first-century Supreme Court decision-making called ‘the Purcell principle.’ Coined in 2016 by UCLA Law Professor Richard Hasen and named after the case it emerged from, Purcell v. Gonzalez (2006), the term refers to the concept that generally guides federal courts to leave in place the status quo of election processes when election day is near. Purcell’s intention is to prevent confusion among voters, but the principle has become an encompassing excuse for the justices to modify election conduct. Its core flaws are thus twofold: the Purcell principle itself is derived from a non-argued and non-binding case, and there is no actual outline as to how close an election must be for the principle to apply. The Court therefore has no procedural reason to abide by Purcell or provide explanation for its decisions beyond a simple invocation of Purcell, leaving lower courts guessing and usually at odds with the Court as to when it should guide their decision-making. With Trump’s constant and calculated attacks on long-standing election processes on the eve of the midterms, Purcell has returned as a dubious factor in many of the federal judiciary’s recent (and in some cases, surprising) decisions, many of which are still being handed down with days to go until the election.

Purcell’s Place in American Jurisprudence

Purcell v. Gonzalez (2006) seems prima facie a landmark merit decision – that is, a case the Supreme Court scheduled oral arguments for, solicited amici curiae (“friends of the court”) briefs for, and handed down with clearly articulated and precedent-setting majority, concurring, and/or dissenting opinions based on the case’s merits. After all, one might assume its significance may be equated to a merit decision such as Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) or Citizens United v. FEC (2010) for its sharp increase in citations by federal courts since 2016 to base precedent-setting judicial review upon.

Reality could not be further from this conclusion. Purcell is instead a case that existed on the Court’s emergency docket – also termed the ‘interim docket’ or colloquially known as the ‘shadow docket.’ The core difference between the Court’s merit and emergency dockets is that unlike merit appeals, emergency appeals are typically brought to a single justice and usually referred to the other justices (rather than voted upon for acceptance), not scheduled for argument, decided rapidly, not usually given any opinion, and do not set Supreme Court precedent. Emergency decisions do hold the same weight of law in that they settle disputes on a national level until further briefing may be held in federal court, but they are not intended to guide future decision-making in the manner merit decisions are.

The controversy at the center of the 2006 decision surrounded a voter-approved 2004 proposition in Arizona prescribing voter IDs as necessary for a ballot to be counted. In early 2006, a midterm election year, a group of Arizona voters sued to block its implementation; after the federal district court kept in place the proposition, they appealed and the circuit court overturned the lower court’s decision and blocked Arizona from implementing the voter ID proposition. When on emergency appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court (the contestation was the circuit court’s order itself, not the merits of the proposition, as by this point there were only days until the November elections), the Court ruled against the circuit court to put back in place the proposition, basing its reasoning on the timeliness of the election and how a revocation of the (then two-year-old) proposition would confuse voters.

All of this occurred on the Court’s emergency docket, but in recent years all levels of federal courts have increasingly referred to that decision when considering whether to stay state election conduct disputes on their own emergency dockets. In essence, every application of Purcell has varied – whether it is in regard to the time or the substantive issue – making it a deeply flawed notion and something seemingly decided on a whim based on jurisdiction or, controversially, ideology. It is meant to constrain federal judges in deciding state electoral matters, but even state courts have taken a separate approach in applying Purcell (if at all). This is key to why it is a principle and not a clause. As UC Law SF Professor Rory Little has argued on principles, “principles are not groundless or invalid. Instead, their application simply needs more clear explanation and definition.” So, it should unsettle the reader who expresses concern for the state of democracy that such an inconsistent idea has made its way into the forefront of deciding whether or not consequential election modifications may take effect.

2026 Election Disputes and Purcell’s Place Now (If At All)

At the time of writing this, there are 371 active federal cases litigating against the Trump administration’s efforts made in the name of national security. At least 24 have directly concerned election law, with half having been filed since August 20th. The issue at hand is not that plaintiffs have been slow to act against executive orders, but rather that the Trump administration accelerated its concerted crusade within these past few months before the general election. The other half of these efforts, however, have already impacted voters for their distance from November. This temporality has seemingly split how the Supreme Court has utilized Purcell for these election disputes.

Take Louisiana v. Callais (2026). Decided April 29, Callais all but gutted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, in essence finding that the requirement of a second majority-minority district constituted a violation of the Equal Protection Clause. This triggered an immediate effort among many Republican-controlled states to redraw their congressional districts and dilute the minority vote to flip a seat from Democrat to Republican. Based on previous applications of Purcell, such as in Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee (2020) or Democratic National Committee v. Wisconsin State Legislature (2020), this ruling should have been considered too close to the election to modify existing congressional districts. In fact, Louisiana even delayed its primary to gerrymander its maps in line with Callais’s logic. If changing the date of an election is not indicative of a court ruling coming too close to said election, I am not sure what more could be.

Mail-in voting has also come under attack, as Trump had attempted to modify how mail-in ballots are postmarked and collected with a March executive order – this was finally implemented with an August 21 administrative rule from the United States Postal Service. On appeal for allowing the rule to take effect after a lower court blocked the rule, the Supreme Court ruled against the Trump administration to block the rule, citing the belief that the government is unlikely to succeed on the merits. But the more curious aspect underpinning this decision is the implicit diversion from Purcell. Justice Kavanaugh offered the only detailed (albeit three-sentence) opinion, framing the issue as related to the Administrative Procedure Act. Where Purcell is inconsistent in this case rests with the lower court preventing the August 21 rule from taking effect. By Purcell’s logic (or, at least what we are able to reasonably infer), this federal court injunction is too close to the November general election and should have been vacated by the Supreme Court. But that’s exactly what the Supreme Court did not do.

On the other hand, there has indeed been some seeming congruence on Purcell. A “procedurally bananas” dispute, as Georgetown Law Professor Stephen Vladeck put it, has emerged in Missouri, in which the state has appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court three times as the justices ruled twice against Missouri’s attempt to implement a gerrymandered 2025 map (Vladeck’s blog gets into the specifics about the procedural ineptitude’s evident here). While not explicitly stated, all of the justices (for lack of any public dissent) seem united in applying Purcell as voters in Missouri have already begun voting using the existing 2022 map.

Another late dispute in line with Purcell emerged with the Supreme Court’s October 23 ruling allowing New Hampshire to proceed with disallowing student IDs as a valid form of voter ID. The law amending New Hampshire’s valid voter ID methods passed in April, to which the district court ruled that, while the law may proceed, with supporting evidence student IDs may be considered. The Supreme Court, citing Purcell, struck down the district court ruling again on the basis of potential voter confusion too close to the election as a result of federal court action. But, compared to the mail-in ballot case, the timeline makes little sense, as its question has been germane far longer, and in both instances federal courts blocked a rule from taking effect.

This is all to say that there is a mystifying legal principle circulating among the federal judiciary’s election disputes, and we have seen a sharp increase in how subjective its application is in recent months, weeks, and even days. Perhaps in the fallout of the midterms we will see the Supreme Court finally decide a case on the merits with regard to Purcell and finally obtain a clear, multi-pronged test for deciding whether an action occurs too closely to an election and its potential for confusing voters. Until then, we Court observers will remain the ones confused.

item.content:encoded:
This post shows how Global South representatives at the United Nations (UN) sought to redefine the concept of international crimes by arguing for the inclusion of colonialism and neo-colonial practices as a crime against peace and security. More specifically, the earlier debates on the criminalisation of colonialism expose the uneven distribution of power and voice in the field and help explain the contemporary reflexive contestation of its vocabulary and punishment mechanisms by Southern actors. Within this framework, reflexive moments form part of a recurring cycle, where Northern legal norms are critically received and re-negotiated by the South, re-injected into the international legal order, and finally re-appropriated by the North in a way that dilutes their transformative potential.

The First Reflexive Moment: After the Second World War

The first major reflexive moment in the post-war development of international criminal law emerged with the drafting of the 1948 Genocide Convention. Global South delegates supported Raphael Lemkin’s proposal for the inclusion of “cultural genocide”, which they saw as an anti-colonial imperative aimed at protecting minority groups from imperial coercion. However, this initiative met fierce resistance from Western colonial powers. In the UN General Assembly’s Sixth (Legal) Committee, they succeeded in deleting the draft article on cultural genocide.1)

The International Law Commission’s (ILC) subsequent work on a “Code of Offences against the Peace and Security of Mankind” offered a better space for contestation. The 1954 Draft Code recognised an additional offence alongside the three Nuremberg-crimes and genocide. It addressed coercive interference in the internal or external affairs of another state through political or economic measures designed to impose the will of the intervening state in order to obtain advantages.2) The offence was proposed by the Cuban ILC member Francisco García-Amador, following proposals for the criminalisation of “economic aggression” submitted by socialist governments. He argued that such a provision expressed a consolidated legal conviction among twenty-one American states that represented then one third of UN members, given that the 1948 Charter of the Organisation of American States already prohibited such acts.3)

This innovation generated intense controversy both within the ILC Commission itself and the Sixth Committee. The proponents’ arguments shared a common foundation, namely that peace and security, as reflected in the purposes of the UN, could be imperilled not only by armed action but also by coercive economic measures that threatened the political independence or sovereign equality of states. Within the General Assembly, opposition came mainly from the representatives of the United Kingdom and the United States who considered the proposal inconsistent with the text of the UN Charter and dangerous for the system of collective security.4)

Two prominent ILC members, Hersch Lauterpacht, and the Special Rapporteur on Aggression, Jean Spiropoulos, objected that although political and economic pressure were morally questionable, criminalising them would drain the concept of crime of its meaning. In response, the former judge of the Tokyo Military Tribunal, Radhabinod Pal, reminded them that in criminal law extortion was also a punishable offence.5) Despite the objections, García-Amador’s proposal was adopted by majority vote, and enshrined in Article 2, paragraph 9 of the 1954 Draft Code.

The 1954 Draft Code, though ultimately cautious, captured the dynamic of the first reflexive moment. It registered an early attempt to translate experiences of non-military forms of domination into the accepted legal categories of the time. By appropriating the Nuremberg and Tokyo Tribunals’ language, states and jurists from Eastern Europe and Latin America sought to reframe externally imposed dependency by means of sustained political and economic pressure as practices analogous to those punished in the landmark post-war prosecutions. In doing so, they exposed the limits of the early post-war vocabulary of international criminal law, while simultaneously demonstrating how that vocabulary could be strategically redeployed to contest hegemonism. The Draft Code thus foreshadowed later debates on neo-colonialism and economic domination that international law would only gradually begin to confront.

Nevertheless, the usual suspects of economic coercion found a way to circumvent the implications of an international criminal system that did not suit their interests. To be sure, García-Amador’s amendment to the Nuremberg Principles was just an additional ground for them to pause the international criminal justice project before it got out of hand. Invoking a lack of consensus regarding the content of the crime of aggression, the General Assembly shelved the Draft Code until the successful liberation struggles of the colonised peoples gave rise to a second reflexive moment.

The Second Reflexive Moment: After Decolonisation

The transformation of the international system through decolonisation fundamentally reshaped the institutional landscape. Within a few years, the UN General Assembly expanded dramatically as dozens of newly independent states entered the organisation, bringing with them political experiences and legal priorities markedly different from those of the post-war founding members. A newly formed majority of formerly colonised countries succeeded in passing several anti-colonial resolutions and bringing back to the UN agenda the Code of Offences against the Peace and Security of Mankind. United by their past as much as by their principal geographical location, states from the Global South insisted that any modern codification of international crimes could no longer rest exclusively on the Nuremberg Principles. Instead, it had to confront and dismantle the legacies of colonialism. The Eastern European and other socialist states aligned with the demands of the Global South.6)

These broader dynamics reverberated directly in the debates of the General Assembly’s Sixth Committee in the mid-1970s, where numerous delegations argued that the Draft Code must expressly reflect recent international instruments, such as the General Assembly’s Resolution 1514 (XV) of 1960, that condemned colonial rule and affirmed the right of peoples to self-determination.7) Several States from the Global South emphasised the need to criminalise not only classical, territorial forms of domination but also neo-colonial practices, such as the exploitation of natural resources. A smaller group advocated the recognition of “economic aggression” as a specific offence.8)

When the ILC finally returned to the Draft Code in the 1980s, these themes became central to the work of the Senegalese Special Rapporteur, Doudou Thiam. In his second report (1984), Thiam observed that the condemnation of colonialism had long acquired the quality of ius cogens. He underscored that the subjection of peoples to alien domination constituted a denial of fundamental rights and an impediment to international peace and security. However, he believed that “economic aggression” belonged more to political discourse than to the “austere language of law”, and that its conceptual boundaries remained too indeterminate for codification.9)

The subsequent discussions in the ILC exposed a profound cleavage on the penal status of colonialism and economic aggression. On one side, a broad coalition of Global South members asserted that colonialism was already per se criminal under peremptory norms of international law, the UN Charter, and the core decolonisation instruments. They stressed that it was not a historical artefact but an ongoing structure of domination, persisting through military occupation, denial of self-determination, and neo-colonial economic control. For these members, colonialism was both morally abhorrent and a threat to peace and security, having systematically produced wars of national liberation and international crises. In addition, its criminalisation alongside economic aggression was indispensable for restoring the sovereign equality of states and completing the unfinished project of decolonisation.10)

By contrast, ILC members from powerful western states such as Ian Sinclair from the United Kingdom and the US-American Stephen McCaffrey argued that the terms “colonialism” and “economic aggression” were political labels and popular slogans that lacked legal precision required for international criminalisation. Critics also considered colonialism an obsolete phenomenon. On the other hand, Christian Tomuschat from Germany commented that, although traditional colonialism would become extinct once Namibia had gained its independence, the persistence of situations of alien domination and exploitation warranted an appropriate provision in the Code.11)

These opposing positions persisted in the UN debates the following years. Already since his third report (1985), Thiam had evidently realised that he was part of a reflexive process. He felt that “[t]his would seem to be a good time to reflect on the vocabulary of international law”.12) In 1989, the ILC was finally able to adopt a provisional article on “colonial domination and other forms of alien domination”, which was reiterated in the text of the draft articles provisionally adopted by the commission on first reading in 1991. Article 18 criminalised the establishment or maintenance by force of “colonial domination or any other form of alien domination contrary to the right of peoples to self-determination as enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations”. The Draft Code also contained some other offences of special interest to States that had experienced colonialism, such as “apartheid”, the “recruitment, use, financing and training of mercenaries”, as well as “wilful and severe damage to the environment”.13)

The establishment of the ad hoc tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda in the early 1990s, with their narrow jurisdictions, dealt a significant blow to the Draft Code’s progressive aspirations. In fact, their creation provided the Global North with the perfect opportunity to re-appropriate the entire international criminal justice project. Soon thereafter, the ILC began capitulating to the political pressures of a newly formed Ad hoc Committee on the Establishment of an International Criminal Court (ICC), staffed by state representatives. Given that the Draft Code’s main purpose was to serve as the subject-matter jurisdiction of the future Court, Thiam had to discard colonialism, foreign intervention, apartheid, mercenary activities, and severe environmental destruction. The rapporteur did not hide that this drastic reduction was due to political factors, essentially noting the strong pushback from Northern States, while reprimanding the Third World for its silence.14)

Very few, like Mexican Alberto Székely, who talked of a “mutilation”, raised a serious objection in the ILC or the Sixth Committee. The argument of the symbolic and deterrent value of colonialism’s recognition as crime against peace and security was also not enough.15) In 1996, the Draft Code of Crimes against the Peace and Security of Mankind passed its second reading with a list of offences that essentially replicated the jurisdiction of Nuremberg and the ad hoc tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, with the addition of “crimes against UN and associated personnel”, at the request of the United States.16) Two years later, the ICC Statute retained a minimal subject-matter jurisdiction for the Court. It is striking that during the Rome Conference only the observer Organisation of African Unity made a brief generic reference to colonialism.17)

The Third Reflexive Moment: Today

In this author’s opinion, the contemporary contestation of the ICC’s legitimacy, especially by African states and scholars of the Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL) movement, is intrinsically linked to the fundamental failure of the Rome Statute to address colonial wrongs. The Court’s disproportionate prosecutorial bias that has led to its condemnation as a neo-colonial instrument is very probably a symptom of a deeper structural deficit. By codifying international criminality almost exclusively around warlike atrocities, while omitting the systemic violence of colonial and neo-colonial practices, the Rome Statute’s substantive architecture practically directs the prosecutorial focus towards Africa. Even in the recent high-profile contexts like Ukraine and Palestine, the ICC does not have the tools to address systemic violence.

This deficit in the Court’s subject-matter jurisdiction seems to have been acknowledged by the drafters of the 2014 Malabo Protocol of the African Union, which provides for an African criminal court. Although colonialism per se does not appear as a stand-alone crime (an omission that itself warrants further inquiry), the Protocol codifies corporate criminal liability and offences targeting manifestations of neo-colonialism, such as the illicit exploitation of natural resources, the trafficking in hazardous wastes, and mercenarism.18) As the case study of the three reflexive moments of colonialism as a crime against peace and security reveals, the contemporary friction demonstrates that international criminal justice has arrived once again at the beginning of a recurring historical cycle.
