item.title: Whose Coup?
item.dc:creator: Kim Lane Scheppele
item.description:
The temporary suspension on 30 October 2026 of the two judges who had usurped the leadership of Poland’s unlawfully composed Constitutional Tribunal produced startling images of a police cordon around the court and a chaotic confrontation with the president of the Republic. Radical-right political movements in Poland and abroad quickly portrayed the intervention as a coup d’état. Legally, however, the intervention marked an important – and necessary - step towards restoring the rule of law.

The post Whose Coup? appeared first on Verfassungsblog.
item.content:encoded:
The temporary suspension on 30 October 2026 of the two judges who had usurped the leadership of Poland’s unlawfully composed Constitutional Tribunal produced startling images of a police cordon around the court and a chaotic confrontation with the president of the Republic. Radical-right political movements in Poland and abroad quickly portrayed the intervention as a coup d’état. Legally, however, the intervention marked an important – and necessary – step towards restoring the rule of law.

For more than a decade, since the radical-right Law and Justice party – known by its Polish acronym PiS – began capturing the Tribunal in manifest and repeated breaches of Polish and European law, we have defended a simple proposition: European rule-of-law standards require Poland to respect the Tribunal’s independence and to constitute and operate it in accordance with the Polish Constitution. That principle remains our starting point. The events of last Friday should be assessed against that constitutional standard. Doing so requires specifying the new leadership’s legal authority, assessing the limited measures they adopted and explaining the political confrontation that followed.

How the Tribunal was captured

Understanding this conflict requires going back to 2015, when PiS won both the national presidential election and majorities in both houses of parliament. Before the parliamentary handover, the outgoing liberal majority elected five judges to the Tribunal. Three of those judges were elected lawfully. The other two improperly anticipated vacancies that belonged to the incoming parliament – a distinction the Tribunal itself confirmed in its judgment of 3 December 2015, which upheld the statutory basis for the first three elections and found the basis for the other two unconstitutional.

Article 194 of the Constitution assigns the election of the Tribunal’s judges exclusively to the Sejm, parliament’s main chamber. This contrasts with the appointment of judges to other courts, which the national president makes on the nomination of the National Council of the Judiciary. Ordinary legislation nevertheless requires elected Tribunal judges to take an oath before the president, but receiving that oath cannot confer an additional appointment (or veto) power on the president that the Constitution deliberately withholds.

Nevertheless, then-President Andrzej Duda, closely aligned with PiS, refused in 2015 to receive the oaths of the three lawfully elected judges. The incoming PiS majority then elected replacements to seats that were already occupied. These unlawfully seated individuals became known in Poland as “duplicate judges”. In its 2021 judgment in Xero Flor v Poland, the European Court of Human Rights held that the participation of any one of these usurpers in any case violates the right of the parties to a tribunal established by law. In M.L. v Poland, decided on 14 December 2023, the ECtHR held that participation was “by itself capable of vitiating the legal force” to be attached to any “judgment” issued by the Tribunal with their participation. In November 2022, Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court held that the unconstitutionally composed Tribunal had been “infected with illegality” to become a body that had “lost, in a material sense, its ability to adjudicate in accordance with the law”.

Two of the original three unlawful appointees died in 2017. PiS irregularly replaced them with further appointees whose seating was likewise unlawful: the deaths of people occupying seats without legal entitlement did not create vacancies in seats belonging to the judges elected in October 2015.

PiS nevertheless treated the replacements as entitled to fresh nine-year terms, prolonging the consequences of the original violations. The surviving original duplicate judge left the Tribunal in December 2024. One replacement’s purported term ended on 18 September 2026; the other’s is scheduled to end on 30 January 2027.

The influence of the original and unconstitutional duplicate judges not only extended beyond the panels on which they sat: they participated in choosing the Tribunal’s leadership. Under the Constitution, the national president appoints the Tribunal’s president and vice-president from candidates presented by the General Assembly (that is, plenary meeting) of all its judges. The duplicate judges voted on those candidates.

On 18 December 2025, in Commission v Poland, the European Union’s Court of Justice held that the Tribunal ceased to constitute a lawful court on account of the serious irregularities vitiating the appointment of three of its “judges” in December 2015 and of its “president” in 2016. On the latter issue, the Court identified two defects: votes cast by unlawfully appointed participants could not supply the required support, and a candidate backed only by a minority could not be treated as the nominee of the General Assembly.

Parliament had meanwhile changed hands in late 2023. The new democratic coalition government subsequently withheld publication of the Tribunal’s “rulings” on the ground that its unlawful composition prevented it from performing its constitutional functions, a logical response to the Tribunal ceasing to be a court meeting the requirements of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.

The democratic coalition initially refrained from filling new vacancies on the Tribunal, arguing that doing so would legitimize the body masquerading as Poland’s constitutional court. But the expiry of existing terms, together with the early retirement of a PiS-appointed judge in December 2025, opened the prospect of filling a majority of the Tribunal’s seats during 2026. The Sejm elected six judges in March, a seventh in June and an eighth in September.

The president’s manufactured veto

The presidential election of June 2025 had ensured that restoring the Tribunal would remain politically difficult. After electing a democratic coalition parliamentary majority in 2023, Polish voters narrowly chose the PiS-backed Karol Nawrocki as president, preserving cohabitation between opposed political camps.

Nawrocki continued his predecessor’s unlawful practice of turning the receipt of a ceremonial oath into a substantive veto. Of the eight judges elected by the current Sejm, he received the oaths of only three. The other five refused to accept that presidential inaction could nullify their election. Four publicly read and signed their oaths on 9 April and delivered notarized copies addressed to the president to his office. The fifth followed the same route in October.

The Venice Commission expressly supported this procedure in its October 2026 opinion. Where the president unjustifiably refuses to receive the oath, it explained, the requirement can be fulfilled without his physical participation through a duly verified document formally submitted to him. The judge should then be able to assume judicial duties. (One may regret that this route was not taken in 2015. Had the three lawfully elected judges then been enabled to take their seats despite Duda’s refusal, much of the subsequent damage might have been prevented.)

In 2026, however, the five judges who took this route were still not admitted to the court. This violates, among other things, the interim measures ordered by the European Court of Human Rights in response to applications submitted by four of the five new judges when their admission to the Tribunal was refused. On 5 May, the Strasbourg Court required Poland to “ensure that its competent authorities refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties” by the newly elected judges until any further decision from the Court. Their continued exclusion defies that court order.

The key actor violating Polish and European law is Bogdan Święczkowski, a former National Prosecutor and deputy to PiS justice minister and prosecutor general Zbigniew Ziobro (now in the United States, having obtained a visa with assistance from senior Trump administration officials to escape charges including abuse of office and misappropriation of public funds). Święczkowski was elected to the Tribunal in 2022 and (irregularly) appointed its purported president in 2024, following a nomination process involving two second-generation duplicate judges. Most recently, Święczkowski’s obstruction has taken a physical form. Earlier in October, one of the newly elected judges reported that Święczkowski – a particularly imposing man – had pushed him out of a corridor and blocked his passage inside the Tribunal. He filed a criminal complaint concerning the incident.

The events of 30 October

One of the excluded judges became a focal actor in this drama. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska is an experienced judge, a former president of the Regional Court in Opole and a leader of Themis, a judicial association active in defending the rule of law.  Rules enacted under the PiS government itself make this background relevant.

The 2016 Act on the Organisation and Procedure of the Constitutional Tribunal identifies which judge should direct the institution when its presidency is vacant and designates the same judge as the substitute when the president cannot authorise the vice-president or another judge to exercise the relevant functions. Under that law, the judge who has the longest combined service on the Tribunal, as a judicial trainee, assessor or judge in the common courts, and in central state administration should preside.  Korwin-Piotrowska has the longest qualifying service across the Tribunal as a whole, including its PiS-era members, since she began her judicial traineeship in 1995.

Acting as the statutory substitute for the Tribunal’s president, she issued two orders temporarily interrupting the judicial duties of Święczkowski and his purported deputy Bartłomiej Sochański – both of whom were nominated in the same flawed procedure. Her orders concerned their duties as judges, including their exercise of the functions of president and vice-president. The stated grounds included the exclusion of lawfully elected judges, manipulation of adjudicating panels and obstruction of the General Assembly meeting needed to adopt the Tribunal’s proposed budget. The power to suspend her colleagues, she argued, comes from the law governing common courts, which the PiS-enacted legislation governing Tribunal judges incorporates through statutory cross-references. The rule permits immediate intervention where a judge’s conduct makes removal from duties necessary to protect the court’s standing or essential interests of the judicial service. The interruption is subject to mandatory review by a disciplinary court composed of Tribunal judges selected by lot. The immediate interruption can last no longer than one month; any further suspension requires a decision of that court.

Korwin-Piotrowska’s orders rested on this statutory framework. Separately, on the same day, the Prosecutor General submitted five applications for consent to criminal prosecution: four concerning Święczkowski and one concerning Sochański. Criminal prosecution requires the consent of the Tribunal’s General Assembly – and that is what was sought with these applications. The applications did not themselves suspend either judge. Korwin-Piotrowska expressly stated that she had not reviewed them when issuing her orders, which rested on other grounds. Disciplinary proceedings are separate and do not require the lifting of criminal immunity. Removal from judicial office is among the sanctions expressly authorized by the legislation governing Tribunal judges. Friday’s orders predetermined neither the criminal nor the disciplinary outcome.

It is important to distinguish Korwin-Piotrowska’s authority to direct the Tribunal from her orders temporarily interrupting Święczkowski’s and Sochański’s judicial duties. Our position is that neither man was lawfully appointed to his leadership office, because the assemblies nominating them included people who were not judges. On that view, the statutory vacancy rule already authorized Korwin-Piotrowska to exercise the president’s functions; no finding of specific misconduct was needed to establish that authority.

Other Polish lawyers, including Włodzimierz Wróbel, defend her intervention on a narrower basis, assuming that the two leadership appointments were lawful. They interpret the statutory substitution mechanism in light of the principle that no one may decide their own case. A court president cannot make temporary intervention in response to his own conduct dependent on his consent or his willingness to authorize someone else to act. Where the conduct of both the president and vice-president is at issue, the statutory substitute must be able to intervene. This argument establishes Korwin-Piotrowska’s authority to issue the orders even if one believes that the leadership positions were lawfully filled.

In practice, however, legal entitlement to direct the Tribunal was insufficient to end Święczkowski’s de facto control of the institution. As described above, his obstruction of the newly elected judges had already become physical, and the Tribunal’s own security staff had previously enforced his restrictions on their access. The suspension orders, subject to mandatory judicial review, provided a basis for excluding both judges from the building and preventing their continued obstruction. They were therefore a means of making lawful authority effective, rather than the source of Korwin-Piotrowska’s authority to act.

Law and the images

The suspension of the Tribunal’s leadership was a temporary measure taken under existing statutes and subject to eventual judicial review. The images told a much more dramatic story.

Korwin-Piotrowska requested police protection for judges and staff. The Prosecutor General also alerted the police to security risks. Officers secured the grounds and the surrounding street; the police expressly stated that they had not entered the Tribunal building. Nevertheless, their deployment after dark was readily portrayed as a nighttime seizure of the court.

The concern for safety was, however, well founded. Protesters and opposition politicians gathered outside. At Święczkowski’s request, a supporter used a power tool to break a gate lock, allowing him onto the grounds, where he confronted a police cordon.

The most dramatic confrontation came around 1 a.m. on Saturday. President Nawrocki had interrupted a foreign trip to return to Warsaw. Korwin-Piotrowska had agreed to receive him alone for talks. Instead, he arrived with companions, including the President of the Supreme Court, Zbigniew Kapiński—himself an illegal Supreme Court “judge” having been appointed to that court through PiS’s unlawfully reconstituted judicial council.

Footage showed Nawrocki, a former boxer with a history of football hooliganism, violently pushing past Korwin-Piotrowska at the entrance. Inside, he was filmed shouting at the newly elected judges. The head of Nawrocki’s chancellery dismissed Korwin-Piotrowska’s orders as ridiculous. One of the judges also reported that people identifying themselves as presidential staff tried to take possession of keys to the Tribunal’s rooms.

Threats of retaliation accompanied the confrontation. PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński raised the possible future application of the “Nuremberg principles”. Other right-wing figures alleged a coup and invoked the prospect of life imprisonment for the judges attempting the return to a lawful bench.

These tactics had an audience beyond the radical right. Prominent liberal legal commentators also questioned the intervention’s legality and warned that the scenes would destroy the Tribunal’s credibility. The Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, while recognising the new judges’ right to take office and rejecting a presidential veto over their election, questioned Korwin-Piotrowska’s authority to issue the orders. It presented a negotiated constitutional reset as the only solution. In our view, that position fails to give sufficient weight to the European judgments requiring the restoration of a lawfully constituted and independent Tribunal, something that would not be fulfilled by a political compromise.

Korwin-Piotrowska and her supporters may have made mistakes in communicating the legal basis for her actions which were not clear on Friday night. But the confrontation also shows where the modern New Right’s cult of force leads. In Poland, that cult has taken literal form: the country’s president and the Tribunal’s purported president have physically assaulted and overpowered judges who stand in their way. When liberal democrats call on the police for protection, as Korwin-Piotrowska did, the resulting images can then be used to portray lawful enforcement as authoritarianism. The more brazen the obstruction, the more suspect the restoration appears.

Law is one of humanity’s great achievements precisely because it denies overbearing men such as Nawrocki and Święczkowski the right to physically prevail over a diminutive woman such as Korwin-Piotrowska simply by overpowering her. The outcome must turn on the strength of the legal arguments, not the strength of the people advancing them.

When the rule of law is shattered by aspirational autocrats who capture the key institutions of state, restoring the independence of those institutions will not be easy. By refusing to relinquish power over the Constitutional Tribunal, Poland’s aspirationally autocratic PiS party has created an unlawful situation that requires decisive action to recover the rule of law. The case law of the Court of Justice and the Court of Human Rights establishes why that situation must be remedied.  Acting under Polish domestic law concerning lawful succession of the Constitutional Tribunal presidency and temporary interruption of judicial duties, Judge Korwin-Piotrowska has taken a lawful – even if poorly communicated – step, subject to judicial review, towards bringing the Constitutional Tribunal back toward compliance with the Polish Constitution and European law.

item.title: The Oath “Towards” the President and the Suspension of the Chief Justice
item.dc:creator: Jakub Jaraczewski

The escalation follows months of conflict in which Polish President Karol Nawrocki refused to receive the oath of the duly elected new judges, a largely ceremonial act that completes their election.

item.content:encoded:
On Friday, 30 October, amid protests and riots in front of the Constitutional Tribunal, a group of judges elected to it this year by the centrist parliamentary majority entered its premises. One of these judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, announced that the current leadership was incapable of acting properly. Invoking the rule that makes the judge with the longest judicial experience acting head of the Tribunal when its leader is incapacitated, she suspended the court’s president and vice-president for 30 days for obstructing its work. The escalation follows months of conflict in which Polish President Karol Nawrocki refused to receive the oath of the duly elected new judges, a largely ceremonial act that completes their election. Indeed, in October 2026 the Venice Commission stated unequivocally that the President cannot obstruct the Sejm’s election of judges by arbitrarily refusing to administer their oath. It added that if the President refuses to take part, the oath can be taken without his physical participation. None of this, however, has stopped President Nawrocki and the PiS-appointed President of the Constitutional Tribunal, Bogdan Święczkowski, from preventing the new judges from taking up their positions. This latest confrontation, which the opposition and its allies in the judiciary has called a coup d’état, marks a sharp escalation in the struggle between Nawrocki and Tusk’s government over how to reverse the judicial changes introduced under the former nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Ceremonial Oaths at the Heart of the Polish Rule of Law Crisis

The Sejm, the lower house of the Polish parliament, elects the judges of the Polish Constitutional Tribunal individually for nine-year terms. Election requires an absolute majority of votes with at least half of all MPs present. After the election, the newly appointed judges swear an oath, as the law on the Tribunal explicitly provides, “towards the President of Poland”. Semantics matter here, as much of the unfolding crisis rests on how “towards the President” (wobec Prezydenta) is interpreted and whether it is equivalent to swearing that oath in the President’s physical presence. This element of the appointment procedure has been controversial on at least two occasions.

After the 2023 parliamentary elections, the parliament initially hesitated to fill an increasing number of vacant seats at the Tribunal. The Sejm reversed this policy in March 2026 elected six new judges: Krystian Markiewicz, Dariusz Szostek, Magdalena Bentkowska, Marcin Dziurda, Maciej Taborowski and Anna Korwin-Piotrkowska. President Nawrocki administered the oath to two of these judges (Szostek and Bentkowska) but refused to do so for the other four. Subsequently, the Sejm elected two more judges, Sławomir Patyra (in June 2026) and Maciej Berek (in September 2026); President Nawrocki administered the oath to Patyra but not to Berek. The head of the Constitutional Tribunal, Bogdan Święczkowski, a judge elected by a PiS majority in 2022 and later in 2024 appointed to lead the court, followed the lead of President Nawrocki. To the three judges, whose oaths have been administered, he allowed to begin working at the Tribunal but refused their seats to the other five. Święczkowski claims that without the President of Poland administering the oath, such judges are not properly installed and may not begin participating in the Tribunal’s work.

This modus operandi is not entirely unheard of. In 2006, the then-President of Poland, Lech Kaczyński, publicly hesitated over Lidia Bagińska, a judge elected by Sejm. The controversy concerned her alleged lack of experience. However, at the end, he chose to hear her oath, famously stating that, despite his misgivings, the law left him with no choice.

In 2015, the outgoing Sejm appointed five judges “in advance”, three to seats that were to be made vacant during that Sejm’s term, and two for seats that would be vacated during the term of the next Sejm. President Duda refused to hear the oath from these judges, barring them from taking their seats. The next Sejm then appointed different judges, whose oaths have been administered by President Duda and who took up their seats. The ECtHR, in Xero Flor v. Poland, and the CJEU, in Case C-448/23 Commission v Poland, ultimately found three of these judges elected to “overwrite” the previous Sejm’s appointments as having been unlawfully appointed.

The Legal Nature of the Oath Before the President

President Nawrocki’s explanation for refusing to administer the oaths has been scattered and incoherent, citing procedural errors in how these appointments were made and claiming he can administer the oath only to judges elected to seats made vacant during his term. None of these explanations reflects a factual or legal reality; in fact, all signs point to President Nawrocki escalating his political conflict with the ruling majority and Prime Minister Tusk by awarding himself the authority to decide who sits on the Tribunal and who does not.

The head of state administering the oath to constitutional court judges as a formal step in completing their appointment is not unique to Poland. Several other European countries, such as Croatia, Austria, and Latvia, include such a step in their judicial appointment procedures. This step, while ceremonial, is not without legal significance; for example, if the elected judge refuses to take the oath, the appointment would not be completed. However, the Sejm, not the President, ultimately decides on appointments to the Tribunal, unlike the President’s explicit power to appoint judges to regular and administrative courts, including the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court. The President’s role in appointing judges to the Constitutional Tribunal is intended to lend the Sejm’s choice additional gravity. I disagree with the view, expressed by the sitting judge of the Constitutional Tribunal Prof. Jakub Stelina, that the President is competent to refuse to administer the oath if they establish that the person elected by the Sejm does not fulfil the formal criteria for a Constitutional Tribunal judge or the Sejm made a procedural error while electing the judge. It is not under the President’s purview to verify whether a judge elected by Sejm can take up a seat at the Tribunal, as opposed to his explicit power to verify the appointment with regard to judges of regular courts.

Reaction by the ECtHR and the Venice Commission

Beyond a domestic legal and political firestorm, the standoff prompted reactions from regional courts and bodies. The four judges who were refused the oath and denied entry to the Tribunal lodged an application with the ECtHR, and in May 2026 the Strasbourg court issued an interim order requiring Polish authorities to remove obstacles preventing the judges from taking up their seats. President Nawrocki and the Constitutional Tribunal unsurprisingly ignored the order.

The next major response came from the Venice Commission, which in October 2026 issued a well-reasoned opinion that clarified the President of Poland’s role in appointing the judges to the Tribunal and the legal nature of his competence to take the oath. The Commission clearly distinguished between the President’s power to appoint judges to other Polish courts, where he has discretion and may refuse to appoint a judge, and the election of judges to the Constitutional Tribunal, where the law provides no explicit possibility of the President refusing to administer the oath. The Venice Commission went one step further, however, by suggesting an alternative course of action if the President refuses to cooperate: the oath could be fulfilled without the President’s physical participation, provided that its essential elements are preserved, and it is addressed and transmitted to the President. In fact, the Sejm has already taken a similar course of action with judges swearing the oath on the Sejm floor or in the presence of the Marshall of the Sejm (speaker). Neither of these alternative means of administering the oath have been recognised by President Nawrocki or Święczkowski, however, as both maintain that such course of action is contrary to the Polish law.

A Powder Keg of Law and Politics

Several legal and political issues converge in this element of the Polish rule of law crisis. First, Polish constitutional law is deficient and does not clearly state what should happen if the President refuses to administer the oaths, including not providing a clear judicial recourse for a person whose oath has been denied. This deficiency stems from a clear source: the drafters’ apparent assumption that the President would never refuse to administer an oath. As with many other institutions of Polish constitutional law, the drafters assumed that such a brazen refusal by the President to cooperate, and an attempt to expand the President’s powers without a sound legal basis, would never occur because of the possible legal and political costs. Yet, as has been the case with many violations of the Polish Constitution and related laws since 2015, it is exactly what happened, and the polarised political landscape seems to encourage such behaviour.

Moreover, this refusal comes at a time when the Constitutional Tribunal is mired in a legal and political struggle between the ruling coalition and the opposition. In particular, the Sejm’s recent election of Maciej Berek, a government minister and close ally of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, to the Tribunal triggered a reaction from PiS and its supporters, who have set up a camp outside the Constitutional Tribunal and vow to protect it from political influence, leading to clashes with law enforcement and visits from PiS politicians and President Nawrocki. Calls for broader political consensus on the need to enact a deep reform of the Constitutional Tribunal, as advocated by i.a. the Stefan Batory Foundation, are gaining traction among politicians but are unlikely to pass without PiS and the ruling coalition reaching a consensus, an elusive prospect given the highly charged polarisation.

Finally, the three new judges – who were able to give an oath and were let into the Tribunal – have refused to start with their work until the crisis is resolved. Accordingly, the “shrinking” court finds itself hard-pressed to carry out regular work and unable to call a general assembly of its judges, which leads to its inability to vote on its 2027 financial plan and pass it over to the government for inclusion in the general budget of the country. Accordingly, the Tribunal is shortly facing the problem with its own financing.

In addition, the judges denied entry are also being denied their salaries, leading to a rather awkward solution of the government paying these out from the budget of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs under the assumption that such action constitutes a partial implementation of the ECtHR interim order.

Concluding Remarks

No clear solution to the oath-taking issue seems to present itself. The oath crisis led directly to the recent ongoing standoff at the Tribunal, whose final result is at this point indecisive. With the European Commission having divested itself of the means to pressure Poland by releasing all funds held back over rule-of-law issues in 2024, and with no political appetite in the Berlaymont to pressure Poland’s pro-European government, there is no external factor that could alter the current trajectory. A judgment of the ECtHR establishing whether the rights of elected judges have been breached will be most welcome, but it will likely take considerable time before such a judgment is issued – and Poland might be in an entirely different political situation after the parliamentary elections next year, were PiS and its allies to return to power.

item.content:encoded:
Working conditions in platform work show an “urgent need for action,” according to the Bundesrat (Federal Council). It recently called on the German government to present a draft bill to implement the Platform Work Directive (“the Directive”) before the 2 December 2026 deadline. Effective regulation in food delivery, the Bundesrat states, could be achieved by requiring platform workers to be employed directly by digital platforms. Indeed, such a prohibition on the use of subcontracted labour would be really helpful.

Fleet Partners: A New Low for Workers

Working conditions in Germany’s food delivery sector have reached a new low. As a first reaction, in January 2026 German law classified platform-based delivery services as a sector at particular risk of undeclared work and illegal employment. However, the German government has yet to indicate how it plans to implement the Directive adopted in 2024. Workers have been calling for an implementation that would address the structural problems posed by the proliferation of intermediaries.

The risks go beyond employment status – delivering food on a bike is also particularly dangerous: a 2026 survey of more than 700 food delivery riders by TU Dresden for the German Road Safety Council (DVR) found that bike workers averaged almost one accident per year, and those in their first year on the job reported around five.

On paper, Germany has been ahead of other legal systems. The Directive’s centrepiece, the presumption of employment (Articles 4 and 5), addresses an issue that German labour law has already more or less resolved, at least for food delivery platform workers. Germany is one of the countries where courts have made clear that delivery platform workers must be classified as employees, rather than disguised as self-employed. Employment became the norm, and with it came labour rights, including the right to strike and to elect works councils. Moreover, the Federal Labour Court established that bike delivery workers have the right to be provided with a suitable bicycle and a mobile phone as essential and appropriate work equipment.

So why is the Bundesrat now calling for action “particularly” on bogus self-employment, labour and social protection, lack of transparency in the organisation of work, and information asymmetry – in other words, on almost every area relevant for worker protection?

Because the Directive’s presumption of employment alone will not fix the problem – an issue we already discussed in a Verfassungsblog symposium in 2023. Since its adoption, food delivery platforms have continued to adapt their business models based on the exploitation of workers, and searched for new ways to disrupt labour law. Their instrument of choice: placing intermediaries, so-called “fleet partners”, between themselves and their workers. Investigative journalists have documented these risks in detail, including footage of fleet partners distributing pay in cash after deducting a 20% cut. Fleet partners, which act as formal employers, sometimes provide no contract at all, or only part-time contracts, while requiring their employees to work full-time.

Wolt, which entered the German market in 2020, has gradually transitioned to a hybrid model that combines some directly employed couriers and those hired by subcontractors. Uber Eats implemented the subcontractor model from the start when it launched in Germany in mid-2021. Lieferando, by contrast, has long remained the only major delivery platform to employ a significant share of its workforce directly. With the announcement in 2025 that Lieferando would also outsource part of its workforce, the shift towards indirect employment is close to complete.

For workers, the consequences have been severe. What began as an outsourcing arrangement has developed into a parallel layer of labour-market intermediaries. Many workers are now managed by small fleet partners that are invisible to the public, and often to the workers themselves. In some cases, workers could identify their supposed employer only by a number in a WhatsApp group. More recently, larger intermediaries have emerged, including Fleetlery, Closer Go and Opriša, some of which have introduced their own apps to manage workers’ shifts and orders. These intermediaries often lack the expertise, resources and willingness to comply with their responsibilities as employers, including legal obligations on health and safety or data protection.

Subcontracting and Structural Enforcement Gaps

The spread of intermediaries came to the EU legislator’s attention relatively late in the adoption of Directive (EU) 2024/2831, but not too late to introduce a fallback clause: Article 3 now obliges Member States to ensure equal treatment of workers engaged through intermediaries.

This provision should be central to Germany’s implementation of the Directive if it is to meet the effectiveness requirements of EU law (Art. 5(1) and 6; Art. 288(3) TFEU; Art. 47 EU-CFR). Employment status alone provides little protection if the employer is an invisible intermediary without the willingness or even the means to fulfil its legal responsibilities. These responsibilities go beyond financial obligations like minimum wage or social security payments. In a sector such as food delivery on bikes, in which workers put their bodies at daily risk, occupational health and safety protection is a major concern – from road traffic accidents and exposure to adverse weather to physical strain and the psychosocial pressures created by algorithmic management.

This is not to say that the legislator has been completely idle. The recent reform of the German Act to Combat Undeclared Work and Unlawful Employment now lists platform-based delivery services among the sectors at high risk of undeclared work and unlawful employment (Sec. 2a(1) No 4 Schwarzarbeitsbekämpfungsgesetz). However, the powers of the federal customs administration exercised through the local agencies for the Financial Control of Undeclared Work (Finanzkontrolle Schwarzarbeit, FKS) focus on compliance with social security obligations, work authorisation for foreign workers, and minimum wage. When FKS officers request working-time records, for example, they typically use them to check minimum wage and social security compliance, not working conditions more broadly. Its right to sanction “exploitative working conditions” (Sec. 2(1) No 7) deters fleet partners with fines and criminal penalties (Secs. 8-11), but creates no rights for workers. Issues of health and safety fall to yet another authority, the Länder Arbeitsschutzbehörden. While larger intermediaries with identifiable premises should be easier to monitor than a myriad of fleet partners, all authorities face the same problem: workers spend their days dispersed across the city, so no inspector sees the full picture.

The Call for a Prohibition on the Use of Subcontracted Labour

Fragmented enforcement underpins calls to prohibit subcontracted labour in the food delivery sector. To pursue this demand, the Lieferando Workers Collective and the trade union NGG organised a protest in September and a strike in October 2025, with immediate media and political reactions. In November 2025, the Länder labour ministers called on the federal government to introduce a direct employment requirement for the food delivery sector (p. 82). The Bundesrat has now followed up on this call.

The prohibition on the use of subcontracted labour, or the requirement of direct employment (Direktanstellungsgebot), is a new instrument of labour law. It was first introduced in the meat-processing industry in 2021, where it prohibits the use of external personnel for core activities in slaughterhouses and meat-processing plants. At the time, it was described as one of the most ambitious and successful social policy measures since the minimum wage. And it delivered: an evaluation found that after subcontracted workers were employed directly, violations of working-time regulations fell. Better access to employment records made legal advice for workers easier, while easier access to overtime records strengthened enforcement. Progress seems to have halted now, but the level of protection has remained higher than before the reform.

The Constitution Is Not an Obstacle

Last year, Federal Labour Minister Bärbel Bas already considered introducing a direct employment requirement for food delivery platforms, but held back because of legal and constitutional concerns. Following the Federal Constitutional Court’s decision confirming, earlier this year, that the instrument is compatible with the German Constitution, these concerns should no longer stand in the way.

In its ruling, the Court addressed the problem of intermediaries with striking clarity: “There is no constitutional entitlement to benefit from one’s workforce without having to address the challenges arising from regular employment relationships” (para. 141). The Court held that the requirement of direct employment is constitutionally justified if it satisfies the principle of proportionality: it must pursue a legitimate aim, such as protecting workers’ health and safety, and be suitable, necessary and appropriate to that aim.

The “necessity” part of the principle is the point of uncertainty in food delivery, as it was in meat processing: are there less intrusive ways to address risks posed by intermediaries? Platforms routinely say they conduct voluntary due diligence on their fleet partners, but reveal little about how. More importantly, sustained public scrutiny of working conditions in the sector, including assessment by the Fairwork project, has not brought substantial improvements. This is, after all, a sector that stands for disruption rather than compliance; unlike the meat-processing industry, most players in the sector do not even claim to embrace the European Social Model.

Why Liability Rules Aren’t Enough

The most obvious alternative to direct employment would be to strengthen liability along the subcontracting chain. German law already establishes a general “chain liability” for breaches of minimum wage legislation by subcontractors (Sec. 13 MiLoG; see also Sec. 28e(3a) and (3g) Book IV Social Code for social security liabilities in the construction and courier, express and parcel services sectors). These provisions give workers a legal claim against an identifiable and financially stronger party. They could also work against digital platforms such as Wolt.

Food delivery workers have in fact already tried to hold platforms accountable in court – and failed. In 2025, a Wolt rider sued for more than €3,000 in unpaid wages. Instead of using the liability rules, she argued that Wolt, not its fleet partner, was her real legal employer. Although the Berlin Labour Court found the evidence insufficient and upheld the corporate veil between platform and fleet partner, the claimant had the right intuition: changing the underlying employment relationship is the only way to address the problems created by diffuse subcontracting. Liability rules address financial obligations and not the significant health and safety risks of delivering food by bike. They merely add a solvent debtor when financial obligations are not met: they do not keep a worker safe on the road. As the Federal Constitutional Court put it: when it comes to workers’ health and safety – “clear responsibilities are a prerequisite for the enforcement of rights” (para. 21).

Food Delivery and Beyond

Since the Constitutional Court’s judgment, a requirement of direct employment has been discussed for various sectors, from parcel services to seasonal employment in agriculture. The health and safety risks make the food delivery sector a particularly strong case for prohibiting the use of subcontracted labour. Employers are obliged to assess risks and take appropriate measures to prevent harm, but these obligations are difficult to enforce where the formal employer is separated from the organisation and control of work. And unlike unpaid wages, a serious work accident cannot be remedied by a subsequent administrative fine. A prohibition on subcontracted labour would make the platform the employer by law, rather than leaving riders with the legal risk of establishing this in litigation, as the current law does.

The Platform Work Directive’s provisions on algorithmic management add another argument: Where subcontractors rely on a platform’s algorithmic tools, it is the platform and not the subcontractor that controls key aspects of the employment relationship: how tasks are allocated, how performance is scored, what targets are set, and which sanctions are imposed. The same applies to the Directive’s transparency and oversight requirements, including the right to an explanation of algorithmic decisions and to request human review (Arts. 7-11); they are hard to enforce against an employer that does not control the technology.

This is, after all, a strong argument for a broader approach: because algorithmic rights can hardly be enforced against subcontractors, a requirement of direct employment should apply across the Directive’s scope, and extend beyond food delivery to platform work in general.

To return to the Constitutional Court: no one should benefit from a workforce without taking on the responsibilities of an employer. Health and safety risks make the case for direct employment in food delivery; algorithmic management makes it for platform work as a whole. A requirement of direct employment is the most straightforward way to ensure the Platform Work Directive is implemented effectively in German law.

item.dc:creator: Tobias Trappe
item.description:
Ausgerechnet jene Hochschulen, an denen die Staatsbediensteten von morgen ausgebildet werden, sind besonders anfällig für autoritäre Einflussnahme. Ihre enge Bindung an Ministerien eröffnet politischen Kräften weitreichende Möglichkeiten, Lehre und Forschung zu steuern sowie Wissenschaft zum Instrument staatlicher Machtausübung zu machen. Die Gefahr reicht damit weit über die Einschränkung der Wissenschaftsfreiheit hinaus. Um ihr zu begegnen, braucht es mehr als gesetzliche Schutzmechanismen.

item.content:encoded:
In der Debatte um Gefahren für die Wissenschaftsfreiheit ist erstmals eine besondere Gruppe von Hochschulen in den Blick genommen worden, von der in der Öffentlichkeit kaum jemand Notiz nimmt: die Polizeihochschulen. Weil sie dem Innenministerium unterstehen, sind sie in besonderem Maße verwundbar, sollte die AfD die Leitung dieses Ressorts übernehmen – ein Befund, auf den Andreas Ruch und Stefan Kersting eindringlich hingewiesen haben. Diese Gefährdung der Wissenschaftsfreiheit betrifft sämtliche sog. „internen“ Hochschulen für den öffentlichen Dienst (HöD), also jene Hochschulen, die ausschließlich für den öffentlichen Dienst ausbilden (§ 73 Abs. 2 HRG). Sie liegt nicht nur in der besonderen Struktur dieser Hochschulen, sondern auch in der für sie kennzeichnenden Kultur begründet. Dabei droht nicht allein die Verhinderung von Forschung, sondern ebenso deren Missbrauch für politische Zwecke (dual use). Um diesen Gefahren zu begegnen, reichen gesetzliche Mittel allein nicht aus. Erforderlich ist vielmehr eine klare Positionierung der Hochschulmitglieder auf allen Ebenen der HöD. Denn was dort gelehrt, erforscht und gelernt wird, bestimmt mit, wie staatliche Herrschaft ausgeübt wird.

Die strukturelle Verwundbarkeit der internen HöD

Die besondere Verwundbarkeit der internen HöD ergibt sich aus ihrer engen institutionellen Anbindung an die Ministerien, für die sie ausbilden. Zwar führen auch externalisierte Studiengänge an regulären Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften (HAW) in den gehobenen Dienst der öffentlichen Verwaltung (einschließlich Polizei), so etwa an der Hochschule für Wirtschaft und Recht (HWR) in Berlin; den Großteil der künftigen Mitarbeitenden bei der Polizei, der allgemeinen Verwaltung, Rechtspflege, Finanzverwaltung und Rentenversicherung bilden jedoch interne HöD aus. Als Einrichtungen im Geschäftsbereich der Ministerien, für die sie ausbilden, fehlen solchen internen HöD laut HRK gerade jene Merkmale, die Hochschulen im strengen Sinne des Wortes ausmachen und die, wie Zillessen und Mono für Sachsen-Anhalt gezeigt haben, vor politischen Übergriffen schützen: gesicherte Entscheidungsautonomie; weitergehende Selbstverwaltungsrechte, einschließlich des Rechts, die eigene Leitung zu bestimmen; eine auf das Recht beschränkte staatliche Aufsicht; der Professorenstatus als Regelstatus der hauptamtlich Lehrenden; die Entscheidungshoheit über Studien- und Prüfungsordnungen oder der Hochschulzugang von Studierenden ohne Anwärterstatus. Eine autoritäre Partei braucht deshalb nicht das Innenministerium, um auf die Exekutive und deren (künftiges) Personal Einfluss zu nehmen; es genügt jedes Ressort, für das eine HöD ausbildet. Dabei ist diese besondere rechtliche Konstruktion interner HöD Absicht: Sie garantiert mit der direkten Steuerbarkeit der Ausbildung nicht nur deren Praxisnähe und inhaltliche Flexibilität, sondern auch eine ebenso bedarfsgerechte wie kurzfristig beeinflussbare Personalgewinnung. Was im Normalfall die Funktionsfähigkeit der Exekutive sichert, kann unter einem autoritär geführten Ministerium in ein leistungsfähiges Instrument zum Umbau dessen umschlagen, was „Verwaltung“ eigentlich ist: der Alltag von Herrschaft.1)

Kulturelle Nähe zwischen internen HöD und Ressort

Politisierungsrisiken2) für interne HöD bestehen indessen nicht nur dort, wo das Recht Wege der Einflussnahme öffnet. Denn: „Machtpolitik ist Personalpolitik, und Personalpolitik ist Politik mit Loyalitäten“.3) Viele Lehrende haben ein zweites Amt – und dieses zweite Amt liegt im Ressort. Wer abgeordnet ist, kehrt in seine Stammbehörde zurück, beurteilt wird er im Fall der Polizei durch die für ihn zuständige Landesoberbehörde. Und die Studierenden sind Anwärterinnen und Anwärter: Ihre Behörde entscheidet über Übernahme und Verwendung. Im Fall der von Ruch und Kersting beispielhaft herangezogenen Hochschule für Polizei und öffentliche Verwaltung (HSPV) NRW stellt sich die Loyalitätsfrage auch bei ihren Führungspositionen: Diese werden durch die Landesregierung bzw. das Innenministerium bestimmt, während der Senat über lediglich beschränkte Mitwirkungsrechte verfügt (§§ 9 Abs. 4, 10 Abs. 1, 17 Abs. 2 und 4, 17a Abs. 1 FHGöD NRW). Der Präsident ist Beamter auf Zeit; seine Lebenszeitstelle besteht fort (§ 9 Abs. 6 S. 5 FHGöD). Und über seine Wiederernennung entscheidet die Landesregierung auf Vorschlag des Ministeriums, unter Umständen auch ohne Ausschreibung (§ 9 Abs. 5 und 6 FHGöD).

Wechselseitige Abhängigkeiten, gemeinsame Interessen, gewachsene Kontakte und dauerhafte Kooperationen schaffen Nähe, Vertrautheit, Einverständnis, so dass das Ressort harte Machtressourcen vielfach gar nicht erst „ausspielen“ müsste. Sie liegen immer schon „in der Luft“. Erst recht, wenn vor Augen steht, dass die Freiheit der Wissenschaft und das Recht auf Selbstverwaltung nichts sind, was in der Ausbildung von Polizei und Verwaltung einfach einen allgemeinen Konsens zum Ausdruck bringen würde. Im Gegenteil: Verwaltungs- bzw. Polizeihochschulen sind vielfach hybride Konstrukte, in denen ganz unterschiedliche Milieus und Kulturen aufeinandertreffen.4) Zahlreiche Kräfte innerhalb wie außerhalb der Hochschule bringen daher einem Verlust des Hochschulstatus viel Sympathie entgegen. Wie das gehen kann, hat Niedersachsen vorgemacht: 2007 löste hier das Land die Fakultät Polizei an der damaligen Niedersächsischen Fachhochschule für Verwaltung und Rechtspflege auf und überführte sie in die Polizeiakademie Niedersachsen. Ein solcher Rückbau ist nicht nur atmosphärisch gegenwärtig und kann kollektive Bestrebungen zu mehr hochschulischer Autonomie bereits im Ansatz dämpfen; ein autoritär geführtes Ministerium könnte ihn auch in die Wege leiten, ohne dass es mit allzu viel Widerstand rechnen müsste.

Insbesondere im Raum der Polizei ist Wissenschaftsfreiheit überdies ein Recht, das mit Blick auf die Ausbildung des eigenen Personals vielfach als problematisch und für die Funktionsfähigkeit der Organisation gefährlich empfunden wird. Zwar finden hier „autoritäre Bedrohungen“ der Wissenschaftsfreiheit keine nennenswerte Akzeptanz. Sie stoßen aber doch auf einen gewissen Resonanzboden, der sich aus langgehegten Zweifeln an einer immer stärker „vergeistigten“ Ausbildung speist. Dazu kommen der Verdacht einer „Praxisferne“ von Teilen einer „akademischen“ Ausbildung sowie ein wachsender Verdruss angesichts einer als zu hoch empfundenen „Drop-out-Quote“, die den polizeilichen „Nachersatz“ und in eins damit das staatliche Sicherheitsversprechen samt Herrschaftslegitimation gefährdet. In Summe spielt all das einem autoritär geführten Ministerium ebenso wie den einstellenden Behörden, aber z. B. auch den Gewerkschaften eine Reihe von plausiblen Argumenten in die Hände, um die Lehre dem „wirklichen“ Bedarf entsprechend anzupassen. Dabei gerieten erwartungsgemäß Einrichtungen wie der „Beauftragte für Menschenrechtsbildung“, aber auch geistes- und sozialwissenschaftliche Fächer, Lehrinhalte und Kompetenzziele besonders schnell auf den Prüfstand: Im Interesse einer „längst überfälligen“ „Entschlackung“ der „überfrachteten“ Ausbildung sind sie es, die sich vergleichsweise geräuschlos entfernen lassen.

Möglicher Missbrauch (dual use) von Forschung an internen HöD

Interne HöD werden vonseiten der für sie zuständigen Ministerien ebenso wie von ihren Bedarfsträgern vielfach als reine Ausbildungsstätten gesehen und auch nur als solche „genutzt“. Einige HöD können inzwischen auf durchaus erhebliche Forschungsaktivitäten verweisen.5) Die dafür zur Verfügung stehenden Ressourcen an Zeit, Geld und Personal sind allerdings in keiner Weise mit denen an Universitäten zu vergleichen. Bei einem nicht unbeträchtlichen Teil handelt es sich dabei um Auftragsforschung für Ministerien, Polizei, aber auch für Städte und Gemeinden. Nach einem Machtwechsel hätte ein extremistisch geführtes Ministerium zwar keinen fachaufsichtlichen Zugriff auf entsprechende Aktivitäten. Durch seine angesprochene strukturelle wie kulturelle Nähe zu den internen HöD könnte das Ressort jedoch kritische Forschung nicht nur verhindern; es könnte Forschung auch ideologisch steuern. Insbesondere über die Auftragsvergabe, aber z. B. auch den Zugang zu Daten und Feld. An internen HöD liegt Forschung in einer Hand: in der des Staates, der sie gleichermaßen beauftragt, finanziert, durchführt, beaufsichtigt und vor allem: nutzt. Wo das geschieht, kann der Staat selbst zum Sicherheitsrisiko werden. Denn Forschung ist „sicherheitsrelevant“, wenn „Dritte“ deren Ergebnisse missbrauchen können, um Menschenwürde, Leben, Freiheit oder das friedliche Zusammenleben zu schädigen. Sie wird „besorgniserregend“ (dual use research of concern, DURC), wenn ein solcher Missbrauch „unmittelbar“ möglich und ein zu befürchtender Schaden „erheblich“ wäre. So definiert es der Gemeinsame Ausschuss zum Umgang mit sicherheitsrelevanter Forschung der DFG und der Leopoldina.

Der durch den Gemeinsamen Ausschuss vorangetriebene Diskurs zu sicherheitsrelevanter Forschung hat dabei erst seit kurzem auch „staatliche Akteure“ als potenzielle „Dritte“ ins Visier genommen, von denen Missbrauchsrisiken der Forschung ausgehen könnten. Mit einer nicht mehr auszuschließenden rechtsförmigen, demokratisch legitimierten Machtübernahme durch antidemokratische oder illiberale Kräfte (autocratic legalism) sind es nicht mehr nur ausländische Akteure, die eine solche Bedrohung darstellen. Eine politisch extreme Ressortleitung könnte über eigene Forschungsaufträge (möglicherweise – hypothetisch gesprochen – zur Kriminalitätsbelastung von Migrantinnen und Migranten in Duisburg) nicht nur gesellschaftliche Diskurse beeinflussen. Sie könnte ganz „unmittelbar“ das Handeln des gewaltmonopolisierenden Staates steuern: durch Regelungsakte, durch Aus- und Fortbildungsinhalte, durch Trainings oder direkte praktische Anleitung. Missbrauchen lassen sich nicht nur Forschungen etwa im Bereich der Waffentechnologie. Sozialwissenschaftliche Studien, die z. B. Menschen klassifizieren und sortieren, sind für dual use ebenso anfällig wie rechtswissenschaftliche Konzepte, die staatliches Eingreifen legitimieren. Ob und inwieweit Forschung an internen HöD überhaupt „sicherheitsrelevant“ ist, bleibt natürlich eine Frage des Einzelfalls. Ist sie es aber, dann birgt sie in der Hand eines autoritär geführten Ministeriums das Risiko einer „unmittelbaren“ und „erheblichen“ Schädigung verfassungsrechtlich geschützter Güter. Hier stellen Kommissionen für Ethik sicherheitsrelevanter Forschung, wie sie der Gemeinsame Ausschuss zum Umgang mit sicherheitsrelevanter Forschung von DFG und Leopoldina empfiehlt, eine Möglichkeit dar, um Forschungen vor autoritär motiviertem Missbrauch zu schützen.

Die notwendige Selbsterkenntnis

Beim Entwurf zum neuen Hochschulgesetz für den öffentlichen Dienst (HGöD-E) in NRW ist es bislang weitgehend versäumt worden, solche oder andere institutionelle Sicherungen der HSPV NRW in den Blick zu nehmen. Ruch und Kersting weisen daher in ihrem Beitrag zu Recht auf die Notwendigkeit gesetzlicher Vorkehrungen hin. Zu ihnen zählen sie neben einer gesicherten Stimmenmehrheit in den forschungsrelevanten Gremien auch das Festschreiben von Lehr- und Lernzielen in den von politischer Einflussnahme besonders bedrohten geistes- und sozialwissenschaftlichen Fächern. Tatsächlich geht der aktuelle Gesetzentwurf einen ersten Schritt in diese Richtung: Er erklärt nun „die ethischen, geschichtlichen und gesellschaftlichen Grundlagen“ eines verantwortlichen Handelns im demokratischen und sozialen Rechtsstaat ausdrücklich zum Befähigungsauftrag der HöD in NRW (§ 3 Abs. 1 S. 3 HGöD-E).

Wie weit eine solche Vorgabe wirklich tragen könnte, dürfte zumindest offen sein. Schließlich hat der „intellektuelle Rechtsextremismus“ gerade diese Fächer als „Schlachtfeld“ (Martin Sellner) seines metapolitischen Strebens nach kultureller Hegemonie identifiziert. Dieses Problem zeigt jedoch: Eine verfassungsresiliente HöD wird mehr brauchen als Regelungen. Sie braucht Menschen, die die Verteidigung der Verfassung als jeweils individuelle, nicht delegierbare Verantwortung anerkennen: in der Lehrendenschaft, in der Studierendenschaft, aber auch und gerade in der Hochschulverwaltung wie -leitung. Das lässt sich vergleichsweise leicht schwören und beschwören, weit weniger leicht umsetzen. Sebastian Haffners „Geschichte eines Deutschen“ ist ein unheimliches Dokument der „Sorglosigkeit“, „Betäubung“, „Zuschauerhaltung“ und der „endlosen Diskussionen“,6) die gerade in staatlichen Einrichtungen eine so attraktive Versuchung darstellen. Solche Anfechtungen auf personeller wie professioneller Ebene zu identifizieren und deren verführerische Kräfte anzuerkennen, ist Aufgabe wie Leistung von Selbsterkenntnis. Diese ist hier wie sonst auch (mit Kant) „aller menschlichen Weisheit Anfang“. Und Ausdruck der Freiheit von Wissenschaft und Forschung: der Freiheit eines unverstellten Blicks – auch auf sich selbst. Das gilt auch und gerade dort, wo das Herrschen gelehrt, erforscht und gelernt wird.

item.title: Statement by Former Presidents of the Constitutional Tribunal on the Crisis in the Constitutional Tribunal
item.dc:creator: Marek Safjan
item.description:
The judges lawfully appointed to the Constitutional Tribunal by the Sejm have taken the necessary steps to restore the functions and status of this constitutional institution, which is essential to the rule of law and the protection of citizens’ rights and freedoms.

The post Statement by Former Presidents of the Constitutional Tribunal on the Crisis in the Constitutional Tribunal appeared first on Verfassungsblog.
item.content:encoded:
The judges lawfully appointed to the Constitutional Tribunal by the Sejm have taken the necessary steps to restore the functions and status of this constitutional institution, which is essential to the rule of law and the protection of citizens’ rights and freedoms.

The Tribunal has been mired in a profound crisis for more than ten years. Its adjudicating panels include persons whose appointments were defective, while excluding lawfully elected judges. The Constitutional Tribunal is headed by a person selected through an improper procedure, and its work has recently been brought to a complete standstill by the failure to convene the General Assembly of its Judges. Judgments of Europe’s foremost courts – the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union – requiring measures to restore the Tribunal’s role as an independent and impartial institution remain unimplemented. Until this is achieved, citizens are denied effective protection of their rights and freedoms and cannot avail themselves of the individual constitutional complaint. This alarming situation called for decisive action to rebuild the authority of the institution and restore public confidence in it. That purpose is certainly not served by the conduct of the President of the Republic of Poland, who, together with Judge Święczkowski, has for many months prevented the judges appointed by the Sejm from taking office and who yesterday made a direct attempt to infringe the autonomy of the constitutional court.

Nothing can justify inaction when the constitutional crisis deepens with each passing day, with all the adverse consequences this entails for the rule of law and for citizens.

The steps now being taken by the judges are intended to restore the functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal in accordance with the Constitution. The judges must be allowed to achieve this aim and to follow the necessary lawful procedures, above all by convening the General Assembly of the Judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and adopting resolutions on the applications submitted to the Tribunal by the Prosecutor General to lift the immunity of Judges Bogdan Święczkowski and Bartłomiej Sochański.

There is no other path to ending the constitutional crisis and restoring the Constitutional Tribunal to the society it serves.

Marek Safjan  Jerzy Stępień  Bohdan Zdziennicki  Andrzej Zoll

Warsaw, 31 October 2026

item.content:encoded:
Democratic self-defence has become a global constitutional habit. Militant democracy in particular, that is the idea that “pre-emptive, prima facie illiberal measures to prevent those aiming at subverting democracy with democratic means from destroying the democratic regime” can be justified,1) has been central to this development. The model, however, has travelled with a European pedigree that has long viewed political parties with suspicion, once as agents of division and now as agents of anti-democratic subversion. I call this party-centrism, that is the assumption that anti-democratic political parties are the primary source of danger for a constitutional democracy and therefore the proper subject of militant regulation.

In many non-European contexts, parties are neither the main form of political organisation nor the main source of threat. The fall of the Arab Spring exposed the futility of searching for anti-democratic forces at party headquarters. But party-centrism is not a “that’s a you problem” for the South, and it simply does not fit a neat North-South divide. Even where politics is organised along party lines, as in the United States (US), much of the assault on democracy runs outside of, or alongside, party politics.

Thinking reflexively about militant democracy requires us not only to point to party-centrism as a flaw, but to take the opportunity to revisit the doctrine as a whole, particularly since it matters to every democratic society facing anti-democratic threats of various kinds. Below, I trace and define party-centrism and argue more narrowly that moving beyond it is valuable not only because it brings more actors into view, but because it extends to them the same level of protection that parties already receive.

Obsessed Much?

For the longest time, political parties have played the main villain in our discussion of militant democracy. Naturally, the electoral arena, where parties are assumed to prey on an “irrational and emotionally unreliable” mass,2) became the main stage for militant intervention. The democratic defence literature holds that the modern threat is, “in many ways, a party threat.”3) As Olsen and Tuovinen advise, “[a]nyone concerned with democracy should thus be concerned with the democratic nature of parties.”4) Party banning, then, has grown to be the archetypical instrument of militant response where parties are routinely “investigated, infiltrated, delisted, and outlawed” in the name of democracy. 5)

Why parties in the first place? The theory holds that while political organisation takes many forms, parties alone “bring opposition into the frame of government.”6) It acknowledges that individuals can hold anti-democratic views, but only group-level organisation can wage that war against democracy.7) Putting a target on the back of parties is, understandably, more convenient. Ethically, banning a party is easier to justify than banishing an individual subverter. Legally, the party is a legible target for a mass movement. It rests on state recognition, and often on state funding. It is an entity, and entities can be easily regulated by law.

There is also another answer than that of convenience. Long before parties were a subject of militant regulation, anti-partyism had established them as the category in which political danger appears. Early modern political thought cast parties as factions, pathological intrusions that corroded the body politic rather than organised it.8) That suspicion shaped state-building on both sides of the Atlantic. The French Revolution, Rosenblum observes, “was the occasion for both constitutional creation and renewed anti-partyism.”9) In the US, Madison warned against the “mischiefs of faction” while conceding that parties would have to be tolerated, on the condition that the government check them rather than the reverse.10) By the nineteenth century parties had been largely normalised. Even totalitarian movements that displayed open hatred toward other parties took the form of a party themselves since the party had become the instrument through which power was won. It was the failure of Weimar and interwar Europe at the hands of anti-democratic parties that produced their rehabilitation after 1945, when rebuilding German democracy, for example, was understood as “above all a question of the relationship of the German people to their parties.”11) In a way, the long hostility toward parties was never abandoned. It was narrowed to a particular type of party.

Today however, elections are no longer the only arena for undermining democracy, and parties are not the only actors whose democratic behaviour should concern us. Dismissing the role of other actors is costly. Müller and others have already taken up the question of individual militant democracy, extending the list of suspects beyond parties to capable individuals.12) Yet the doctrine has remained party-centric, and the extension has not been followed through into what it asks of the framework.

Stranger Danger?

Any account of the current global democratic crisis that treats it as a party problem is already too narrow. In several parts of the world, parties are not the main mode of political organisation. The Arab World’s failed transition was closed by establishment figures, sectarian networks, and foreign patrons, and none of them fell within reach of the party-banning provisions the new constitutions had just adopted.

My intention is not to dismiss party threats, least of all while the Alternative for Germany (Alternative für Deutschland, AfD) is surging in Germany.13) But the view that democratic defence belongs to parties alone is mistaken, even where party politics is the default. Democracy is undone not just at party venues and election polls, but also at hate marches, Twitch streams and bot farms, fundraising receptions, and campus booths. Anti-democrats are thriving, and aiding and abetting anti-democratic agendas in the public sphere should not be treated as less serious than campaigning on them.

The past three years in the US make this plain. There is certainly a self-perpetuating, anti-democratic agenda carried out by the party in power, but alongside it sit financiers, courtiers, and foot soldiers who answer to no party and stood before no voter. The richest man in history, Elon Musk, has backed anti-democratic parties across Europe and the Americas, amplified far-right voices online, and promised million-dollar giveaways to voters in a Wisconsin Supreme Court election, all from inside a federal post with sweeping reach over the civil service. Bill Ackman financed the campaign against university presidents after the war on Gaza, helped reshape campus policy on student and academic freedom, and has since pledged to bankroll anyone willing to challenge New York’s mayor. Neither has a reported party affiliation.

This is not just the usual story of money and influence. Others have wielded informal power and used it to reshape public institutions and set the national agenda, through having the ear of the President or his allies, as erratic influencers like Laura Loomer and Christopher Rufo do, or long-game architects like Leonard Leo of the Federalist Society. Tellingly, Loomer lost two congressional races and ended up with more power than a seat would have likely given her. On the streets, Jake Lang in the US and Tommy Robinson in the United Kingdom (UK), both with convictions to their name, have mobilised mass protest around anti-immigration causes without running through any party organisation.

The point is that even in a stronghold of party politics like the US, every one of these actors would survive if the country decided to go militant tomorrow. Dismantling democracy is no longer a party scheme. It has become a joint venture, and while its participants may all favour the same party, none of them belongs to it or depends on it.

Rights, Not Parties

The problem runs deeper than the distinction between parties and non-parties. Even a fully equipped militant democracy would struggle to constrain the figures above, and not only because they are not parties. Militant democracy’s logic is electoral. It triggers scrutiny when someone runs for office or forms a party to do so, and the figures above did neither. What they exercised instead were rights that can be just as subversive and have never been treated as militant democracy’s concern.

Part of the trouble is how we define the object of regulation. I propose we think of militant democracy as a category of state action rather than a particular instrument of party control. Simply put, it is the constitutional capacity for pre-emptive restriction of political rights on democracy-protection grounds. It becomes a question about rights restriction rather than a question about parties. This is less of a departure than it sounds. Militant democracy, as Loewenstein envisioned it in 1937, was never only about party banning, and his catalogue was wider and agnostic to the form of organisation. Germany, which embedded the doctrine in its Basic Law, has a dormant constitutional provision aimed at individuals specifically.14)

In practice, states already reach past parties. The UK has proscribed a protest group (Palestine Action), the US has designated a movement with no membership or structure to speak of (Trump’s anti-antifa orders), and lone figures have been debanked and deplatformed (Nick Fuentes, though largely at the hands of private actors rather than the state). These cases differ considerably, and none was framed as militant democracy, but they show that actor legibility, the ease with which a target can be identified and served, is a problem states have already overcome. States do restrict the political rights of actors beyond parties, and largely at will, without the demanding safeguards that make militant democracy defensible in the first place.

Opening the category means militant democracy can pursue those who subvert democracy through any political right at their disposal. Troy can now watch for the Greeks in whatever shape they arrive. And this carries an important implication. Militant democracy is not only a licence to restrict. It carries constraints too, normative considerations and procedural safeguards, and there is no reason these should not travel from parties to individuals and other groups. Applied properly, it would be demanding, and it would mean that when a state reaches past the party, as it already does, it meets the same burden it meets when it reaches a party.

In substance, addressing party-centrism closes an important doctrinal gap. A billionaire is no longer restriction-proof, and a protest movement gets the same protections and safeguards a party would receive. But the project carries a broader significance. The Southern story that animates this inquiry treats the Global South neither as a laboratory for testing militant democracy nor as a recipient of the latest democratic innovations, but as an interlocutor and a source of conceptual insight, relevant to Europe, the United States, and democracies everywhere.
