item.content:encoded:
Research on political parties has become a global enterprise. A field that for a long time concentrated heavily on Europe and North America now includes productive research agendas with a focus on Africa, Asia and Latin America. As a result of this geographical expansion, new experiences have been brought to bear on established concepts, theories and findings, leading to a better understanding of their actual scope. Even more fundamentally, the global expansion of party research has led to innovations in comparative theorising about parties. New concepts have emerged, old ones have been challenged and refined, and more inclusive comparative frameworks have emerged. Among the topics transformed by this globalisation of party research is the study of clientelism and patronage, ethnic mobilisation, dominant party systems, electoral authoritarianism and party system institutionalisation.1)

However, this movement towards more genuinely comparative theorising has been uneven. One area where it remains incomplete is in the treatment of political authority, and specifically, how the condition of plural authority shapes parties – what they do, where they come from, and how they should be regulated. This is a serious gap because, in much of the world, parties operate alongside traditional, customary, religious and other institutions that exercise politically consequential authority. These institutions were “discovered” by scholars from various disciplines a long time ago.2) Yet, what the presence and operation of these traditional authorities means for general theories of party politics remains unclear.

This blog draws on African experiences to consider what plural authority means for party theorising. Its central argument is that taking plural authority seriously raises new questions about parties and challenges some of the assumptions embedded in established theories. African experiences therefore do more than reveal the limits of existing party theory; they provide critical resources for reconstructing it as a more genuinely global comparative theory.

A Hidden Assumption of Party Theory

The problem can also be understood from the standpoint of party theory itself. From here, it appears as a background assumption that is often taken for granted, but which in fact reflects a more particular historical and geographical condition than is commonly recognised. That assumption is the idea that parties operate within a unified framework of political authority centred on the state. For example, in his canonical text, Giovanni Sartori described parties as “the central intermediate and intermediary structure between society and government.”3) This insight captures a familiar model of representation and governance that runs from society, through parties, to the state. But it warrants closer examination on the grounds that it may oversimplify the reality of representation and governance if parties do not operate in a unified authority framework centred on the state. That assumption is widely shared even though the party scholarship has been attuned to institutional complexity, as shown by the significant attention it gives to territorial arrangements such as federalism, decentralisation, regional autonomy and multilevel governance.4) But, crucially, these arrangements distribute authority among different territorial levels within what is still an encompassing state-centred order. The deeper question, then, is whether the state provides the only source of authoritative ordering in the first place.

The concept of legal pluralism helps to clarify the alternative. It draws attention to settings in which state law operates alongside customary, religious, indigenous and other normative orders.5) The orders may overlap, compete or become incorporated into one another, and individuals can be situated within multiple orders simultaneously. Legal and political authority are not the same thing, but these non-state legal orders are sustained by institutions that organise communities, perform governance functions (e.g. adjudicating disputes), command allegiance, and draw on their own sources of legitimacy – in short, they exercise independent political authority. This possibility of multiple political authorities complicates the familiar image of party politics. Parties are often understood as organisations that aggregate interests within society and compete with one another for control of the state. But what if the society in which parties operate is already politically organised through institutions that the party neither creates nor controls? And what if acquiring control of the state does not give parties control over all the sources of authority that matter for governance?

Two Cases of Plural Authority

Plural authority structures, grounded in traditional and religious institutions, are common in Africa. Consider the case of Ghana. It provides a particularly clear case of institutionalised traditional authority. This is reflected in its Constitution which guarantees the institution of chieftaincy and traditional councils, while also establishing National and Regional Houses of Chiefs and assigning them functions relating to customary law and chieftaincy.6) Nigeria illustrates a different form of pluralism. Its constitution doesn’t go so far as to institutionalise traditional roles, like the Ghanaian constitution, but it accommodates multiple legal systems based on Sharia law and customary law.7) Thus, both countries depart from a straightforwardly monist order, in which the state exists as the sole political authority, but in different ways.

Interestingly, both constitutions also recognise and place nation-building obligations on political parties. Article 55 of Ghana’s Constitution requires parties to have a “national character” and prohibits membership based on ethnic, religious, regional or other sectional divisions. Similarly, Nigeria’s Constitution prohibits ethnically or territorially restricted parties.8) It also requires the composition of a party’s governing body to reflect the country’s “federal character,” including representation from at least two-thirds of the states in its executive committee.9) In both cases, then, constitutional recognition of multiple sources of authority coexists with constitutional recognition of political parties and, more specifically, rules designed to make parties cross territorial and communal divisions. It seems reasonable to say that these constitutions express a certain division of labour in which traditional authorities undertake local governance functions, while parties provide a means of national political integration. The standard society-party-state model does not seem to capture the more complex modes of governance imagined by these constitutions or seen in practice in these societies.

Rethinking Parties under Plural Authority

Ghana and Nigeria suggest why plural authority matters for thinking about the role of parties. But what changes more generally if we rethink parties from this alternative standpoint? The implications are potentially significant. Consider, first, party origins. Influential accounts explain how social cleavages become mobilised through parties,10) and how politicians organise to pursue electoral and policy objectives.11) Under plural authority, however, party formation is not simply a matter of organising society for competition over the state. Parties may emerge in political landscapes already organised through other institutions possessing leaders, constituencies and legitimacy of their own. Botswana illustrates the point: modern party politics developed amid established Tswana polities whose chiefs already occupied positions of political authority.12)

Party organisation looks somewhat different from this perspective too. Classic models of cadre, mass, catch-all and cartel parties describe very different relationships among party elites, members, social constituencies and the state.13) Yet under plural authority, citizens may also be organised through, and subject to the power of, non-party and non-state institutions. In northern Nigeria, for example, party development was shaped by established emirate institutions. As CS Whitaker shows, traditional structures influenced party organisational strategies especially within the developing Northern People’s Congress.14) In settings such as these, an account of party organisation must extend beyond the party itself to encompass the networks connecting party actors with other centres of authority.

Party competition may also need to be understood more expansively. Sartori famously conceptualised party systems through interparty interactions. That relational insight remains powerful, but under conditions of plural authority the relevant relationships may extend beyond parties to include traditional authorities, who cannot simply be treated as analogous to party factions or interest groups because they can possess independent sources of authority and legitimacy within their communities. Parties must therefore take these authority holders into account as they compete to win control of the state. In Ghana, for example, parties court traditional leaders, seeking their support during election campaigns.15) Party competition should be understood in such contexts not simply in terms of interparty interactions, but also in terms of parties’ relationships with other authority holders.

Finally, plural authority raises questions about party regulation. Party law is normally concerned with matters such as registration, political finance, internal democracy, and associational freedom. These remain important concerns. But regulation in a plural political order also structures relationships between parties and other authority holders. For example, a constitution, like that of Uganda, may recognise traditional or cultural leaders while prohibiting them from participating in partisan politics. Rules such as these raise important questions about the boundary between traditional and party-political authority. The new, revealed questions include whether regulation should aim to separate or connect political orders, and whether familiar regulatory approaches facilitate or impede parties’ capacity to represent within plural orders and indeed mediate across them.

Recognising plural authority does not require endorsing or romanticising it. Traditional institutions can reproduce hierarchy, exclusion and unaccountable power, sometimes worsened by the legacies of colonial intervention.16) But evidence of such pathologies does not by itself establish state-centred monism as the only or most appropriate democratic endpoint. The better normative inquiry is to ask what parties ought to do under conditions of plural authority, and especially, when should they accommodate, challenge or seek to reform other authority holders, and under what conditions might parties promote political integration without institutional assimilation?

Party Theory and Reflexive Globalisation

Existing party theories are not mistaken simply because they assume a unified, state-centric framework of political authority. In many contexts, that assumption may be entirely appropriate. The problem arises when such theories are treated as having a broader scope than their underlying assumptions warrant. One response is to specify their scope more carefully. Another response – as I’ve argued here – is to rethink concepts and theories informed by experiences that initially appear exceptional. This latter move has affinities with Dipesh Chakrabarty’s project of “provincialising” apparently universal ideas originating from European intellectual traditions.17) The point is not to reject concepts because of where they originated, but to reimagine them in light of encounters with new experiences. As Chakrabarty puts it, “European thought is at once both indispensable and inadequate in helping us to think through the experiences of political modernity in non-Western nations.”18)

The idea of reflexive globalisation, developed by Philipp Dann and Florian Jeßberger, pushes this argument in a complementary direction.19) They contrast an earlier understanding of globalisation as a unidirectional “Westernisation” with a new, “fundamentally multidirectional” dialogue between South and North, metropole and periphery. The implication is that globalisation should involve more than a one-way journey for concepts; feedback from diverse global experiences should contribute to conceptual refinement and reconstruction. Party scholarship has already undergone this kind of reflexive exchange in other areas. Plural authority provides another opportunity. African experiences make visible a political condition that is neither uniquely African nor historically unusual: parties can operate amid several politically consequential sources of authority. Taking that possibility seriously changes the questions we ask about party origins, organisation, competition and regulation. The broader lesson is that genuinely comparative theory cannot be produced simply by applying concepts developed in one setting to an ever-wider range of cases. Globalising theory also means allowing different political experiences to rebound back upon and change those concepts.

item.content:encoded:
If we can still believe the pollsters, Democrats are headed for a very good night next Tuesday. Across the United States, candidates running as Democrats are either leading or running even with their Republican opponents. That the president’s party loses ground in the midterms, often decisively, is one of the more reliable patterns in American politics. But if such a blue wave materializes, we should neither read it as voters’ repudiation of the Republican Party, nor as an endorsement of the Democrats. It is better understood as evidence that American democracy can still deliver on some, if not all, of its promises.

Democracy is not only majority rule. It is also a system of accountability, meant to guarantee some degree of responsiveness between those who govern and those who are governed. On that measure, American democracy is alive and kicking. This is despite the manifold ongoing and strategic assaults on its electoral mechanics. And assaults, some of them successful, there are many. These include the Supreme Court’s gutting of Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 earlier this year, making it far harder to challenge maps that dilute minority votes; the Administration’s attempts to change rules for mail in voting and voter registration, and, most recently, its frivolous lawsuits in California and Alaska. In California the Administration seeks to toss out roughly 20,000 votes. Up North in Alaska, in a rather bizarre twist, Democrats apparently managed to crowd the state’s four-person ballot with an additional candidate sharing the Republican candidate’s exact name, Dan Sullivan. Now, the Administration seeks to block potential certification of a Democratic winner because of potential mix-ups among Republican voters. Both lawsuits are unlikely to go anywhere, and legal scholars have dubbed them “preemptive election interfering” (a framing that arguably also fits the Dan Sullivan stunt).

President Trump returned to the White House on promises with appeal across ideological and party lines. To an electorate squeezed by rising living costs, concerned (whether justifiably or not) about “unregulated” immigration, and disillusioned with the neoliberal status quo, he offered lower prices, an end to foreign wars, and a secure southern border. America first, in short. Two years on, a record share of voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of inflation and the violence with which untrained ICE agents brutalize immigrants and citizens alike. Gas prices are above $4 a gallon (3.8 liters), more than a dollar higher than a year ago. Trump has repeatedly said he doesn’t care for affordability, all while maneuvering the country into yet another open-ended and extremely expensive war in Iran. Next week, voters appear poised to register their discontent and hold accountable those who promised to represent them and instead served the party line, or their own bottom line. After all, little has been done, overall, to ease the strain on a country whose workers put in some 1,800 hours a year (compared with roughly 1,340 in Germany) and still, increasingly, struggle to get by.

We should not dismiss the significance of such electoral accountability. Yet it is only part of what democracy promises. The modern democratic bargain fundamentally rests on the concept of representation. Those we elect shall represent our interests. Our choices at the ballot box should shape what government actually does in a way that is responsive to our needs and demands. On this front, American democracy has arguably been failing for quite some time. Trump turned this failure of representation, whether perceived or real, into a winning electoral strategy, succinctly summarized in his promise to “drain the swamp.”

Democrats in competitive races have learned from this. Many are campaigning on much the same populist message that carried Trump to victory two years ago. Freed from the complications that come with running the government, now it is the Democrats chastising the Trump administration for the high cost of living, and calling out corruption and the way in which elites – and especially the President and his family – undermine good governance on behalf of ordinary people. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, James Talarico in Texas, and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, a state that has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, all run some version of this pitch. It has worked well enough to make races in red and purple states intensely competitive.

Yet despite their shared economic populist agendas, these candidates differ in important ways, both from each other and from their own party. Each has run less as a standard-bearer for the Democratic Party than against its perceived establishment. El-Sayed, a practicing Muslim, Rhodes Scholar, and son of Egyptian immigrants, ran as an unapologetic progressive, and won a bruising primary against a more established rival. Talarico, a state legislator and Christian pastor, talks about his faith as readily as about school funding and grocery bills, and has toured Texas under a slogan borrowed from a TV drama about small-town high-school football. Hamilton, a Methodist minister who founded the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, is courting a largely rural electorate unhappy with the administration’s policies by leaning into a populism of “decency.”

Taken together, these candidates offer a version of American identity that is much more complex and diverse than that embraced by the Trump Administration. America is an immigrant society with a strong progressive streak in its cities. It is also a deeply religious, and specifically Christian, country. And it is utterly divided between urban and rural places whose interests and sensibilities often diverge. The Democratic candidates doing well this year are not papering over these differences. They speak to particular places on their own terms, campaigning on what they think is good for Michigan, or for Texas, or for Kansas. This multiplicity contrasts sharply with the identity (and otherings) offered by Trump in 2024 and many Republican House and Senate candidates today.

Trump’s identity politics rests on a narrow ethnonationalist “we,” tied to whiteness and grievance, coupled with a hyper-libertarian economic creed that materially rewards only those at the very top. The ethnonationalist movements of the last century at least understood that belonging had to be paid for, not only in social status but in jobs and benefits for the in-group. But the Trump administration sought to claim the electoral benefits of ethnonationalist identity politics, without delivering their – remarkably diverse – supporters a material return on their investment. Voters’ change of course is not a rejection of white ethnonationalism as such. In 2024, many arguably voted Republican despite the party’s embrace of white ethnonationalism, not because of it. If anything, the coalition’s fraying shows that Trump squandered a chance to manifest future Republican majorities by building a socially conservative but ethnically diverse coalition focused on economic relief in a country that will soon be majority non-white.

But suppose these Democratic candidates win. Could they deliver on what they promise, and ease the malaise, grievance, and disillusionment that have long characterized the American experiment? Not if relief depends on legislation. If Democrats take only the House, they likely cannot legislate at all. The Senate filibuster lets 41 senators block almost any bill. Even if Democrats flipped the Senate, they would still face the presidential veto of any bill they shuffle through both chambers of Congress, and a Supreme Court with open contempt for progressive legislation. The realistic outcome is two years of hearings and stalemate rather than cheaper groceries or lower rents, followed by a 2028 presidential race about who is to blame.

However, for Democrats, gaining ground in the Senate now is essential to laying the groundwork for legislative success after 2028. Senators serve six-year terms, with a third of the chamber up every two years. This year’s results will shape the Senate a potential future Democratic president would have to work with. The 2026 map initially looked unfavorable, with many of the seats up for election in heavily Republican states. But the toxic national environment for Republicans has turned it into a real opportunity, as the administration’s low approval ratings now threaten Republican senators who were considered safe only months ago. That window may not reopen in 2028, when the map offers Democrats few plausible pickups and several competitive seats of their own to defend. So even if Democrats win the White House in 2028, governing with a comfortable majority will depend largely on gains made in the Senate this year.

The local energy for change currently on display is real and meaningful. Yet it faces an old and intractable problem. Washington’s sclerotic institutional design will likely absorb and stifle much of said energy’s transformative potential over the next two years. For now, this leaves American voters in a bind. They can change who governs, but not really what government does. Elections continue to deliver voters the satisfaction of throwing someone out. Yet their capacity to facilitate policy change responsive to voters’ needs remains weak.

Over time, this teaches voters a concerning lesson: casting a ballot is at best a form of protest, but not one of self-government. Mature democracies can decay – or rot, as Jack Balkin called it – this way, without any dramatic break, through a long series of elections that change who is in charge and leave much of the rest as is. A blue wave would show that Americans can still hold their government accountable. But whether the midterms will deliver much more – on policy, especially affordability and the Iran war, or in terms of restoring a broader sense of responsive government – remains doubtful.

Emmanuel Carrère led me to Eduard Limonov, and Limonov led me to Sankya, Zakhar Prilepin’s thinly veiled autobiographical novel. Its hero is a young Russian in the 1990s whose fury at a rotten, corrupt state eventually tips him into terrorism. Prilepin himself now churns out anti-Ukrainian propaganda for Vladimir Putin and sits on the EU’s sanctions list. And a small far-right press in Germany has just reissued the book. The Week on Verfassungsblog

summarised by EVA MARIA BREDLER

If you still have some holiday to use up before the end of the year, how about Norway? On Sunday, Trump crowned the Scandinavian country the latest “shithouse country” after he was, once again, denied the Nobel Peace Prize. Norway has responded with humour and promptly turned it into an advertising campaign for its – admittedly rather lovely – loos.

If you are less demanding about design, you could also travel to the US – or, if you happen to be a defeated, potentially corrupt presidential candidate: less than two days after the election, Flávio Bolsonaro left for the United States, in defiance of a court order suspending his passport and prohibiting him from leaving the country. THOMAS BUSTAMANTE and EMILIO PELUSO NEDER MEYER (ENG) trace how Lula managed to overturn a significant loss in the first round, above all due to the extraordinary mobilisation of civil society.

Democratic resistance was also decisive in the Serbian elections. On 25 October, the Student List won an absolute majority in parliament. Like Poland and Hungary, Serbia is one of the states whose courts and other key institutions have been captured by the ruling party. BOJAN SPAIĆ and M. VICTORIA KRISTAN (ENG) show what this election will allow Serbia to leave behind.

What Serbia is leaving behind may still lie ahead for Canada: founded in 2025, the “Restoring the Foundations of Judicial Power” project now wants to bring “common good constitutionalism” to Canada. It all sounds very good and very common, but according to DAVID DYZENHAUS (ENG), it is an anti-pluralist project – and he recognises in it the playbook Orbán and PiS used to build their illiberal democracies.

To prevent an illiberal democracy in Saxony-Anhalt, the CDU now plans to leave the chamber during the secret election of the Minister-President, so that no votes from its own ranks can go to the AfD candidate. Why are heads of government elected by secret ballot in the first place, asks MARKUS LEBER (GER) – and calls for the practice to be abolished.

Abolition is also on the agenda in France, where the target is fossil fuel advertising. The ban is already on the statute books. On 2 October, the Conseil d’État reminded the government that it must also give it practical effect, with a clear regulatory framework. MARTA TORRE-SCHAUB (ENG) explains what the judgment means for the balance between climate protection, commercial freedom and the prevention of misleading environmental claims – and why it could set an example well beyond France.

Less resolute is the UK. It has approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea – without any requirement to address the emissions from actually burning the gas. CHRIS HILSON (ENG) argues that the government waits where it should push, on scope 3 and scope 1 emissions alike.

The Bundestag, by contrast, is done waiting. It is currently debating stricter rules in the Associations Act to keep out the influence of foreign states, or even terrorist organisations. PHILIPP OVERKAMP (GER) analyses the planned special rules for “foreign associations” and shows why they are legally problematic and do little for security.

A similar diagnosis applies to a new regulation in the north: with immediate effect, Bremen bans religious symbols and religiously connoted clothing in the police service. ADIL DEMIRKOL (GER) explains why the regulation is incompatible with federal law.

Incompatible with EU law, on the other hand, is the General Equal Treatment Act, which is no longer a teenager. Twenty years after its entry into force, it is finally to be reformed to protect those affected more effectively against discrimination. Yet the draft only partly lives up to that promise, concludes FABRIZIA VON STOSCH (GER).

This week, our symposium “Thinking Machines, Thinking Lawyers” (ENG) is drawing to a close. GAURAV MUKHERJEE and TUHIN CHAKRABARTY ask what it actually means to “think like a lawyer” – and what we lose when lawyers let LLMs do their writing for them. YOAN HERMSTRÜWER and ALICE MARGARIA argue that computational methods may facilitate a form of estrangement valuable to qualitative and, in particular, ethnographic inquiry: they can help make the familiar strange. JAKE GOLDENFEIN traces how AI firms have entered the contest over who gets to profit from information.

And another symposium: “Reflexive Globalisation and the Law: Expanding and Deepening its Understanding” (ENG) kicked off with the inaugural Sharifu Lecture of the RefLex Centre at HU Berlin, in which B. S. Chimni of Jindal Global Law School spoke about “Different Pasts, Multiple Presents: Towards a Materialist History of Imperialism and International Law”. The first contribution comes from THEUNIS ROUX, who argues that globalisation did more than spread Western constitutionalism: it also transformed it into an open, experimental tradition.

Norwegian toilet architecture can pass for an open, experimental tradition, too. This specimen – all gold, soaring, with a red door – looks like something Trump might actually enjoy. Worth a trip after all?

That’s it for this week. Take care and all the best!

item.content:encoded:
Wenn man den Umfrageinstituten noch trauen darf, steht den Demokraten am kommenden Dienstag ein ziemlich guter Wahlabend bevor. Im ganzen Land liegen demokratische Kandidat:innen entweder vorn oder liefern sich mit ihren republikanischen Konkurrent:innen ein Kopf-an-Kopf-Rennen. Dass die Partei des Präsidenten bei den Midterms an Zustimmung verliert – oft sogar deutlich –, gehört zu den verlässlichsten Mustern der US-Politik. Eine solche „Blue Wave“ sollte aber weder als Abrechnung mit den Republikanern noch als Blankoscheck für die Demokraten missverstanden werden. Sie wäre vielmehr ein Zeichen dafür, dass die amerikanische Demokratie zumindest einige ihrer Versprechen einlösen kann – wenn auch nicht alle.

Demokratie ist eben nicht nur die Herrschaft der Mehrheit. Sie ist auch ein Kontrollsystem, das ein Mindestmaß an Verantwortlichkeit zwischen den Regierenden und den Regierten garantieren soll. Gemessen daran ist die amerikanische Demokratie quicklebendig – und das trotz der vielfältigen, anhaltenden und strategischen Angriffe auf ihr Wahlsystem. Und solche Angriffe gibt es viele, einige waren sogar erfolgreich. So hat etwa der Supreme Court Anfang des Jahres Paragraf 2 des Voting Rights Act von 1965 entkernt – und damit deutlich erschwert, gegen Wahlkreiszuschnitte vorzugehen, die die Stimmen von Minderheiten verwässern. Oder man denke an die Versuche der Regierung, die Regeln für die Briefwahl und für Wählerregistrierung zu manipulieren, oder ganz aktuell an die absurden Klagen in Kalifornien und Alaska. In Kalifornien versucht die Regierung, rund 20.000 Stimmen für ungültig erklären zu lassen. Weiter nördlich in Alaska gelang es den Demokraten in einer ziemlich bizarren Wendung offenbar, den Vierer-Wahlzettel des Bundesstaates mit einem weiteren Kandidaten zu überfüllen, der genau denselben Namen wie der republikanische Kandidat trägt: Dan Sullivan. Nun versucht die Regierung, eine mögliche Bestätigung eines demokratischen Siegers zu verhindern, aufgrund der potenziellen Verwechslungen unter republikanischen Wählern. Es ist unwahrscheinlich, dass beide Klagen Erfolg haben werden. Jurist:innen kritisieren sie treffend als „präventive Wahlbeeinflussung“ (eine Bezeichnung, die wohl auch auf das Manöver von Dan Sullivan passt).

Präsident Trump ist mit Versprechen ins Weiße Haus zurückgekehrt, die über ideologische und parteipolitische Grenzen hinweg Anklang fanden. Einer Wähler:innenschaft, die unter explodierenden Lebenshaltungskosten leidet, sich (ob zu Recht oder nicht) über „unkontrollierte“ Zuwanderung sorgt und vom neoliberalen Status quo enttäuscht ist, sagte er ein billigeres Leben, ein Ende der Kriege im Ausland und eine geschlossene Südgrenze zu. Kurzum: America first. Zwei Jahre später straft die Wähler:innenschaft Trump indes ab: Die Unzufriedenheit mit seiner Inflationspolitik hat ein Rekordhoch erreicht, ebenso wie die Empörung über die brutale Willkür, mit der schlecht ausgebildete und maskierte ICE-Agent:innen sowohl gegen Eingewanderte als auch gegen US-Bürger:innen vorgehen. Benzin kostet wieder über vier Dollar die Gallone (das sind 3,8 Liter) – über einen Dollar mehr als vor einem Jahr. Trump hat immer wieder durchblicken lassen, dass ihm bezahlbare Lebenshaltungskosten schlicht egal sind. Und gleichzeitig zieht er das Land in den nächsten langwierigen und extrem kostspieligen Krieg hinein, diesmal im Iran. Die Wähler:innen scheinen nun mit all jenen Kongressmitgliedern abrechnen zu wollen, die mehr auf die Parteilinie oder das eigene Portemonnaie bedacht sind als auf das Wohl ihrer Wähler:innen. Schließlich hat die Politik kaum etwas unternommen, um den Druck auf die Bevölkerung zu lindern: Im Schnitt arbeiten US-Amerikaner:innen rund 1.800 Stunden im Jahr (zum Vergleich: in Deutschland sind es etwa 1.340) und kämpfen trotzdem zunehmend damit, über die Runden zu kommen.

++++++++++Anzeige++++++++++++++

Hier brennt noch Licht.

Irgendwo liest gerade jemand den Verfassungsblog. Morgens um zehn, nachts um eins. Vor einer Klausur, vor Gericht, nach der neuesten Volte eines verkorksten Gesetzgebungsverfahrens. Rund um die Uhr liest oder schreibt hier jemand. 716 Leser:innen spenden bereits regelmäßig, damit hier das Licht anbleibt. Bis Mitte Januar brauchen wir 1.000.

Werden Sie Teil der Verfassungsblog-Community: ab 5 Euro im Monat, jederzeit kündbar. Diesen Raum offenhalten: Jetzt spenden

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Eine solche „Denkzettel-Wahl“ ist nicht zu unterschätzen. Doch Demokratie verspricht mehr als bloße Denkzettel. Demokratie jenseits der Verhinderung völliger Abwege basiert auf Repräsentation: Die von uns Gewählten sollen unsere Interessen vertreten. Unsere Entscheidungen an der Wahlurne sollen das konkrete Regierungshandeln so lenken, dass es auf unsere im Wahlakt ausgedrückten Bedürfnisse und Forderungen eingeht. In diesem Punkt liefert die amerikanische Demokratie schon seit längerem nicht mehr wirklich. Trump hat dieses Versagen daher in eine erfolgreiche Wahlkampfstrategie verwandelt – mit seinem Versprechen, den „Sumpf trockenzulegen“ (drain the swamp).

Demokraten in hart umkämpften Wahlkreisen haben daraus gelernt. Viele bestreiten ihren Wahlkampf mit genau derselben populistischen Botschaft, die Trump vor zwei Jahren ins Amt brachte. Frei von direkter Regierungsverantwortung sind es nun die Demokraten, die die Trump-Regierung für hohe Lebenshaltungskosten und Korruption kritisieren und anprangern, wie Eliten – insbesondere der Präsident und seine Familie – Politik auf Kosten der einfachen Leute machen. Ob Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, James Talarico in Texas oder Adam Hamilton in Kansas (einem Bundesstaat, der seit 1932 keinen Demokraten mehr in den Senat entsandt hat): Sie alle setzen auf diesen Kurs. Das hat so gut funktioniert, dass selbst traditionell konservative und umkämpfte Bundesstaaten („Red und Purple States“) für die Republikaner zu Zitterpartien geworden sind.

Trotz gemeinsamer wirtschaftspopulistischer Agenden ticken diese Kandidat:innen bei wichtigen Themen völlig unterschiedlich – sowohl untereinander als auch im Vergleich zu ihrer eigenen Partei. Sie inszenieren sich weniger als klassisches Aushängeschild der Demokratischen Partei, sondern als Rebellen gegen das eigene Establishment. El-Sayed, praktizierender Muslim, Rhodes-Stipendiat und Sohn ägyptischer Einwanderer, positionierte sich als kompromissloser Progressiver und gewann eine schmutzige Vorwahl gegen den etablierteren Rivalen. Talarico, Abgeordneter und christlicher Pastor, spricht ebenso unverhohlen über seinen Glauben wie über marode Schulen und Supermarktrechnungen und tourt mit einem Slogan durch Texas, den er sich von einer Football-TV-Serie geliehen hat. Hamilton, methodistischer Pfarrer und Gründer der größten Gemeinde des Landes, wirbt um eine überwiegend ländliche Wähler:innenschaft, indem er auf einen „Populismus der Anständigkeit“ setzt.

Gemeinsam entwerfen diese Figuren eine amerikanische Identität, die wesentlich komplexer ist als jene enge Schablone der Trump-Regierung. Amerika ist eine Einwanderungsgesellschaft mit stark progressiven Metropolen. Zugleich ist es ein sehr religiöses, speziell christlich geprägtes Land. Und es ist tief gespalten zwischen urbanen und ländlichen Lebenswelten, die ganz unterschiedliche Interessen haben. Die erfolgreichen demokratischen Kandidat:innen kaschieren diese Widersprüche nicht. Sie sprechen bestimmte Regionen in deren eigener Sprache an – und haben dabei im Blick, was Menschen in Michigan, Texas oder Kansas konkret brauchen. Das klingt ganz anders als die spaltende Ausgrenzungspolitik von Trump und vielen republikanischen Kandidat:innen.

Trumps Identitätspolitik stützt sich auf ein exklusives, ethno-nationalistisches „Wir“, geboren aus weißem Groll und Kulturkampf, kombiniert mit einem hyper-libertären Wirtschaftscredo, das nur die gesellschaftliche Spitze belohnt. Die völkischen Bewegungen des letzten Jahrhunderts wussten wenigstens noch, dass Zugehörigkeit ihren Preis hat: Sie mussten die eigene Gruppe mit sozialem Status, Arbeitsplätzen und Sozialleistungen entlohnen. Die Trump-Regierung wollte zwar die Früchte der Identitätspolitik ernten, ließ aber ihre extrem diverse Anhängerschaft wirtschaftlich im Regen stehen. Dass sich die Wähler:innen jetzt abwenden, ist also keine Absage an den weißen Ethno-Nationalismus als solchen. Viele haben 2024 wohl eher trotz als wegen der ethnonationalistischen Ausrichtung republikanisch gewählt. Wenn überhaupt, dann zeigt das Bröckeln dieser Allianz, dass Trump eine historische Chance vertan hat: Er hätte eine republikanische Mehrheit zementieren können, und zwar mit einer sozialkonservativen, aber ethnisch diversen Koalition, die auf wirtschaftliche Entlastung setzt – in einem Land, das schon bald mehrheitlich nicht-weiß sein wird.

++++++++++Anzeige++++++++++++

.
Ob Geheimdienstreform, Palantir oder Anti-Terror-Maßnahmen, das Straf- und Sicherheitsrecht steht ständig vor neuen Herausforderungen. Das VB Security & Crime Dossier ordnet einmal im Monat die zentralen Entwicklungen für Sie ein: ein Kommentar an der Schnittstelle von Verfassungs-, Straf- und Sicherheitsrecht, ein Überblick über die laufenden Debatten sowie unser „Aktenvermerk” als kompakter Impuls. Fundiert zusammengefasst, direkt in Ihr Postfach.
.
Jetzt kostenlos abonnieren: https://verfassungsblog.de/newsletter-mpi/

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Doch angenommen, diese demokratischen Kandidaten gewinnen: Könnten sie ihre Versprechen einlösen? Könnten sie den Frust, die Wut und die tiefe Enttäuschung lindern, die das amerikanische Experiment seit Jahren lähmen? Wohl kaum, solange echte Fortschritte von neuer Gesetzgebung abhängen. Sichern sich die Demokraten lediglich das Repräsentantenhaus, ist parlamentarischer Stillstand garantiert. Der Filibuster erlaubt es 41 Senator:innen, nahezu jede Gesetzesvorlage zu blockieren. Selbst wenn die Demokraten überraschend eine Mehrheit im Senat erzielen sollten, drohen das Veto des Präsidenten und ein Supreme Court, der progressive Gesetze offen verachtet. Das realistischere Szenario: zwei Jahre Anhörungen und Stillstand statt billigerer Lebensmittel oder sinkender Mieten – gefolgt von einem Präsidentschaftswahlkampf 2028, in dem sich beide Seiten gegenseitig die Schuld in die Schuhe schieben.

Für die Demokraten ist es jetzt dennoch entscheidend, im Senat zuzulegen. Nur so können sie gesetzgeberische Erfolge nach 2028 vorbereiten. Senator:innen werden für sechs Jahre gewählt, alle zwei Jahre wird ein Drittel der Kammer neu besetzt. Deshalb bestimmen die diesjährigen Ergebnisse jenen Senat, mit dem ein künftiger demokratischer Präsident arbeiten müsste. Die Ausgangslage für 2026 wirkte anfangs schlecht für die Demokraten, da viele wackelige Sitze in tiefroten Staaten lagen. Doch das für die Republikaner mittlerweile toxische nationale Klima hat das Blatt gewendet. Die miserablen Umfragewerte der Regierung bedrohen nun plötzlich auch solche Senator:innen, die vor wenigen Monaten noch als unantastbar galten. Dieses Momentum wird sich 2028 vermutlich nicht wiederholen, da Trump nicht nochmal antreten kann und die Demokraten 2028 viele eigene umkämpfte Sitze verteidigen müssen. Selbst wenn das Weiße Haus 2028 also an die Demokraten gehen sollte – breite regierungsfähige Mehrheiten im Kongress entscheiden sich maßgeblich bereits jetzt bei den Midterms.

Die so entstandene Aufbruchsstimmung auf demokratischer Seite erscheint kraftvoll. Doch selbst wenn sich die Aufbruchs- oder gar Wechselstimmung in Mehrheiten manifestieren sollte, droht Washingtons institutionelle Architektur einen Großteil dieser Energie in den nächsten zwei Jahren zu ersticken. Die US-Wähler:innen stecken momentan in einer Zwickmühle. Sie können zwar verändern, wer regiert, aber kaum, was die Regierung tut. Wahlen verschaffen ihnen nach wie vor die Genugtuung, unbeliebte Politiker:innen zum Teufel zu jagen. Doch echten politischen Wandel, der auf ihre Bedürfnisse eingeht, können die Wähler:innen zumindest bei diesen Wahlen kaum bewirken.

Auf Dauer lehrt das die Wähler:innen eine bittere Lektion: Ein Stimmzettel taugt im besten Fall als Warnschuss, aber nicht zu echter Interessenrepräsentation oder gar self-governance. Reife Demokratien können genau auf diese Weise zerfallen – oder verrotten, wie Jack Balkin es nannte –, Stück für Stück, ganz ohne dramatischen Bruch. Es genügt eine lange Reihe von Wahlen, bei denen zwar das Führungspersonal rotiert, aber im Grunde alles beim Alten bleibt. Eine Blue Wave würde beweisen, dass die US-Amerikaner:innen ihre Regierung sehr wohl zur Rechenschaft ziehen können. Ob die Midterms darüber hinaus viel bewirken, bleibt zweifelhaft. Das gilt vor allem für die Lebenshaltungskosten und den Iran-Krieg – und für die Hoffnung, das verlorene Vertrauen in einen funktionierenden Staat wiederherzustellen.

*

Editor’s Pick

von MAXIMILIAN STEINBEIS

Copyright: Maximilian Steinbeis

Über Emmanuel Carrère bin ich vor kurzem auf Eduard Limonov und darüber auf Zakhar Prilepins quasi-autobiografischen Roman „Sankya“ gestoßen: einen Roman über einen jungen Russen in den 90er Jahren, den die Wut und der Widerstand gegen den korrupten russischen Staatsapparat in den Terrorismus treiben. Heute steht Prilepin als anti-ukrainischer Propagandist in Wladimir Putins autoritären Diensten und auf der Sanktionsliste der Europäischen Union, und ein Fascho-Kleinverlag hat kürzlich eine Neuauflage von „Sankya“ herausgebracht. Warum ein Buch eines solchen Autors lesen? Noch dazu ein Buch über einen brutalen nationalistischen Schlägertypen, der für Demokratie und Menschenrechte nichts als Hass und Verachtung übrig hat? Den man irgendwie… versteht? Der einem geradezu ans Herz wächst? Würde ich das auch lesen wollen, wenn es ein Nazi aus Eisenhüttenstadt wäre, von dem da die Rede ist? Und wenn nein: warum eigentlich nicht?

Zakhar Prilepin: Sankya, Matthes & Seitz 2012, 362 S.

*

Die Woche auf dem Verfassungsblog

zusammengefasst von EVA MARIA BREDLER

Falls Sie für das Jahresende noch Urlaub zu verplanen haben, wie wäre es mit Norwegen? Das skandinavische Land wurde am Sonntag von Trump zum jüngsten „Shithouse Country“ gekürt, nachdem ihm wieder einmal der Friedensnobelpreis vorenthalten worden war. Norwegen reagiert humorvoll und macht daraus kurzerhand eine Werbekampagne für seine – tatsächlich ziemlich hübschen – Toilettenhäuschen.

Wer weniger strenge Designanforderungen an den stillen Ort stellt, kann auch in die USA reisen – oder wer als unterlegener, potenziell korrupter Präsidentschaftskandidat Asyl sucht: Weniger als zwei Tage nach der Wahl hat sich Flávio Bolsonaro in die USA abgesetzt, nachdem ein Gericht ihm zuvor den Pass entzogen und die Ausreise untersagt hatte. THOMAS BUSTAMANTE und EMILIO PELUSO NEDER MEYER (EN) zeichnen nach, wie Lula eine deutliche Niederlage im ersten Wahlgang noch drehen konnte, vor allem dank einer organisierten Zivilgesellschaft.

Demokratischer Widerstand war auch bei den Wahlen in Serbien entscheidend. Am 25. Oktober hat die Studentische Liste dort die absolute Mehrheit im Parlament gewonnen. Wie in Polen und Ungarn hatte die Regierungspartei auch in Serbien Gerichte und andere Schlüsselinstitutionen unter ihre Kontrolle gebracht. BOJAN SPAIĆ und M. VICTORIA KRISTAN (EN) zeigen, was Serbien mit dieser Wahl hinter sich lassen kann.

Was Serbien hinter sich lässt, könnte Kanada noch bevorstehen: Das 2025 gegründete Projekt „Restoring the Foundations of Judicial Power“ will nun den „Common Good Constitutionalism“ nach Kanada bringen. Was erstmal gut gemeinwohlig klingt, ist laut DAVID DYZENHAUS (EN) jedoch ein antipluralistisches Projekt – er erkennt darin die Taktik, mit der Orbán und die PiS ihre illiberale Demokratie errichtet haben.

Um die illiberale Demokratie in Sachsen-Anhalt zu verhindern, will die CDU nun bei der geheimen Ministerpräsidentenwahl den Saal verlassen: So kann es keine Stimmen aus den eigenen Reihen für den AfD-Kandidaten geben. Warum werden Regierungschefs überhaupt geheim gewählt, fragt MARKUS LEBER (DE) – und fordert, dies abzuschaffen.

Abschaffen will Frankreich die Werbung für fossile Brennstoffe. Das Verbot steht schon im Gesetz. Am 2. Oktober hat der Conseil d’État die Regierung daran erinnert, dass sie es auch durchsetzen muss, und zwar mit klaren Regeln. MARTA TORRE-SCHAUB (EN) erklärt, was die Entscheidung für das Verhältnis von Klimaschutz, unternehmerischer Freiheit und Greenwashing bedeutet, und warum sie über Frankreich hinaus Schule machen könnte.

Weniger entschlossen ist Großbritannien. Die Regierung hat das Gasfeld Jackdaw in der Nordsee genehmigt, ohne Auflagen für die Emissionen, die beim Verbrennen des Gases entstehen. CHRIS HILSON (EN) meint: Die Regierung wartet ab, wo sie Druck machen müsste, bei Scope-3- wie bei Scope-1-Emissionen.

++++++++++Anzeige++++++++++++

Owning the Past: The Omnipresence of Divergent Historical Narratives in Law and Politics

Edited by Angelika Nußberger and Paula Rhein-Fischer 

“‘Owning the Past’ shows the importance of investigating history, memory laws, and politics not as separate but closely intertwined fields of research. Drawing from various disciplines, this edited volume elaborates in a comparative perspective how the way of remembering the past shapes significantly domestic and foreign policy of our present and future. A most timely and compelling publication!”

– Fabian Klose, University of Cologne

Get your copy here – as always, Open Access!

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Nicht länger abwarten will dagegen der Bundestag. Er berät derzeit eine Verschärfung des Vereinsgesetzes, um ausländische (gar terroristische) Einflüsse zu verhindern. PHILIPP OVERKAMP (DE) analysiert die geplanten Sonderregeln für Ausländervereine und zeigt, warum sie rechtlich problematisch und sicherheitspolitisch wenig zielführend sind.

Eine ähnliche Diagnose ließe sich auch neuen bremischen Regelungen stellen. Ab sofort verbietet Bremen religiöse Symbole und religiös konnotierte Kleidungsstücke im Polizeidienst. ADIL DEMIRKOL (DE) erklärt, warum die Verordnung nicht mit dem Bundesrecht vereinbar ist.

Mit Unionsrecht nicht vereinbar ist dagegen das Allgemeine Gleichbehandlungsgesetz, das inzwischen kein Teenager mehr ist. Zwanzig Jahre nach seinem Inkrafttreten soll es nun endlich reformiert werden, um Betroffene effektiver vor Diskriminierung zu schützen. Doch diesem Anspruch wird der Entwurf nur teilweise gerecht, resümiert FABRIZIA VON STOSCH (DE).

Unser Symposium „Thinking Machines, Thinking Lawyers“ (EN) nähert sich dem Ende. GAURAV MUKHERJEE und TUHIN CHAKRABARTY fragen, was es eigentlich heißt, „wie Jurist:innen zu denken“, und was verloren geht, wenn Jurist:innen ihre Texte von großen Sprachmodellen schreiben lassen. YOAN HERMSTRÜWER und ALICE MARGARIA zeigen, dass computergestützte Methoden eine Art „Verfremdung“ ermöglichen, von der qualitative und gerade ethnografische Forschung profitieren kann: Sie lassen das Vertraute fremd erscheinen. JAKE GOLDENFEIN zeichnet nach, wie KI-Unternehmen in den Streit darüber eingestiegen sind, wer an Informationen verdienen darf.

Und ein weiteres Symposium: „Reflexive Globalisation and the Law: Expanding and Deepening its Understanding“ (EN) hat mit der ersten Sharifu Lecture des RefLex-Zentrums an der HU Berlin begonnen. B. S. Chimni von der Jindal Global Law School sprach darin über eine materialistische Geschichte von Imperialismus und Völkerrecht („Different Pasts, Multiple Presents“). Der erste Beitrag kommt von THEUNIS ROUX. Er argumentiert, dass die Globalisierung den westlichen Konstitutionalismus nicht nur verbreitet, sondern auch verändert hat: hin zu einer offenen, experimentellen Tradition.

Auch die norwegische Toilettenarchitektur kann als offene, experimentelle Tradition durchgehen. Dieses Exemplar – ganz in Gold, aufstrebend, mit roter Tür – sieht so aus, als könnte es Trump gut gefallen. Vielleicht doch eine Reise wert?

item.content:encoded:
African constitutionalism is often approached through the language of reception. International human rights standards are incorporated into constitutions, treaties are given domestic effect, courts draw upon international jurisprudence, and regional instruments adapt international commitments to African contexts. Yet this perspective leaves a fundamental question unresolved: What happens to the legal meaning of an international norm when it is interpreted and applied within an African constitutional or regional order?

This post argues that African constitutionalism should be understood not simply as a practice of reception, but also as a practice of legal translation. International norms, understood here as norms embodied in, or derived from, positive international law, including treaty obligations, internationally recognised rights, and rules and principles of international law, are therefore not treated as abstract claims of universal validity. Rather, the argument concerns how legally recognised norms acquire meaning through their interpretation and application across different legal orders. Legal translation denotes the process through which an international norm acquires a distinct juridical meaning when situated within another normative and institutional environment. The focus thus shifts from the movement of norms across legal systems to the transformation of their meaning through that movement. As such, reception concerns entry, whereas translation concerns reconstruction, circulation concerns the movement of a reconstructed meaning, and feedback concerns the circumstances in which that meaning subsequently acquires legal significance beyond its original setting. Decolonisation gives this process its epistemic dimension by asking who is recognised as capable of producing legal meaning.

Reception is Not Translation

The movement of norms across legal orders has long been examined through concepts such as legal transplants, vernacularisation, localisation, and norm diffusion.1) These approaches demonstrate that norms do not necessarily travel unchanged. Legal translation builds on this insight but places particular emphasis on their juridical reconstruction. A norm may be formally received while the relationships, assumptions, and legal consequences through which it operates are reconfigured in its new setting. Translation is therefore distinct from reception, asking not simply whether a norm has entered a legal order, but what legal meaning it acquires there.

In the African context, this process can be observed at two interconnected levels. Constitutional translation occurs when international norms are interpreted through constitutional texts, principles, institutions, and domestic adjudication. Regional translation occurs when African regional institutions situate internationally recognised rights and obligations within distinctive regional frameworks and forms of legal reasoning. African legal orders consequently become not only sites of implementation but also sites of juridical meaning-making.

From Reception to Translation

African constitutions establish different institutional pathways through which international law enters constitutional reasoning. For example, Article 2(5) of the Constitution of Kenya provides that the general rules of international law form part of Kenyan law, while Article 2(6) gives ratified treaties and conventions domestic status. The Constitution of South Africa adopts a different approach, with section 39(1)(b) requiring courts to consider international law in interpreting the Bill of Rights, while section 233 directs courts interpreting legislation to prefer interpretations consistent with international law. Such provisions do more than determine the domestic status of international law; they create institutional conditions in which international norms can acquire constitutional meaning.

South African jurisprudence illustrates this process through the use of ubuntu. For example, in Dikoko v Mokhatla, the Constitutional Court connected the concept with human dignity guaranteed by the South African Constitution but also recognised as a human right in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).2) Ubuntu thus operates not merely as a cultural reference but as a resource for constitutional reasoning. Its significance lies in the way it participates in determining the relationships among constitutional values, including dignity and the interests of communities affected by the exercise of property rights. The point is not that ubuntu itself constitutes or replaces an international norm. Rather, an African normative resource participates in the constitutional interpretation through which internationally recognised rights acquire concrete juridical meaning within a particular legal order.

A similar process can be observed at the regional level. While the rights to property (article 17 UDHR), health (articles 1 and 12 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights) and the “right of peoples to dispose of their wealth” (article 1 of the ICCPR) are firmly anchored in international human rights law, their corresponding provisions in the African Charter, the African Commission treats these rights not merely as separate guarantees. For example, in Social and Economic Rights Action Center (SERAC) and Center for Economic and Social Rights v Nigeria, the Commission interpreted them in an interconnected manner in assessing the environmental destruction in the Niger Delta of southern Nigeria.3) Environmental harm was therefore understood through its cumulative and communal effects on a broader constellation of individual and collective rights. This approach was not a practice of mere compliance, nor did the Commission create new rights. Instead, it transcended international fragmentation by establishing a specific, relational framework between environmental protection, health, property, natural resources, and collective interests. Ultimately, SERAC demonstrates how an African regional institution can give concrete, autonomous juridical content to universally recognised human rights through an interpretation shaped by the specific institutional and normative context of the African Charter.

The Endorois and Ogiek jurisprudence develops this relational approach further. In Enorois, the Commission addressed the relationship between land, culture, property, development, and community rights. Rather than treating these rights as separate guarantees, the Commission examined the community’s displacement from its ancestral land through their combined effects on cultural identity, property, development, and access to resources.4) The African Court’s Ogiek judgment likewise connected land, culture, natural resources, and collective interests, treating the protection of the community’s ancestral territory as closely connected to the preservation of its cultural and collective life.5) These cases illustrate legal translation not simply because African institutions applied internationally recognised rights, but because they articulated their juridical significance through relationships among individual, collective, cultural, developmental, and land-related interests. The relevant rights were therefore not merely reproduced in their abstract for their application was reconstructed through the particular normative and institutional configuration of the African regional human rights system.

From Translation to Circulation and Feedback

Translation does not necessarily produce legal influence beyond the order in which it occurs. A meaning reconstructed within an African constitutional or regional order may remain confined to that setting, influence neighbouring jurisdictions, or circulate internationally without acquiring legal significance. This makes circulation distinct from translation. Circulation refers to the movement of a translated legal meaning beyond the order in which it was first articulated, whether through judicial citation, regional jurisprudence, treaty-body reasoning, State practice, legislation, international litigation, or institutional uptake. It is related to judicial dialogue, but the concepts are not identical as dialogue concerns interaction among legal actors, whereas circulation entails the movement of meaning across legal orders.

Circulation alone, however, does not establish that African legal reasoning has influenced international law. A judgment may be cited abroad without acquiring authority, and a concept may become internationally visible without affecting the interpretation of a legal obligation. Feedback requires legal uptake in a process capable of influencing the interpretation, application, or development of international law. The possibility of such feedback rests on ordinary processes of international legal interpretation. Article 31 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties requires treaties to be interpreted in good faith according to the ordinary meaning of their terms, in their context and in light of their object and purpose. Article 31(3)(c) further requires consideration of relevant rules of international law applicable between the parties.6) Treaty interpretation therefore takes place within a broader normative environment.

African legal practice may become part of that environment where its interpretations, treaty practice, or state practice enters processes capable of influencing legal reasoning beyond the context in which they originated. Once taken up in judicial interpretation, regional jurisprudence, international litigation, treaty practice, or other legally consequential settings, a meaning generated within an African legal order may acquire relevance to the further interpretation or development of international law. African investment treaty practice provides a useful illustration. For example, the Morocco–Nigeria Bilateral Investment Treatylinks investment protection to environmental and human-rights considerations. The African Continental Free Trade Area Investment Protocol embeds regulatory autonomy and sustainable development within investment governance. What is distinctive is their explicit integration of these objectives into the design of African investment rules, rather than treating them solely as external constraints on investment protection.7)

Their significance lies in showing how internationally recognised legal commitments can be recombined within African treaty instruments and potentially enter wider processes of transnational legal reasoning. Feedback should therefore not be understood as a reversal of legal influence. It describes the possibility that meanings generated within African legal practice may travel beyond their original setting and, when legally taken up, contribute to the continuing interpretation and development of international law. By framing authority as relational and co-constituted across jurisdictions, this approach moves past a rigid, unidirectional model of influence, highlighting circulation as a dynamic process where legal meanings are constantly rearticulated across geographic boundaries.8)

Decolonisation

The decolonial significance of this architecture lies in its directionality. When international legal norms are presumed to possess their authoritative meaning before entering African legal orders, African law is positioned as secondary by being relegated to receiving, implementing, adapting, or resisting norms whose meaning has already been determined elsewhere. Legal translation unsettles this hierarchy by drawing attention to the interpretive processes through which meaning is reconstructed within African constitutional and regional orders. Decolonisation, from this perspective, does not require a return to precolonial forms of governance or a rejection of international law. It concerns the recognition of African constitutional and regional institutions as legitimate sites of legal meaning-making. African philosophies like ubuntu matter not as alternatives to law, but as active forces that shape legal interpretation and the application of constitutional rights. This also means that decolonisation should not simply reverse the direction of legal influence. The objective is neither to reproduce a hierarchy in which norms move outward from Europe or the Global North and are received in Africa, nor to construct an opposite hierarchy in which African meanings replace all others. It is to recognise a more plural process in which legal meaning is produced, translated, and circulated across international, regional, and constitutional orders, with each capable of contributing to its further development.

Conclusion

African constitutionalism has often been examined through the international norms it receives. That perspective, however, captures only one direction of legal movement. Reception concerns the entry of an international legal norm into an African legal order. Translation concerns its juridical reconstruction within that order. Circulation concerns the movement of that reconstructed meaning beyond its original setting. Feedback concerns the circumstances in which it subsequently acquires legal significance within wider processes of international legal interpretation or development. The central question is therefore not simply how Africa receives international law, but what happens to international law when Africa interprets it. African constitutionalism is neither a site of passive reception nor a self-contained legal order detached from international law. It is a practice of legal translation in which international legal norms encounter constitutional institutions, regional frameworks, and African normative resources, acquiring new juridical relationships in the process.

Some meanings may remain locally situated; others may circulate more widely and, through subsequent legal uptake, participate in the continuing development of international law. The decolonial implication is ultimately an epistemic one, whereby African legal orders should be understood not only as places where international law is implemented, but as sites from which legal meaning can emerge, travel, and potentially feed back into the international legal order.

Ultimately, this trajectory from translation to feedback epitomises the dynamics of reflexive globalisation at the heart of the RefLex research agenda. Legal orders can no longer be viewed as insulated spheres where norms simply travel in a unidirectional path from the global to the local. Instead, they constitute interconnected spaces where global norms shape domestic constitutional law, while domestic constitutional interpretations simultaneously contest, reconfigure, and potentially reconstruct the authority and meaning of global law. The African constitutional and regional experience demonstrates that globalisation is not merely a process of top-down dissemination, but a reflexive loop where the periphery actively co-constitutes the global legal order.

item.description:
What does a Bollywood soundtrack have to do with the future of constitutionalism? More than one might think. Just as Chutney music defies notions of cultural purity, constitutionalism has emerged from centuries of entanglement between Western and non-Western ideas. Challenging both Eurocentric histories and romanticised visions of an authentic indigenous past, the idea of confluence constitutionalism opens up a different path to decolonisation.

item.content:encoded:
In 2012, filmmaker Anurag Kashyap released “Gangs of Wasseypur”, a two-part Hindi film that depicts the trials, tribulations, and testaments of gang members from what is now the state of Jharkhand in eastern India. Based as it was on the real-life experiences of those involved with the coal mafia over seventy years spanning the colonial and post-colonial periods, the film endeavoured to authentically represent the socio-political landscape of Wasseypur and its neighbouring districts. In this spirit of authenticity, responsibility for the film’s music – which played a significant role in bringing it critical acclaim – was given to Sneha Khanwalkar, a young composer known for her distinctive blend of electronic and folk music. For “Wasseypur”, Khanwalkar, in her characteristic mode, left the confines of the “Bombay studio” and entered the “field” to learn, record, and represent the music of Bihar, the state from which Jharkhand was carved out in 2000.1) Through extensive travel, she constructed an “auditory archive” of Bihar,2)which she then used to compose tracks that critics have described as “strikingly flavourful and headily authentic.”3)

Interestingly, Khanwalkar’s travels for “Wasseypur” were not limited to the state of Bihar or the broader region of which it is a part. To trace back the sounds of the region from the colonial era, she travelled to the Caribbean, where many Biharis had been forcibly shipped to serve as indentured labour following the official ban on slavery in the British Empire. From the Caribbean, Khanwalkar brought to Indian audiences “Chutney music,” a Caribbean blend of Bihari music, which, as its name suggests, was born out of a fusion of Indian and Caribbean sounds and rhythms. Redolent of Salman Rushdie’s term “Chutnification,” Chutney music reminds us that “authentic” sounds – or, more broadly, authenticity – do not exist out there and beyond time. Instead, much like a chutney (a mix of herbs and spices), it is a blend of the old and the new, the colonial and the pre-colonial, the oriental and the occidental, and the global and the local.

Constitutional History and Theory as Already Chutnified

What does all of this have to do with constitutional law and the idea of reflexive globalisation? Recent decades have seen the rise of right-wing populists who have collectively ushered in a crisis of constitutionalism by disregarding the rule of law and championing a form of strongman politics. In this context, many in the Global North, being disgruntled with liberal legalism, have argued for a form of decolonising constitutionalism, at the core of which is the “imperative to go South and learn from the South.”4) In parallel, in the Global South, many, in support of their populist leaders, have advocated for a revivalist form of decolonial constitutionalism which seeks to rediscover an authentic, indigenous, and non-Western self.5) Despite their differences in terms of their political orientation and relations with state power, these approaches share two key presuppositions: firstly, they assume that constitutionalism, at its core, is of Northern/Western authorship; and secondly, they contend that the non-West exists in a museumised form, outside of time and space, thereby making a return to it possible.

Relying on the idea behind the Chutney, I challenge these two presuppositions and, in their place, advance a theory of decolonising constitutionalism that centres on the idea of “confluence constitutionalism.” The choice of the term confluence here is largely motivated by scholarship on confluence philosophy, championed by Arindam Chakrabarti and Ralph Weber, among others.6) As a method, confluence, unlike comparison, allows for dialogue across national and other imaginary boundaries and highlights the entangled nature of our present, in which ideas from all parts of the world have flowed into one another, often despite best efforts to keep them apart.

Using the lens of confluence, I question the standard genealogy of constitutionalism to open the possibility for the South to claim constitutionalism as part of its own legacy, while simultaneously proffering a mode of thinking about the future of constitutionalism that is neither indigenist nor parochial. Scholars of constitutional law and politics – acting either out of a sense of academic modesty prompted by a lack of knowledge of the non-West or following the received wisdom of colonial historiographers who were invested in describing Europe’s past and non-Europe’s present as dark and irredeemable – typically narrativise constitutionalism’s origin story by referring exclusively to what are considered Western sources.7) They either locate the emergence of contemporary constitutionalism exclusively in the modern revolutions in France and the United States,8) or draw a direct line from modern Euro-America to ancient Greece and Rome, which are together regarded as the birthplaces of constitutional thought.9)

Drawing on scholarship on connected histories and Eurocentrism,10) both of which emphasise the Chutnified nature of our past and present, I critique this narrative and, in so doing, redeem the place of the non-West/South in the history of constitutionalism. Relying on Aditya Nigam’s metaphor of modernity as a “constellation” composed of pre-existing elements,11) I contend that while the constitutive elements of modern constitutionalism were present both outside of the West and in the West, the crucial task of assembling them and giving them a bourgeois orientation took place in the West during the turn to modernity. In making this claim, I acknowledge modern Europe’s contributions to constitutionalism, while nonetheless recognising that modernity did not construct an entirely new politico-legal order but instead ushered in a new orientation towards existing political concepts.

In parallel, drawing on Samir Amin’s critique of Eurocentrism,12) I contend that Europe was never sequestered from the rest of the world in a way that would allow for an undisturbed pathway to be created between it and ancient Greece and Rome. Instead, being enmeshed in a broader landscape, European modernity was informed by a whole host of ideas, many of which flowed in from the East and got radicalised in the West. This entanglement only increased with colonialism, when those in the colonies mobilised, critiqued, and, in the process, transformed the received wisdom of modernity and modern constitutionalism.13) Acknowledging this movement of ideas helps recognise the syncretic nature of modern constitutionalism, while opening the door for its critique on universal rather than parochial grounds.

Decolonising Constitutionalism as Confluence Constitutionalism

Moving from the past to the future, I contend that once it is accepted that the history of contemporary constitutionalism is a product of a confluence of Western and non-Western thought(s), experiences, and institutions, a critique of it along lines of inauthenticity or lack of indigeneity becomes indefensible. In other words, if it is accepted that “no type of thinking [here, constitutionalism] can be considered purely ‘Western’ or purely ‘Indigenous’ without further scrutiny,”14) the road to an alternative constitutionalism – or even an anti-constitutionalism – from the South cannot take the form of performing an exorcism to rid the rest of the world of the West. Rather, alternative imaginings, be they presented from the West/North or the South, must proceed from a critique of constitutionalism that is itself universal in nature. Decolonising constitutionalism in this key cannot be a return to a pure past, for no such past exists. Rather, as Frantz Fanon put it in “The Wretched of the Earth”, it must be an attempt to “work out new concepts, and try to set afoot a new man.”15)

For the emergent task of re-imagining constitutionalism, the Global South has a historical advantage. In the South, where constitutionalism was not assembled and where its violence and limits are for all to see, alternative imaginings other than modern constitutionalism have always been afoot. These alternatives, examples of which include M.K. Gandhi’s 1939 constitution for the princely state of Aundh,16) exist as an archive of possibilities and as a source of inspiration for thinking otherwise. They remind us that modern constitutionalism is neither natural nor inevitable and that other futures can emerge “for Europe, for ourselves and for humanity.”17) Using the language of the Chutney, they suggest that the present mix that we refer to as constitutionalism is not the only recipe in town. Other ingredients can be added, and some can be taken out. In so doing, new mixes can be created, and through this, something altogether different can emerge.
