item.content:encoded:
The Centre for Advanced Studies “Reflexive Globalisation and the Law” (RefLex) at Humboldt University starts from the insight that legal globalisation cannot adequately be understood as a unidirectional process in which legal concepts and institutions developed in the Global North are exported to the rest of the world. Global legal development is increasingly characterised by multidirectional exchange, contestation and transformation, including a critical engagement with colonial legacies and enduring asymmetries in knowledge production.

In my book project, Liberal Constitutionalism and its Critics, I argue that liberal constitutionalism can be understood in similar terms. Critics associate it with five distinct pathologies: gross economic inequality, rampant individualism, democratic disempowerment, stubborn coloniality, and a dithering inability to confront existential challenges such as climate change. Its defenders, in turn, end up aiding and abetting these critiques by proceeding from a relatively fixed image of what a liberal constitution is: a familiar institutional package centred on rights, judicial review, separation of powers and limits on government. However, globalisation has not simply involved the diffusion of a Western constitutional model. It has also involved the transformation of the tradition itself. Liberal constitutionalism is no longer the hegemonic global governance ideology or model it used to be. Rather, it can be understood as an evolving, interpretively open, experimentalist tradition. Starting from these premises, my book engages the five critiques set out above.

In this blog post, I will first propose a definition of liberal constitutionalism as a tradition rather than a fixed governance ideology or model. Against this background, I will outline how I respond in my book to three of the five major criticisms identified above, that is the Left critique, the democratic critique, and the decolonial critique. I conclude with some reflections on how my book contributes to debates on the contemporary crisis of liberal constitutionalism and how it connects with the Centre’s concern for reflexive globalisation.

Defining Liberal Constitutionalism

My forthcoming book begins with a conceptual question: what is liberal constitutionalism? I argue that it is better understood as a tradition rather than a particular institutional configuration. Its central commitments – including freedom, equality, the rule of law, democratic government and constraints on arbitrary power – have never yielded a single, determinate institutional form. They have instead generated continuing arguments about how those commitments should be realised in changing social and political circumstances.

This matters because many contemporary criticisms of liberal constitutionalism implicitly take the classical US-American model as their point of reference. That model places particular emphasis on negative liberty, rights against government and strong-form judicial review. But liberal constitutionalism changed significantly after 1945. The German Basic Law, the Indian Constitution and, later, the South African Constitution are examples of a more programmatic form of liberal constitutionalism. These constitutions do not merely restrain the state. They also impose positive obligations, recognise socio-economic rights, pursue substantive equality, regulate private power, protect democratic participation and create institutions designed to sustain constitutional democracy.

Seen in this way, the history of liberal constitutionalism is a history of institutional experimentation. A remark in Frank Michelman’s “Constitutional Essentials” is helpful here because it conceives of liberal constitutionalism as an ongoing conversation about how political institutions should give practical meaning to liberal commitments.1) The relevant question is consequently not whether liberal constitutionalism has one correct institutional form, but how constitutional orders have responded to new problems and to criticism of existing arrangements.

The idea of liberal constitutionalism as a tradition changes how we should think about constitutional circulation. Constitutional ideas obviously do travel across borders, but they do not necessarily arrive intact. Rather, constitutional ideas are appropriated, translated, combined with local political traditions and sometimes radically re-signified. India and South Africa are especially important examples of this phenomenon. Their constitutions cannot adequately be understood simply as instances of the transplantation of European or US-American constitutionalism. They were produced through distinctive political struggles over colonialism, race, inequality, democracy and political membership. Their constitutional experiences have, in turn, contributed to wider understandings of what liberal constitutionalism might mean.

This perspective provides a distinctive way of addressing the major criticisms of liberal constitutionalism examined in my book. The point is not to refute them in turn. Rather, it is to use them as an opportunity to reflect on how liberal constitutionalism might address its internal contradictions and external challenges.

The Left Critique

Consider first the Left critique of liberal constitutionalism and inequality. One version of this critique holds that inequality is effectively “baked into” liberal constitutionalism because liberal freedom is intertwined with private property, market relations and the separation of the economic realm from the political.2) The South African experience, however, provides little support for such a strong claim. The 1996 Constitution contains extensive egalitarian resources: substantive equality, socio-economic rights, a property clause expressly linked to land reform and transformation, and mechanisms for regulating both public and private power. Post-1994 governments also used constitutional and policy instruments to reduce absolute deprivation and expand access to basic services and social security.

This does not mean that liberal constitutionalism has no responsibility for global economic inequality. But it does suggest a more contingent account has greater explanatory force: political choices, implementation failures, corruption, weak state capacity and the persistence of apartheid’s material legacy have all mattered. Even this account has limits. National constitutional orders operate within a global political economy characterised by mobile capital, investment pressures and competition for economic growth. The resulting scale mismatch helps explain why domestic constitutional resources cannot by themselves overcome all the forces generating inequality. The conclusion is therefore nuanced: inequality is neither intrinsic to liberal constitutionalism nor wholly within the capacity of national constitutional politics to eliminate.

The Democratic Critique

The book responds to the democratic critique of liberal constitutionalism in a similar way. Critics such as Mark Tushnet,3) Jeremy Waldron4) and Richard Bellamy5) have drawn attention to the democratic costs of constitutional rights adjudication, especially where courts possess strong authority to invalidate legislation. These criticisms have considerable force when directed at particular institutional arrangements. But they do not exhaust what courts do within contemporary programmatic constitutionalism. Courts can also protect democratic institutions themselves by requiring legislatures to comply with participation requirements, holding executives accountable and protecting independent institutions.

This suggests that republican constitutional theory and liberal constitutionalism need not be treated as mutually exclusive traditions. The republican concern with freedom from domination and meaningful participation has increasingly been incorporated into programmatic forms of liberal constitutionalism. There remains a genuine question about whether judicially enforced rights can sometimes displace political agency. But the relationship is not one of inherent opposition. Constitutional institutions can both constrain democratic politics and create conditions in which democratic citizenship is more meaningful.

The Decolonial Critique

The decolonial critique poses a still more fundamental challenge. It asks not simply whether liberal constitutional institutions work, but why the liberal concepts on which many postcolonial constitutions are based should be treated as universal.6) Liberal constitutionalism, on this view, emerged from the European Enlightenment, and its global spread was entangled with imperialism. However much they might have been adapted to local circumstances, postcolonial liberal constitutions therefore perpetuate epistemic hierarchies and forms of cultural and political power after formal colonial rule has ended.

The response developed in the book is not to deny that liberal constitutionalism draws significant resources from the Euro-American intellectual tradition. It is rather to argue that its Western origins do not settle the question of whether it can be appropriated and transformed elsewhere. Anti-colonial and postcolonial actors have repeatedly taken constitutional ideas developed elsewhere and made them their own. The Indian and South African constitutional experiences are important precisely because they complicate the distinction between imposition and appropriation. They raise the possibility that constitutional borrowing can be an exercise of political agency and that the meaning of liberal constitutional principles can change through their encounter with different histories and normative traditions.

This does not dispose of the decolonial critique: the possibility of colonial assumptions persisting within apparently emancipatory institutions remains an important object of scrutiny. But it does change its point of focus, away from assumed epistemicide to questions of political agency.

The Book’s Contribution to Debates on Reflexivity

Taken together, these arguments suggest a different way of understanding the contemporary crisis of liberal constitutionalism.7) The question is not whether liberal constitutionalism has failed once and for all, nor whether it should be defended as the world’s best form of government. My claim is more modest, but also more historically defensible. Liberal constitutionalism is a tradition whose ideals have generated continuing disagreement about institutional design, and whose institutional forms have changed in response to political struggle, criticism and changing circumstances.

That conception also changes how we should understand the globalisation of constitutional law. If liberal constitutionalism is a tradition, then its global history is not simply a story of diffusion from a Western centre to passive recipients. It is a history of circulation and transformation. Constitutional ideas move across borders, but they are altered in the process. The Global South is not merely a site in which liberal constitutionalism is implemented. It is also a site in which its meaning is contested and remade.

It is in this respect that the book’s argument connects most directly with the Centre’s concern for reflexive globalisation. The globalisation of constitutional ideas becomes reflexive when the process of circulation itself becomes an object of scrutiny: when legal traditions confront their own histories, when previously marginalised actors challenge inherited categories, and when the exchange of ideas changes both sides of the exchange. Liberal constitutionalism, understood as a tradition rather than a fixed model, is capable of precisely this kind of reflexivity.

The conclusion is not that liberal constitutionalism is universally applicable, or that it is necessarily preferable to all alternative traditions of political ordering. Nor does it follow that liberal constitutionalism imposed from the outside cannot be damaging. Popular support and local political struggle remain essential to constitutional legitimacy. The more limited claim is that liberal constitutionalism should not be understood as exclusively Western simply because many of its formative ideas originated in Europe. Its subsequent history has been shaped by actors and struggles far beyond Europe and North America.

The book’s broader purpose, then, is to change the terms of the debate between liberal constitutionalism and its critics. Criticism need not be understood only as an external challenge to a settled tradition. It can also be a source of constitutional learning. The Left critique exposes the limits of nationally bounded constitutionalism in a global political economy. The democratic critique forces attention to institutional forms that protect rather than displace democratic agency. The decolonial critique requires continuing interrogation of the tradition’s origins, categories and claims to universality.

None of this guarantees that liberal constitutionalism will remain politically influential, or that its principles will always be interpreted in emancipatory ways. It does, however, suggest that the tradition’s capacity for adaptation is part of what it is. Liberal constitutionalism has changed because political actors have contested it, appropriated it and forced it to confront problems that its earlier forms did not adequately address. Its future therefore depends less on defending a fixed institutional model than on maintaining the political and intellectual capacity to revise constitutional arrangements in light of experience.

In that sense, liberal constitutionalism may itself be an example of reflexive globalisation: a tradition that began in particular historical circumstances, travelled across borders, encountered radically different political and social worlds, and was repeatedly transformed through those encounters. The question for constitutional scholarship is not simply whether that tradition should be accepted or rejected. It is how we understand what it has become through its global circulation – and what it might yet become.

item.content:encoded:
Zwanzig Jahre nach Inkrafttreten des Allgemeinen Gleichbehandlungsgesetzes (AGG) soll es reformiert werden. Im Juni hat der Bundestag den Entwurf in erster Lesung beraten und an den Rechtsausschuss überwiesen. Dort wurde er am 5. Oktober in einer öffentlichen Anhörung diskutiert. Die Reform soll Betroffene effektiver vor Diskriminierung schützen, die Rechtsdurchsetzung stärken und offene Auslegungsfragen klären. Diesem Anspruch wird der Entwurf jedoch nur teilweise gerecht.

Hintergrund der Reform

Die Reform des AGG ist überfällig. Seit 2015 läuft wegen mangelhafter Umsetzung der Richtlinie 2004/113/EG (Gleichbehandlungsrichtlinie) ein Vertragsverletzungsverfahren der Europäischen Kommission gegen Deutschland. Außerdem hat die Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes das AGG 2017 evaluiert und konkrete Schutzlücken benannt. Anfang 2023 hat ein Bündnis aus rund 100 zivilgesellschaftlichen Organisationen eine Ergänzungsliste veröffentlicht. 2025 ist die Reform sodann auf die politische Agenda gekommen, denn der Koalitionsvertrag bekennt sich explizit zur Stärkung und Verbesserung des Diskriminierungsschutzes (S. 92, Rn. 2952-2954). Schließlich mussten die EU-Richtlinien 2024/1499 und 2024/1500 (Standardrichtlinien) bis zum 19. Juni 2026 in nationales Recht umgesetzt werden.

Was das AGG leisten soll

Neben den verschiedenen Richtlinien, die die Reform (teils unzureichend) umsetzen soll, ist ein wirksamer Diskriminierungsschutz auch verfassungsrechtlich determiniert. Dies folgt aus den Gleichheitsverbürgungen in Art. 3 GG. Im sogenannten Triage-Beschluss hat das Bundesverfassungsgericht klargestellt, dass sich für den Staat aus Art. 3 Abs. 3 S. 2 GG ein Auftrag ergibt, „Menschen wirksam davor zu schützen, wegen einer Behinderung benachteiligt zu werden“ (Rn. 89). Damit hat das Gericht die Schutzfunktion des Art. 3 Abs. 3 S. 2 GG adressiert. Die Schutzfunktion ist allen Grundrechten immanent (dazu auch Hong). Sie gilt daher auch für die übrigen Absätze und Sätze des Gleichheitsgrundrechts. Die Aussagen im Triage-Beschluss lassen sich folglich auf den gesamten Art. 3 GG übertragen. Art. 3 Abs. 2 GG formuliert sogar explizit den Auftrag an den Staat, auf die Beseitigung bestehender Nachteile zwischen Frauen und Männern hinzuwirken. Aber auch Art. 3 Abs. 3 S. 1 GG schützt seinem Sinn und Zweck nach diskriminierungsgefährdete Gruppen (Dritte Option, Rn. 50). Da Art. 3 Abs. 3 GG den allgemeinen Gleichheitssatz „konkretisiert und verstärkt“ (Teilzeitbeamter, Rn. 48), greift Art. 3 Abs. 1 GG schließlich als Auffangnorm für solche Diskriminierungskategorien, die in Art. 3 Abs. 2 und 3 GG nicht aufgeführt sind. Art. 3 GG verpflichtet den Staat folglich, Private umfassend vor Diskriminierung zu schützen.

Wirksamer Diskriminierungsschutz zahlt sich aus

Wirksamer Diskriminierungsschutz ist nicht nur verfassungsrechtlich geboten, sondern wirkt sich auch positiv auf die Wirtschaft aus. OECD-Daten zufolge führt Diskriminierung dazu, dass Menschen Tätigkeiten unterhalb ihrer Fähigkeiten ausüben, ihre Erwerbschancen verlieren oder geringere Anreize haben, in Ausbildung und Weiterbildung zu investieren. Dies reduziert das gesamtwirtschaftliche Produktionspotenzial (vgl. S. 72). Umgekehrt fördert ein effektiver Diskriminierungsschutz also die Produktionskapazitäten, was wiederum der Gesamtwirtschaft dient.

Was sich inhaltlich verbessert

Die Neufassung des § 3 AGG-E weitet den Schutz vor Benachteiligung wegen Schwangerschaft, Mutterschaft sowie vor sexueller Belästigung nun endlich auf den Zivilrechtsverkehr aus. Bislang schützt das AGG vor Benachteiligung wegen Schwangerschaft und Mutterschaft sowie vor sexueller Belästigung allein in Beschäftigungsverhältnissen (§ 3 Abs. 1 S. 2, Abs. 4 AGG) und nicht in anderen zivilrechtlichen Schuldverhältnissen. Diese Begrenzung ist sachlich nicht nachvollziehbar. Die strafrechtlichen Regelungen zum Schutz vor sexueller Belästigung genügen nicht, da sie allein körperliche Übergriffe erfassen. Auch §§ 280, 241 Abs. 2 BGB genügen nicht. Ein hieraus resultierender Entschädigungsanspruch ist – anders als § 15 Abs. 2 AGG – nicht verschuldensunabhängig. Außerdem findet die besondere Beweislastregelung des § 22 AGG keine Anwendung, die für den Rechtsschutz bei Diskriminierungen – und damit auch bei sexuellen Belästigungen – eine Erleichterung der Darlegungslast, eine Absenkung des Beweismaßes und eine Umkehr der Beweislast vorsieht (BAG, Urt. v. 29.1.2026 – 8 AZR 49/25, Rn. 25). Der fehlende Schutz vor sexueller Belästigung außerhalb von Beschäftigungsverhältnissen widerspricht zudem den unionsrechtlichen Vorgaben. Auf das diesbezügliche Vertragsverletzungsverfahren sei nochmals hingewiesen. Gemäß Art. 4 Abs. 1 lit. a), Abs. 3 der Richtlinie 2004/113/EG (Unisex-Richtlinie) ist der Schutz vor Benachteiligung wegen Schwangerschaft und Mutterschaft sowie vor sexueller Belästigung in Zivilrechtsverhältnissen sicherzustellen. Die vorgesehene Ergänzung ist insoweit überfällig.

Der Entwurf will den Schutz vor geschlechtsbezogener Diskriminierung auch im Übrigen ausweiten. § 19 Abs. 2 AGG verbietet bei zivilrechtlichen Schuldverhältnissen im Sinne des § 2 Abs. 1 Nr. 5 bis 8 AGG bislang lediglich eine Benachteiligung wegen der „Rasse“ oder wegen der ethnischen Herkunft. Für die übrigen Diskriminierungsmerkmale gilt der Schutz nur für sogenannte Massengeschäfte, also für solche, die ohne Ansehen der Person in einer Vielzahl von Fällen zu vergleichbaren Bedingungen zustande kommen (§ 19 Abs. 1 Nr. 1 AGG). Künftig soll die geschlechtsbezogene Diskriminierung für Schuldverhältnisse im Sinne des § 2 Abs. 1 Nr. 8 AGG, also den Zugang zu und die Versorgung mit Gütern und Dienstleistungen, verboten sein, sofern das Schuldverhältnis ohne Ansehen der Person geschlossen wird (§ 19 Abs. 2 S. 2 AGG-E). Damit wird zwar die unionsrechtswidrige Begrenzung der geschlechtsbezogenen Diskriminierung auf Massengeschäfte aufgehoben. Ohne Not wird jedoch weiterhin zwischen verschiedenen Diskriminierungsmerkmalen unterschieden: Während für Benachteiligungen wegen der Religion oder Weltanschauung, einer Behinderung, des Alters oder der sexuellen Identität ein sehr eingeschränkter zivilrechtlicher Schutz greift, gilt für Benachteiligungen wegen des Geschlechts ein etwas weitergehender Schutz. Für rassistische Diskriminierung greift die geringste Begrenzung. Wirksamer Schutz muss jedoch für alle Diskriminierungsformen gleichermaßen gewährleistet sein. Das Bundesverfassungsgericht hat insoweit in seinem Beschluss zur Dritten Option zutreffend ausgeführt: „Zweck des Art. 3 Abs. 3 Satz 1 GG ist es, Angehörige strukturell diskriminierungsgefährdeter Gruppen vor Benachteiligung zu schützen“ (dort Rn. 59). Daran ändern auch die europarechtlichen Vorgaben nichts. Die Hierarchisierung verschiedener Diskriminierungsmerkmale ist demnach nicht gerechtfertigt.

Verbesserter Rechtsschutz

Bislang mussten von Diskriminierung Betroffene ihre Rechte gemäß §§ 15 Abs. 4 S. 1, 21 Abs. 5 S. 1 AGG innerhalb einer Frist von zwei Monaten schriftlich geltend machen. Diese (zu) kurze Frist haben nicht nur eine Vielzahl von zivilgesellschaftlichen Organisationen kritisiert, sondern auch der CEDAW-Ausschuss (Rn. 16) sowie die damalige Menschenrechtskommissarin des Europarats Dunja Mijatović (S. 14). Die nun geplante Erweiterung auf vier Monate ist ein Schritt in die richtige Richtung, genügt jedoch nicht. Die regelmäßige Verjährungsfrist von Ansprüchen beträgt drei Jahre (§ 195 BGB). Vor diesem Hintergrund ist die kurze Ausschlussfrist nicht nachvollziehbar. Sie kann auch nicht mit den im Arbeitsrecht geltenden kurzen Fristen begründet werden, da die Frist nicht nur für Arbeits-, sondern auch für Zivilrechtsverhältnisse gilt. Außerdem gelten auch im Arbeitsrecht für Entschädigungs- und Schadensersatzansprüche keine kurzen Fristen. Die Fristen sollten daher deutlich großzügiger gefasst werden.

Der Entwurf stärkt die Antidiskriminierungsstelle des Bundes und verbessert auch so den Rechtsschutz. Die Antidiskriminierungsstelle soll künftig im Rahmen der Beistandschaft (§ 90 ZPO, § 11 Abs. 6 ArbGG) Betroffene in Gerichtsverfahren unterstützen sowie auf Aufforderung eines Gerichts zu grundsätzlichen Rechtsfragen schriftlich Stellung nehmen können (§§ 27 Abs. 6, 7 AGG-E). Sie soll zudem als außergerichtliche Schlichtungsstelle dienen (§§ 27a AGG-E). Auch wenn der Entwurf die wichtigen Forderungen nach einer Prozessstandschaft oder einem Verbandsklagerecht (S. 6) nicht umsetzt, sind diese punktuellen Verbesserungen ein Schritt in die richtige Richtung hin zu einem effektiveren Rechtsschutz für Betroffene.

Verbleibende Schutzlücken

Nicht alle Schutzlücken schließt der Entwurf. Für eine umfassende Darstellung des verbleibenden Reformbedarfs fehlt hier der Raum – insofern sei auf die umfassenden Stellungnahmen der Verbände verwiesen. Zwei Aspekte seien jedoch kurz hervorgehoben: der unzureichende Schutz von Selbstständigen und Organmitgliedern und der fehlende Schutz vor diskriminierenden algorithmischen Entscheidungssystemen (ADM-Systeme).

Gemäß § 6 Abs. 3 AGG gilt der Diskriminierungsschutz für Selbstständige und Organmitglieder, insbesondere Geschäftsführer*innen und Vorständ*innen, nur für den Zugang zur Erwerbstätigkeit und den beruflichen Aufstieg; während sie ihre Tätigkeit ausüben, greift er nicht. Der Bundesrat hat im laufenden Gesetzgebungsverfahren zumindest gefordert, den Schutz vor sexueller Belästigung für Selbstständige und Organmitglieder auszuweiten (S. 3). Dieser Aufforderung ist die Bundesregierung nicht nachgekommen. Doch auch Vorstandsmitglieder können durch Geschäftspartner*innen oder andere Organmitglieder diskriminiert und belästigt werden. Die homogene – männerdominierte – Zusammensetzung von Leitungsorganen (dazu hier und hier) erhöht das Diskriminierungsrisiko für Personen, die nicht der homogenen Gruppe entsprechen. Zudem gilt für Selbstständige die Richtlinie 2010/41/EU (Selbstständigen-Gleichbehandlungsrichtlinie). Diese verlangt, dass jede Diskriminierung aufgrund des Geschlechts zu unterbleiben hat (Art. 4 Abs. 1); dazu zählt auch die (sexuelle) Belästigung (Art. 4 Abs. 2). Barnard und Blackham diskutieren einen auf den Zugang zur Selbstständigkeit begrenzten Anwendungsbereich (S. 9 f.). Sie begründen dies damit, dass Art. 4 Abs. 1 die Gründung, Einrichtung oder Erweiterung eines Unternehmens als Beispiele nennt. Diese Beispiele sind jedoch nicht abschließend. Sie lassen eine solche Beschränkung nicht zu. Das Diskriminierungsverbot gilt folglich auch bei der Ausübung der selbstständigen Tätigkeit. Bei einem Verstoß müssen die Mitgliedstaaten sicherstellen, dass Betroffene für den dadurch entstandenen Schaden oder Verlust einen Schadens- und/oder Entschädigungsanspruch erhalten (Art. 10). Jedenfalls beim Merkmal Geschlecht lässt sich der Ausschluss von Selbstständigen auch deshalb nicht rechtfertigen.

Das AGG schützt zudem nur unzureichend vor diskriminierenden ADM-Systemen. Der Entwurf schweigt hierzu, obwohl der Einsatz solcher Systeme – etwa bei Bewerbungen, Kreditentscheidungen oder der Leistungsvergabe – rapide zunimmt und die Diskriminierungsrisiken künstlicher Intelligenz hinlänglich bekannt sind (siehe dazu etwa hier). ADM-Systeme entscheiden auf der Grundlage von Daten und erkennen dabei statistische Muster. Sie perpetuieren historisch gewachsene Ungleichheitsstrukturen und diskriminieren nicht nur direkt, sondern auch über stellvertretende Ersatzmerkmale, sog. Proxy-Merkmale (siehe dazu hier, S. 18 f., 21 f.). Weil die ADM-Systeme technisch komplex und intransparent sind, bleibt die Diskriminierung oft für die Beteiligten verborgen. Daher sind konkret auf diese Art der Diskriminierung zugeschnittene Vorschriften erforderlich, die durch Auskunftsansprüche Transparenz schaffen, durch Beweislastregelungen das Informationsdefizit ausgleichen und Verantwortlichkeiten bei dem Einsatz diskriminierender ADM-Systeme regeln.

Fazit

Die AGG-Reform geht in die richtige Richtung. Einen hinreichend wirksamen Diskriminierungsschutz, wie ihn die Verfassung erfordert, gewährt sie jedoch nicht. Die erhoffte strukturelle Reform ist ausgeblieben – nicht zuletzt wegen der eiligen Umsetzung der unionsrechtlichen Vorgaben und gescheiterter Ressorteinigungen (siehe dazu die FAQs des BMJV zum Entwurf, S. 5). Ob das Gesetz seinem eigenen Anspruch gerecht wird, entscheidet sich im weiteren Gesetzgebungsverfahren. Der Bundestag muss den Entwurf nachschärfen und seiner unionsrechtlichen wie auch verfassungsrechtlichen Verpflichtung nachkommen.

item.content:encoded:
On 19 October 2026, the UK Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero agreed to the grant of consent by the Oil and Gas Authority for the Jackdaw gas field project under the Offshore Oil and Gas Exploration, Production, Unloading and Storage (Environmental Impact Assessment) Regulations 2020. The decision deserves close attention by climate and energy lawyers both for its compatibility with the remaining global carbon budget and for its treatment of scope 3 emissions. The current piece focuses on the latter, arguing that the conditions placed on scope 3 emissions were inadequate, as were some for scope 1.

The Decision in Context

Jackdaw is a small field with all of its gas likely to be used domestically. A further decision is expected on the much larger Rosebank oil field, where much of the oil would be exported. The Jackdaw consent decision did not license a new gas field – the field licence already existed. The decision involved allowing project operations in the field to begin. There had been an earlier decision to grant consent to the project on 27 May 2022. However, that became unlawful as a result of the 2024 UK Supreme Court Finch ruling that an environmental impact assessment (EIA) had to assess the downstream, scope 3 combustion emissions from an oil and gas project.

The EIA at the heart of the 2022 decision had not included consideration of scope 3 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions – only scope 1 emissions arising directly from the operations. The new consent process, which culminated in the October 2026 decision, addressed this deficit, with the revised decision based on an EIA which assessed scope 3. The project developer, Adura (a joint venture between Shell and Equinor), actually started operations in 2025, well before the recent decision, completing drilling in February 2026 (Decision, para. 6). It would have been subject only to the 2022 scope 1 conditions at that stage. Some potential scope 1 conditions are now academic (such as requiring the jack-up drilling rig to be powered by renewables), but many scope 1 conditions remain relevant to the project’s ongoing operations, and the developers were no doubt keenly awaiting what scope 3 conditions, if any, might be required of them. There were no scope 2 emissions (para. 35).

Conditions on Emissions

As the recent MACH Energy v Denman decision in Australia illustrates, considering emissions is not the same as considering whether to impose conditions on those emissions. The wording of the New South Wales legislation explicitly required the latter, but it should be read as a legal requirement more generally where a decision maker has found climate effects of a project to be significant, as the Secretary of State did in her October 2026 decision. The decision states initially that “No project-specific mitigation [had] been proposed for scope 3 emissions for EIA purposes, which reflects the developer’s position that the project would not have significant effects” (para. 177). However, applying a precautionary approach, the Secretary of State disagreed, arguing that, for EIA purposes, it was “not possible to rule out likely significant effects as a result of the project’s GHG emissions”, including its scope 3 emissions  (para. 178).

As Acland Bryant has noted, it seems odd for the minister to have disagreed on significant effects and yet approved the project without imposing any conditions on scope 3 under regulation 4(4) of the 2020 regulations. The June 2025 government guidance on scope 3 emissions (drawn up after Finch) requires conditions to be considered, stating that “where the assessment of GHG emissions identifies a likely significant adverse effect from a proposed project, consideration must be given by the developer to identifying suitable mitigation measures” (Guidance, p. 13). The guidance goes on to spell out that suitable mitigation measures available to a developer to control significant adverse effects on the environment from scope 3 emissions are likely to be limited. It states that offsetting lies at the bottom of an appropriate mitigation hierarchy, and that “emissions removal measures currently appear to be most appropriate for addressing any likely significant effects on the environment from scope 3 emissions” (p. 13).

Scope 3 Conditions

In her October 2026 decision, the Secretary of State did consider conditions on both scope 1 emissions and scope 3 emissions from Jackdaw. On scope 3, the decision rejected calls for a carbon takeback obligation (CTBO), which would require the developer to capture and store a progressive fraction of CO2 corresponding to the project’s downstream combustion emissions. The reason given was that the creation of a CTBO would be a major policy change requiring legislation rather than being introduced via consent conditions (para. 235). However, while the Secretary of State says that she did not consider it appropriate to impose a CTBO as a condition on Jackdaw (para. 235), she does not tell us what other scope 3 conditions she considered. While correctly associating a CTBO with CCS as one form of circular economy CO2 “waste” management, the decision unhelpfully fails to actively consider CCS as a possible condition in its own right, independent of a surrounding CTBO policy framework. The government’s scope 3 guidance does not mention CCS. As seen above, it instead lists carbon removal as the most appropriate measure for tackling scope 3 project emissions. CCS is not by itself typically classified as a removal technology. However, the decision does not consider removals like direct air capture as a potential scope 3 condition either.

In fact, the decision does consider CCS, but only passively in light of the developer mentioning that “some mitigation measures may be possible in future for some projects, for example if there is a market for carbon capture and storage” (para. 232). However, the Secretary of State simply takes at face value the developer’s assertion that “such measures require progressive government policy supported by collaboration between government, customers and private organisations” (para. 232).

As the “waiting or pushing” part of the current piece’s title suggests, this involves government regulation of scope 3 accepting the wait for a market-based and subsidy-driven arrival of CCS (which has already involved a wait of many years, with the climate movement widely seeing it as a technological smokescreen designed to delay the transition away from fossil fuels). Effective scope 3 governance should, instead, be actively pushing CCS and making it happen through conditions. But even if CCS were to be seen as too stringent a regulatory requirement, what about offsets as a condition for scope 3 emissions? Those are also often viewed with suspicion by the climate movement, but some high-integrity carbon credits are available. It looks as if the government has unlawfully failed to follow its own scope 3 guidance in not considering, let alone imposing even the lowest rung on the mitigation hierarchy. Nevertheless, its scope 3 guidance does not exactly help in that respect, expressing the view “that it is unlikely that the purchase of credits will be an effective mitigation measure for the purposes of the Offshore EIA Regulations” (p. 14).

Scope 1 Conditions

What then of scope 1 GHG emissions? First, the 2026 decision covers methane emissions, referring to the 2021 North Sea Transition Deal policy’s commitment to methane reduction targets and zero routine flaring and venting by 2030. Again, though, the government is prepared to wait rather than push here. That ban on flaring and venting of methane only comes in 2030 – it is not imposed via conditions now in 2026. We are simply told that “Methane emissions from the UK’s oil and gas sector are a relatively new area of focus”, that “the industry is still developing its capability in methane measurement, monitoring, reporting and abatement” and that “the developer is currently at an early stage in this process” (para. 67).

Methane can be released not only by routine flaring and venting but also via leaks. There, the decision again acknowledges an industry commitment to halve methane emissions by 2030, rather than imposing specific conditions to this effect more quickly. Based on this commitment, the government simply accepts that the developer’s forecast methane intensity figure for the project (0.44 kgCO2e/boe) is much lower than the global average (15kg CO2e/boe) (paras. 67-68) (defining GHG intensity as “the emission quantity of CO2e relative to the amount of hydrocarbon production” (para. 57)). And that is despite the fact that the forecast is an estimate, with the developer not having provided any underlying methodology and data (para. 67).

Second, the other part of the scope 1 emissions picture beyond methane is CO2. Carbon dioxide emissions from operations may arise from the drilled gas itself, and this CO2 has historically often been vented to the atmosphere. Other scope 1 CO2 emissions come from combustion of the fossil fuels used to power Jackdaw’s (now removed) drilling rig and (ongoing) wellhead platform (WHP) operations in the North Sea, and from power used in processing and transport. The 2026 decision discusses these scope 1 CO2 emissions (paras. 50-56) and the emissions intensity of the project with them included [57-59], and then reiterates the 2022 scope 1 conditions to control the venting of CO2 and for WHP power (para. 236). That WHP power is currently supplied by on-platform diesel generation rather than renewables (as found on many greener platforms in Norway). The 2026 decision does not actively seek to push conditions to reduce Jackdaw’s CO2 emissions intensity by requiring the latter. Instead, it notes the 2022 condition requiring the WHP to “accommodate a potential electrification retrofit should green power become available”, while simply accepting that the developer had provided no updated information on this for the 2026 decision (para. 236). Again, we have a passive waiting for renewables inscribed in a weak condition rather than an active pushing for them via a stronger consenting approach.

Fortunately, the Secretary of State does not oversell the scope 1 emissions-intensity advantages of the project. First, she notes the difference in scale between the project’s scope 1 emissions and its vastly greater scope 3 emissions (paras. 48, 169). Second, she acknowledges the uncertainty around the level of emissions intensity reduction associated with production from Jackdaw, and goes on to state that she would have agreed to the grant of consent even if the project did not deliver any reduction in emissions intensity (para. 182). That would make any legal challenge to the decision on the ground that scope 1 emissions intensity was based on shaky assumptions difficult – because that was not a significant basis for the decision anyway. However, it does not address whether the decision ought to have considered more intensive conditions for scope 1 CO2 emissions than its 2030 waiting approach on methane and its laissez-faire wait-and-see stance on renewables for platform power.

Conclusion

It is odd that the Secretary of State found there to be significant likely climate effects from the Jackdaw project and yet decided not to impose any conditions on its scope 3 emissions. It is true that she considered imposing conditions, but she actively considered just the CTBO measure at the top of the scope 3 mitigation hierarchy, only to reject it as requiring a legislative foundation. CCS was mostly treated as part of the CTBO package; insofar as it was considered in its own right, it was similarly held to be something for the future, needing more support to bring it into being. Also noteworthy is the tension of the scope 3 guidance wanting to see measures from a scope 3 mitigation hierarchy while dismissing offsets as a measure from that hierarchy. It is perhaps no surprise that the government felt compelled to leave offsets out of its October 2026 decision altogether, but the legality of that (and the underlying scope 3 guidance) appears questionable. Based on the guidance, it seems to be carbon removals or nothing, which is not much of a mitigation hierarchy for scope 3 emissions. But, given that, it is strange that removals were not considered in the decision at all.

In contrast, conditions for the less climate-impactful scope 1 emissions are not only considered but actually imposed. There too though, one might have expected less of a waiting until 2030 approach on methane conditions as well as a more active push on renewable platform power rather than being so accommodating of industry by requiring only renewables readiness. The climate crisis is now. The government’s decision involves too much waiting and not enough pushing.

item.title: What We Lose When Lawyers Let LLMs Write
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Mukherjee
item.description:
One of the first things a bleary-eyed first-year law student has to hear ad nauseam in their first week of law school is that, over the next three years, they will be taught to “think” like a lawyer. What does that mean exactly? And how is that likely to change in the face of rapid adoption and spread of Large Language Models (LLMs) across law schools, law firms, and in-house legal departments? What do we lose when lawyers let LLMs do their writing for them?

item.content:encoded:
One of the first things a bleary-eyed first-year law student has to hear ad nauseam in their first week of law school is that, over the next three years, they will be taught to “think” like a lawyer. What does that mean exactly? And how is that likely to change in the face of rapid adoption and spread of Large Language Models (LLMs) across law schools,1) law firms,2) and in-house legal departments?3) What do we lose when lawyers let LLMs do their writing for them?

These questions arrive at a fraught time for the legal profession. A recent Thomson Reuters Institute survey found that judges already report declining litigation and communication skills among attorneys in their first five years of practice, with nearly 60% saying client advocacy is being harmed.4) Of course, answering these questions depends less on what LLMs can do in the abstract and more on what a given lawyer chooses to do with them, and at what stage of their career. Consequently, the implications of an LLM writing the first draft of the first essay that our harried first-year law student must write in law school differ radically from when, say, it does a final read-through of a share purchase agreement for a third-year law firm associate.5) Similarly, delegation will not affect everyone uniformly: a law student incubating their legal judgment through iterative exercises in law school will be affected differently from a more advanced legal professional whose judgment is already settled.

In this symposium post, we unpack how “thinking like a lawyer” is changing in the age of LLMs. At the outset, it’s important to clarify that we understand the term to mean a bundle of specific cognitive acts, comprising the skills of reasoning, argumentation, sequencing, and revision that legal training is built around,6) and it is likely that they’re going to change in unpredictable ways once LLMs can do each of these on demand. Of course, some of this lawyerly thinking occurs orally, whether that’s in oral argument in a courtroom, or when an instructor engages in Socratic dialogue with a law student. But we focus here on writing because that is where legal reasoning is captured in a form upon which others rely, and where LLMs are most likely to take over.

We make two arguments. First, we argue that LLM-assisted writing is likely to negatively affect creative lawyering. The common law’s adversarial system is contingent upon a triadic division of cognitive labour: we see modes of what the creativity literature calls ‘divergent thinking’ from advocates putting forth opposing readings of the same factual record, resolved by ‘convergent thinking’ by a third actor — usually a court — that decides which is the winning proposition between the two. When advocates on both sides draft with the help of an LLM trained on the same corpus of published legal writing, that divergence can narrow even while the disagreement looks intact on paper.

Second, we argue that legal writing often constitutes legal reasoning. Legal reasoning does not fully exist until it ‘survives’ the act of documentation, of being written down. As a result, delegating the writing risks delegating away a crucial intermediate step which legal professionals use to ask if the reasoning holds up in the first place.

What happens when we’re all drinking from the same well?

The first aspect of lawyering we address is how offloading cognitive tasks to LLMs affects creative lawyering, or the capacity to think and reason outside the box. Cognitive offloading is the use of an external aid that reduces the mental demand a task places on us.7) Think shopping lists or calendar invites.

Creativity research distinguishes two modes of thought: convergent thinking narrows toward a single best answer that derives from a fixed set of premises, which, for example, multiple-choice tests reward. On the other hand, divergent thinking generates the widest possible range of dissimilar responses to the same prompt. Much of the early work on human intelligence treated the latter as central to creativity itself — likely because it was believed that a mind capable of only one answer per question cannot be said to be inventing anything.8)

In a foundational work in the genre, Carrie Menkel-Meadow argued that good legal creativity requires ‘separating inventing from evaluating’, that is, the ability to generate options before judging them, while saying that much of legal education is aimed at training the critical, convergent half of these two rather than the generative, divergent half.9) This leaves law students with a honed capacity to narrow an argument down but impoverishes their capacity to widen the search space in the first place.

The adversarial legal system we inhabit manufactures divergent thinking through design: two advocates work with a (usually) agreed-upon factual record and have access to a similar body of doctrine. Yet, they’re (usually) required to produce maximally different, yet maximally motivated readings of both, before a court performs the convergent operation of choosing between them. The jurist Karl Llewellyn treated this division of labor as one of the ‘steadying factors’ that made common law decision-making predictable.10)

Recent creativity research may help here. A study of LLM-assisted writing found that even when individual stories became more creative and better written, the assemblage of LLM-assisted stories became measurably more similar to one another than stories written by humans alone.11) The gains for individual stories came at the cost of collective novelty. Research on algorithmic monoculture offers an explanation: systems built on shared components tend to produce homogeneous outcomes.12) When we apply this finding to two opposing counsels, it shows how our adversarial system’s inbuilt mechanisms to produce divergent thinking are imperiled. What follows is that each side of a legal dispute writes a locally better brief while the ideational distance between the two briefs — the meat on which a convergent judicial decision is supposed to operate — becomes smaller.

Recent work from Finke and Casper finds that models from major LLM developers typically discuss their creators’ controversies in a differentially positive manner.13) Let’s imagine a situation where the legal question under consideration implicates the LLM developer’s own exposure, such as fair use considerations for AI training. In such cases, both sides’ briefs risk reading as more defendant friendly.

Choi and Schwarcz’s finding that LLM assistance narrows the spread of legal-writing quality toward a shared mean may be analogous indirect evidence of such a mechanism.14) The productive tension between opposing sides of a legal argument may become narrower as we see wider adoption of LLM tools, which might play out in unanticipated ways in how the law mediates between opposing parties on things that we deeply disagree about in a plural human society.

Is Cognitive Offloading Domain-specific?

The second question we tackle is whether there is something unique about the relationship between legal reasoning and legal writing, and how LLM-assisted writing affects it. The empirical literature on LLMs and cognitive offloading asks whether such reliance erodes the capacity that it replaces. A 2025 study of essay writing with GPT-4o found that 83.3% of LLM-assisted writers could not remember a correct quotation from their own essay when compared to 11.1% of unassisted writers.15) Indubitably, a failure to recall one’s own sentences isn’t the same as a failure to grasp their content, so this finding should be treated with caution. Yet, our interest lies in the premise these studies share: that writing involves a separable cognitive process, and that the question is whether outsourcing degrades a process that would have happened anyway. While writing shapes how thinking occurs in virtually every field, the law is a domain where there is a specific difference: while, say, a news story or a lab report describes something that exists apart from it, much of legal text is itself the legal act. Most forms of legal writing, as a result, do not necessarily operate the same way.

Take judicial opinions, for example. On one view, opinions function as rules, which must exist as a text before binding anyone: there isn’t a pre-textual holding waiting to be reported on.16) Most participants in the legal system work this way. This is not to say that legal reasoning only occurs through the written word: oral arguments in courtrooms and snappy back-and-forth between a law professor and their student would readily disprove that notion. But when legal reasoning binds a set of people, it usually takes a written form.

Before a judge begins to write a decision, they may know how they want to rule but might not have the exact reasoning behind it. A legal argument doesn’t act as a holding until it’s written very clearly to guide the next case. Legal editing therefore carries a lot of value as it points out flaws in reasoning. An argument can sound convincing in theory, but when expressed in words, it can fall apart very quickly. In his new work on AI and judicial opinions, Richard Re makes a similar point, noting how an opinion merges “directive and justification” into one document.17) As LLMs make writing judicial opinions easy, judges may find it hard to discover flaws in their reasoning through the writing process. This is because fewer drafts will appear unworkable or need to be abandoned. Prior work on cognitive offloading has focused on how overreliance on tools for writing can impact our ability to think independently over time. Legal drafting challenges a key assumption of that work: that reasoning occurs before writing and apart from it. In legal writing, they are intertwined.

One objection is apparent: haven’t judges long delegated their writing to law clerks?18) Yes, but unlike LLMs, clerks serve as an additional check against opinions rooted in tenuous legal reasoning. In contrast, LLMs will likely return elegant prose when prompted, making judges less likely to edit it substantially and more likely to be anchored to it.19) Prudential guidelines like the Judicial Writing Manual from the Federal Judicial Center insist that while clerks may assist judges in some of their tasks, “the opinion must always be the judge’s work”.20) Of course, precise empirical work on authorial attribution remains notoriously difficult in this domain.

Our argument tracks an intuitive curricular distinction: 1L legal writing courses are often split between predictive and persuasive writing.21) Predictive legal writing (for example, where a first-year law student is asked to write a memo) tells you (or your client) what a court will likely do, in a seemingly neutral voice that weighs both sides, while eschewing the pull toward the answer the writer wants to be true. Persuasive writing is a zero-sum game. It takes the form of a brief that tells a court what it should do, marshalling only the facts and authority that support your client’s position. The object of persuasive writing is to win, and most faculty will admit that even its neutral-sounding Statement of Facts is an advocacy tool. While these two share some scaffolding, they pursue starkly different purposes, which explains why law schools teach them a semester apart. When LLMs draft for us, we forgo a step that can surface a shaky legal proposition, doomed to fail, before a client hears it from opposing counsel.

Moreover, we believe LLMs are likely to fare worse under delegation for two structural reasons. First, they’re trained mostly on published, persuasive-register text, while predictive memos are privileged and essentially absent from training data. A model’s sense of ‘neutral’ therefore comes largely from the performed neutrality of advocacy documents, which looks the same on the page as the real discipline of predictive writing. Second, alignment training pushes models toward hedging, and hedging softens unfavorable predictions more than favorable ones. Notably, this is unlikely to be symmetrical: we predict that briefs drafted by models would be more favorable to the client than attorney-drafted ones, holding authority constant. We believe this isn’t because the model learned advocacy’s performed neutrality, but because hedging erodes unfavorable predictions more than favorable ones.

Conclusion

So, what do we lose when lawyers let LLMs do their writing for them? Surely, we can’t peg it to the production of competent, grammatical prose, nor to an uncanny ability to whip up razor-sharp legal authority, both of which can be done well by an LLM, with newer models doing even better. We hope to have shown that lawyers use writing as a check on their own reasoning. Similarly, when lawyers argue on opposing sides, the productive tension creates the glue of genuine divergence that adversarial adjudication needs to bind itself together. Additionally, the domain-specificity of cognitive offloading has a surprising implication: law may be one of the domains where writing was not a snapshot of thought to begin with, which is why the stakes of outsourcing it look different here than elsewhere.

item.content:encoded:
In one of the most dramatic elections in the history of Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has achieved a dramatic victory against the far-right incumbent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is now under house arrest following a conviction to more than twenty-seven years for a coup attempt in January 2023. Less than two days after the election results were announced, Flávio left the country to seek asylum in the United States, in defiance of a court order suspending his passport and prohibiting him from leaving the country. The restraining order was issued in the context of an investigation into allegations of corruption and money laundering involving Flávio. In this article, however, we will concentrate on the main events of the electoral process and on how democratic resistance has been organized through street demonstrations and coordinated responses on social media. The elections attracted the world’s attention both for the president’s impressive overturn of a significant electoral loss in the first round and for the extraordinary capacity of mobilization and reorganization of civil society resistance against the extreme right in a very short period of time.

First-Round Results and Electoral Losses in Congress

The results of the first round of the presidential elections favoured Flávio Bolsonaro and his party – the so-called “Liberal Party” (Partido Liberal). Flávio Bolsonaro had few concrete proposals for ruling the country. They included the promise of cutting social benefits and implementing what he called a Big Scissors Treatment (Tesouraço) for dealing with public debt in the style of Javier Milei’s “chainsaw program” in Argentina. Most of his supporters were moved, however, by the electoral promises of granting full amnesty to his father and hundreds of military officials, politicians, and ordinary persons formally convicted for the coup attempt of January 2023, and by the commitment to impeach Justices in the Federal Supreme Court. The main target was Justice Alexandre de Moraes, the rapporteur of the trial for Jair Bolsonaro’s coup attempt. Moraes now faces, in fact, serious suspicions of receiving money under contracts of his wife’s law firm with a now-imprisoned former banker. Although these are separate cases, they raise serious legitimacy concerns towards the Federal Supreme Court and its justices.

In the first round of the election, Flavio Bolsonaro’s strategy produced effective electoral outputs, leading to a victory against Lula by a margin of 2% (47.03% against 45.16% of the valid votes), and to major wins in the Federal Senate and in the House of Representatives. The largest electoral victory was in the Senate, where the far-right parties altogether achieved a supermajority of 49 out of 81 Senators. Bolsonaro’s party, for instance, went from the current total of 15 Senators to 28 Senators in the next legislature, whereas Lula’s Workers’ Party remained with the current number of 9.

Extreme Speeches and Behavioral Impact

The electoral campaign was marked by acts of political violence. According to Terra de Direitos and Justiça Global, 134 incidents were documented during the 50-day campaign preceding the first round, including 64 threats, 33 cases of verbal abuse, 19 physical assaults, 11 attempted attacks, and two killings. In the second round, things got worse. Marcelo de Oliveira Rocha, a 30-year-old environmental engineer and master’s student, died after being assaulted following an event associated with a pro-Lula gathering in Santos, São Paulo. Elisabete Martins Chaves, aged 54, died after being struck by a car while waiting for a pro-Lula campaign caravan in Vargem Alegre, Minas Gerais. Witnesses alleged that the driver supported Flávio Bolsonaro. In Campo Novo do Parecis, Mato Grosso, police investigator Emilson Ormond Souza, aged 56, was shot dead in a bar after a man reportedly asked patrons about their political preferences. According to initial witness accounts, the suspect asked who supported the Workers’ Party (PT) before opening fire. In General Carneiro, Mato Grosso, city councillor Marcos Aurélio Bento Pena was arrested on suspicion of firing shots toward a group celebrating Lula’s electoral victory, leaving two women injured. Other reported incidents of political violence during Brazil’s 2026 elections included a shooting at a pro-Lula demonstration outside the Federal University of Sergipe (UFS), in São Cristóvão, on October 8. In Minas Gerais, on October 24, city councillor Iara Pimentel (PT) was injured when objects, including stones and bottles, were thrown at a sound truck during a pro-Lula campaign caravan in the city of Montes Claros.

External Interference and Imbalance in Social Media

Reporting on the Trump administration’s involvement in Brazilian politics points to efforts to strengthen U.S. influence by supporting the Bolsonaro family’s return to power. During Lula’s 2023–2026 presidential term, Eduardo Bolsonaro relocated to the United States in March 2025 and lobbied U.S. officials to take punitive measures against Brazilian authorities. His efforts formed part of a broader pressure campaign that included Global Magnitsky sanctions against Federal Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, the revocation of visas held by other justices and Brazilian officials, and additional tariffs on Brazilian goods. These measures sought to pressure Brazilian institutions over the prosecution of former president Jair Bolsonaro for plotting a coup. Ahead of the 2026 elections, Rockbridge Network, a U.S. conservative network co-founded by J.D. Vance, also took steps to establish a presence in Brazil. Allegations that individuals associated with the network were supporting Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign prompted a request to the Federal Supreme Court for an investigation into possible foreign campaign financing.

Another feature of the presidential election was the accusation of a lack of balance between political forces in social networks. Meta faced mounting allegations of unequal treatment of political candidates and of potentially interfering with the electoral process through the management of its social media platforms’ algorithms. Reports indicated that content associated with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his campaign had experienced restrictions, reduced visibility, or technical obstacles, while content associated with his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, was allegedly more readily recommended or amplified. These allegations gained further significance when reports based on internal company communications suggested that Meta employees had acknowledged problems affecting Lula’s accounts. The controversy prompted Lula’s campaign to seek intervention from Brazil’s electoral authorities and to announce a complaint to the Organization of American States.

Legislative Measures, Street Protests, and the “Janones Effect”

Nonetheless, neither the episodes of street violence by supporters of Bolsonaro nor the external interference from the so-called “Big Techs” proved to be decisive in the presidential run. To begin, the Federal Government reacted by approving measures backed by broad public support.

In September 2026, just a few days before the first round, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva issued a provisional measure banning fixed-odds betting in Brazil, including online sports betting and casino games. The government justified the measure on public-health and socioeconomic grounds, citing gambling addiction, household indebtedness, and the diversion of family income to betting platforms. By the same token, on September 17, 2026, the president announced a 15.04% adjustment to Bolsa Família, Brazil’s flagship cash-transfer program, with payments at the new rate beginning in October. The government described the measure as an inflation adjustment intended to preserve beneficiaries’ purchasing power. Announced just 17 days before the first round of the presidential election, the increase sparked political controversy, with critics questioning its timing and challenging its legality under electoral rules.

Though these measures were not sufficient to secure a win in the first round, they contributed to raising the approval of the government in ordinary family households. And the package of good news became more generous in the second round. After the first round, Lula was finally able to deliver one of his most important promises, which he pursued during the bulk of his term but failed to gather sufficient support in Congress. Shortly after the first-round election results were announced, the Federal Senate finally approved a constitutional amendment to reduce the working week from six to five days, with a maximum of 40 working hours per week.

Nonetheless, these popular measures were not enough to overturn the unfortunate electoral results. The turning point was reached, instead, through two decisive factors: first, the engagement of ordinary citizens in public rallies and demonstrations, and second, an unprecedented effort of coordinated action in social networks.

During the final two weeks of the presidential runoff, Lula’s supporters organized a nationwide wave of demonstrations aimed at reversing his first-round deficit and mobilizing voters for the October 25 election. On October 19, Lula claimed in a television interview that nearly 1,700 marches and motorcades had taken place across the country during the preceding weekend. His campaign also reported organizing events in approximately 500 cities on October 18. On the last Saturday before the election, October 24, Lula organized what his campaign described as the largest political rally in Brazil since the “Diretas Já” campaign during the country’s transition to democracy, filling a 2.8-kilometre stretch of Avenida Paulista, São Paulo’s main thoroughfare.

The second and arguably most decisive movement was orchestrated by Congressman André Janones, who led a huge campaign on social media in support of Lula. After Lula’s defeat in the first round, Janones received the mission of giving a response to the far-right dominance of social networks in Brazil. He devised a strategy to turn Meta’s algorithm in favour of Lula and dominate Instagram, Threads, and Facebook. Janones went viral in a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” (Exército do Lula) during the three weeks of the second round. Created as an independent initiative in the aftermath of Lula’s first-round setback, the channel grew at extraordinary speed, reaching approximately 10.8 million followers by election day. Its success reflected not merely an enormous audience, but its capacity to transform passive support into coordinated political engagement. Janones regularly assigned followers specific tasks, such as sharing campaign videos, promoting hashtags, boosting posts on social media and recruiting new participants through their personal networks. Ready-made messages and clear instructions made participation accessible to millions of supporters, turning the channel into a decentralised mobilisation network capable of amplifying Lula’s campaign across multiple platforms.

The initiative helped restore the morale of a political camp that had entered the runoff facing the prospect of defeat. Janones’s own popularity rose dramatically during this period. His personal commitment became particularly evident when he was hospitalised with a cardiac arrhythmia in the early hours of 19 October, following the televised presidential debate. Even while in hospital, he resumed issuing instructions to his followers and coordinating online mobilisation. Upon his discharge the following day, he immediately rejoined the campaign effort, meeting supporters outside the hospital and declaring himself ready to return to work. The channel’s rapid expansion, the increased visibility of its founder and the mobilisation of millions of supporters demonstrate how digital activism can become a powerful instrument of political coordination and collective confidence.

Indirect Disenfranchisement, Judicial Responses, and Post-Election Responses

Until the 2026 elections, no candidate who lost the election in the first round had been able to overturn their disadvantage in the second round. Nonetheless, Lula was able to achieve a remarkable victory when the polls were open. In all regions of Brazil, Lula da Silva was able to improve by a large margin the votes that he received in the first round. Overall, he improved by more than 10 million the number of votes that he received in the first round, becoming the best-voted President in Brazilian history, with more than 64 M votes (reaching 51,79% of the valid votes), in contrast to more than 59 M votes (48,21% of the valid votes) of his opponent. Lula improved his results by a wide margin, in all territories, even where his opponent won.

This ascending trend had been captured by the polls and led to the repetition of a strategy of disenfranchisement that had been adopted in the second round of the presidential election of 2022, when roadblocks were set up by the Federal Highway Police (Polícia Rodoviária Federal, PRF) to prevent voters from reaching the ballot boxes in states where Lula traditionally wins. In December 2025, Brazil’s Federal Supreme Court (STF) convicted Silvinei Vasques, former head of the Federal Highway Police (PRF), and Marília Alencar, a former intelligence director at the Ministry of Justice, as part of the group that operationalized the attempted coup following the 2022 election. Anderson Torres, Bolsonaro’s former Minister of Justice, was separately convicted in the broader coup proceedings. The court considered the alleged PRF operations to obstruct voters in Lula-supporting areas of the Northeast as part of the wider plot against the democratic order, rather than as a separate voter-suppression offence.

A similar strategy was adopted, again, in the 2026 elections, at least in two major capitals: the city of Salvador, in Bahia, with a large black majority who support Lula, and in the capital city of the State of São Paulo (Brazil’s largest city, with a metropolitan area of 20 million inhabitants). In both cities, the city council reduced the number of buses circulating and taking voters to voting sites. In the city of Salvador, a court order determined the arrest of the Secretary of Urban Mobility, and the full re-establishment of the bus routes. A few hours later, another court order was issued by Justice Cristiano Zanin, from the Federal Supreme Court, to keep the ballots open for two hours after the voting time. The court was motivated by requests from both candidates. On the side of Flavio Bolsonaro, they asked for a term extension due to the heavy rains in the southern states, whereas on the side of Lula da Silva, the request was due to the failures in the transport systems in these two major cities.

The impact of the extra voting hours, however, has been insignificant. While Lula won by a margin of 4,430,191 votes (3.6% of the valid votes), fewer than 35,000 people voted in the extra time. Nonetheless, Flavio Bolsonaro refused to acknowledge the result of the election and claimed that the extension of the voting hours was grounds for annulling the whole electoral process. This allegation was widely regarded as not only desperate but disingenuous, since his own campaign requested it and it is widely documented that it could not possibly have any sort of interference in the result. The grounds were so weak that even the president of his party rejected it, and he gave up on this argument in less than twenty-four hours.

On the day after the elections, all Brazilian media outlets announced that Justice Alexandre de Moraes notified Flávio Bolsonaro to surrender his passport due to pending inquiries in corruption cases. As this article is being finished, it is widely reported that Flávio Bolsonaro has fled the country towards the United States.

A Less Authoritarian Brazil?

Brazil’s history of slavery, racism, patronage politics, extreme inequality, elite rent-seeking, and dictatorship has often made the country emblematic of authoritarian persistence. The 1988 Constitution, however, may have altered this trajectory. Although Jair Bolsonaro won the presidency in 2018, a majority of Brazilian voters appears unwilling to endorse the consolidation of an illiberal political project.

Regardless of Flávio Bolsonaro’s fate, Lula da Silva has achieved a major electoral win. For the fourth time, he has been elected President of Brazil, and he had the highest number of votes any president has received in a presidential election. While the fear of a new Bolsonaro presidency may have motivated such a very high electoral turnout, the election is representative of a historical effort of the progressive camps, both with left-wing and right-wing orientation, toward the preservation of constitutional democracy and the rule of law.

item.description:
On 25 October, the Student List won an absolute majority in Serbia's parliamentary election.  Aleksandar Vučić conceded within minutes of the polls closing. The significance of this election goes beyond the composition of parliament and lies in what its result will allow Serbia to leave behind, since, like Poland and Hungary, Serbia is one of the states whose courts and other key institutions have been captured by the ruling party.
