item.content:encoded:
On 25 October, the Student List won an absolute majority in Serbia’s parliamentary election.  Aleksandar Vučić conceded within minutes of the polls closing. The significance of this election goes beyond the composition of parliament and lies in what its result will allow Serbia to leave behind, since, like Poland and Hungary, Serbia is one of the states whose courts and other key institutions have been captured by the ruling party. The new majority must now make constitutional guarantees and legal duties effective in institutions the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) still largely staffs.

What makes the Serbian case distinctive is that, two years after the canopy of the Novi Sad railway station collapsed, a leaderless movement born in occupied faculties now holds a parliamentary majority (OSW). With 8,155 polling stations processed, the Student List had 52.73% of the vote (2,257,863 votes) and Vučić’s United Serbia 39.15% (1,676,138 votes) (Vreme), and according to the final projection by Ipsos and CeSID the Student List will have 141 of the 250 seats, with 103 for United Serbia and six for four minority lists. According to CeSID’s projections, it will have 140 of the 250 seats, with 103 for United Serbia and seven for minority lists. Now that the question of whether SNS could be voted out is settled, the harder problem, and the subject of this piece, is what a new majority may lawfully do with institutional arrangements and informal structures built to outlast those who built them.

Serbia’s history shows why this question is of crucial importance, since the country found itself in a similar situation in 2000: on 5 October of that year, after Slobodan Milošević refused to concede the September election, Ljubisav Đokić drove a bulldozer into the state television building in Belgrade, and Milošević conceded the following day (JusticeInfo/AFP). However, the state he had built largely survived him, beginning with its security apparatus, whose “Red Berets” unit supplied the men who assassinated Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić in March 2003 (NBC News). Many of those who went on to build today’s SNS state had served the old one, including Vučić, who served as Milošević’s information minister from 1998 (Global Voices). This means that winning the election did not restore the Rule of Law, and the students draw on that experience.

What Was on the Ballot

The protests leading to the election were the students’ response to institutional inaction, driven largely by a decade of political pressure and the dominant ruling party’s erosion of judicial independence. The founding moment of the movement came on 1 November 2024, when the canopy of the railway station in Novi Sad collapsed, killing sixteen people. A consortium of two Chinese state companies, China Railway International and China Communications Construction Company, had reconstructed the station building as part of the Belgrade–Budapest railway, a Belt and Road project financed largely by Chinese loans (Vreme), and it reopened only four months before the collapse. The companies and the government insisted that the canopy had not been part of the reconstruction; the authorities had refused to disclose the reconstruction contracts, and “Corruption kills” became the slogan of the protests. In the weeks after the collapse, students blockaded more than 60 faculties behind a Rule of Law demand: publish the documents, prosecute those responsible, and let institutions do their job (BTA). Violeta Beširević called it a demand for government under the Rule of Law rather than rule by one man (Beširević).

What happened over the following months explains why the students came to see an election as the way to get those institutions working again. In May 2025, they called for early elections, and in August, TOK, the Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime, detained a former construction minister and senior railway officials over financial flows in the station’s reconstruction (N1), after which the police director pulled 17 officers out of the task force tracing that money (N1). In January 2026, as parliament cut short prosecutors’ secondments to the office, TOK stated that the withdrawal of investigators and repeated failures to hand over documents had made obtaining the evidence practically impossible (TOK statement; Danas), a pattern of political pressure that the Commission’s July report confirms.

To contest the election they had demanded, the students built a list of their own: Student List – Students Win, a citizens’ list whose candidate criteria, set by 105 student plenums and open assemblies in every higher-education unit, excluded students, officials of opposition parties and former members of the ruling coalition (Jacobin). Several opposition parties withdrew in its favour (BTA). It asked voters for a mandate to make institutions work, and that is the standard by which it will be judged.

The election result will most certainly change Serbia’s future, but it will also matter in retrospect. Namely, the vote decided who controls accountability for the past. In his last days as president, Vučić announced pardons for 49 people whose names have not been published (N1). To this day, only a handful of names are public, and speculation, along with public hints from Vučić (Radio Free Europe), suggests the pardon included officials investigated and charged with corruption related to the fall of the canopy and other high-profile affairs (Guardian). Two days later, Radar published Sky communications in which Vučić reportedly appears as “Oskar” and a pardon is mentioned as a way of correcting an unfavourable court outcome for the drug trafficker Darko Šarić (N1). These accounts need independent investigation, and nothing so far shows that Šarić is among the 49, although the arrangement they describe, in which legal consequences can be negotiated through closeness to power, is the one that the students’ slogan, “Serbia or Mafia”, put before voters. Vučić also chose the timing and form of the vote, dissolving parliament on 9 September (Balkan Insight) and resigning on 27 September to run for prime minister.

How the vote was held is itself a Rule of Law question, as a BIRN investigation published on 20 October shows: it documented public employees pressed to deliver votes, attend SNS rallies and do party work under threat of transfer or dismissal (BIRN). While these testimonies cannot establish how widespread the practice was, they show the mechanism by which dependence on a public job becomes political obedience, as ODIHR’s interim report of 9 October had already noted (ODIHR). Captured public authority thus helps produce the electoral support later invoked to justify its partisan use, making the thirteen-point margin a measure of how strong the demand for change was, achieved under unacceptable conditions.

Vučić’s election-night concession removed the risk of a contested result (Euronews), and ODIHR’s preliminary findings describe high turnout and generally well-run voting in a contest seriously skewed by ruling-party advantages, misuse of state resources, intimidation and media bias (ODIHR). However, none of this changes the diagnosis of a Rule of Law crisis that reaches the foundations of institutional life. In politically sensitive areas, law has become a thin layer over informal autocracy, legitimising the government abroad while failing to organise public action or constrain those who hold power (Vuković, Spaić; BiEPAG). We therefore use the word “restoration” with some care, since in many areas no functioning legal order is held in reserve, and the students are striving to make law effective in government and institutions, in some domains for the first time.

Why it Matters

With the antecedent of 2000 in mind, the student and later popular movement set out to turn protest into electoral authority (Bloomberg), and because it won power under the existing constitutional rules, it will be expected to exercise that power within them as well. Comparisons with Poland and Hungary illuminate inherited appointments and entrenched power, and also highlight what is specific to the students’ project: practical force for existing guarantees and duties, a goal for which a constitution-amending majority is the wrong yardstick.

What the students face goes beyond laws designed to entrench a ruling party, since political instructions, selective enforcement, appointments, and dependence on public employment can displace the rules while leaving the text untouched. As early as 2022, Beširević observed that Vučić sought to control how every institution functioned (Beširević), resulting in institutions doing routine work yet still failing wherever an investigation, appointment, or regulatory decision threatens a protected interest, making governance through general, publicly knowable rules unreliable. Calling every institution an empty shell would overlook the individual judges, prosecutors, and many universities whose sustained resistance has supported the movement.

We believe three questions must be kept apart: whether a norm is legally valid, whether it is effective, and whether the exercise of power meets Rule of Law standards. A valid norm does not, by itself, guide official conduct, and effective coercion does not make conduct lawful, since arbitrary commands can be enforced very efficiently. In Serbia’s case, where informal authority displaces legal duties, and no effective remedies exist against that displacement, restoration requires officials who treat the law as a reason for action even after an unwelcome phone call, and citizens who can obtain compliance when officials fail them.

European actors share responsibility, as the European Parliament’s July assessment finds a persistent gap between legislative alignment and implementation, which Beširević traces to the EU’s long preference for regional stability over Serbia’s democratisation (Beširević). The gap has also been politically useful: legal reform has earned the government credentials abroad as informal control continued at home, so European scrutiny should examine what institutions do when the law requires action those in power do not want.

The Day After October 25

The transfer of power still runs through constitutional procedure, under which the acting president proposes a candidate for prime minister who must obtain the votes of a majority of all MPs. If SNS wins the presidential election in December, its president could return legislation to parliament and delay it, with the obligation to promulgate any law parliament passes again by a majority of all MPs (Constitution, Articles 109, 113, 120 and 127). Within this constitutional framework, what the new majority can do will depend on the programme on which the Student List was elected.

The Student List’s eleven-point programme puts institutional independence and respect for the Constitution and laws at its centre and proposes no constitutional amendment. It translates the claim behind “Serbia or Mafia”, that public offices should perform their legal functions, into measures that work within the existing constitutional order: a special prosecutorial police unit, action against unlawful wealth, review of public procurement contracts, a functioning media regulator and appointments on professional criteria (Student List programme). Many of the obstacles these measures target are practical, and removing them will require legislation, money and enforceable procedures, guided in each case by the question of what stops a lawful investigation, audit or appointment from taking effect.

The hardest problem is that a single institution can contain compromised leadership, unlawful practices and professionals who have kept their independence. Treating the judiciary or the prosecution service as captured wholesale would destroy the capacity the reform depends on. Yet personal independence is of little use when a prosecutor cannot get the police to comply. Restoration must therefore protect those trying to do their jobs, establish responsibility for obstruction, and give lawful decisions operational effect, with allegations of misconduct assessed individually and the validity of appointments treated as a separate question.

This calls for a distinction between restoring the conditions of legality and retaliating by legal means, what Mark Tushnet calls “constitutional hardball” (Tushnet). Restoration changes the conditions of public decision-making, so officials must give legal reasons and answer for departing from them. Retaliation uses legal instruments to decide beforehand who will lose office, be prosecuted, or be favoured, and is, in that sense, a form of abuse: a legal form put to ends the rule does not authorise. Whether a given measure amounts to one or the other depends on its design and operation, whatever its authors say they intend, and the distinction matters most for personnel, where two separate questions arise. The first concerns removal: a judge or prosecutor appointed under SNS cannot be removed for having been appointed during that period, still less for presumed loyalties, and removal requires grounds established in law, evidence of individual conduct, a hearing and review by an independent body. The second concerns invalidity, which arises where the appointing body was itself constituted in breach of the rules conferring the power to appoint and raises the question of whether the office was ever validly conferred (Kristan). This second question is categorical and should be settled through a competent procedure, with proportionality applying to the effects of the decisions taken in that office and the appointee’s status following from the finding on validity. Where someone holds office lawfully, reform should reduce the room for abuse within that office without inventing grounds for dismissal, a standard that also protects officials whose lawful decisions displease the new government.

The practical agenda should begin where legal duties have been defeated, as when TOK’s lawful instructions simply went unexecuted. We regard this as a violation because those under a duty to provide the means of investigation induced the incapacity, which distinguishes it from a deficiency in institutional capacity (Kristan). The proposed prosecutorial police unit is meant to ensure investigators follow a prosecutor’s instruction even when the executive prefers inaction, but whether it achieves this, or becomes a new partisan force, will depend on who commands it, how its members are appointed, what resources it controls, and who oversees it. Its success should be measured by whether a lawful instruction reliably produces investigative action, including against the powerful.

The pardons and the Sky revelations show another way to hollow out the capacity to investigate power, and accountability therefore requires disclosure and lawful scrutiny of the September clemency decisions, along with the conditions for independent investigation. The constitutional grant of the pardon power leaves open whether a given pardon served a public purpose, and a pardon that complies with the clemency power while protecting a network of private loyalties would be a misuse of power, an act within the letter of a competence that defeats the principle justifying it (Kristan). An electoral mandate neither establishes anyone’s criminal responsibility nor authorises the new government to disregard existing legal acts, so the new majority must rebuild the procedures through which responsibility is established and consequences imposed, procedures that will also bind it.

For the same reason, we do not adopt a stance of equidistance: documented evidence of coercion and an unsupported denial cannot carry equal weight, and legal analysis owes its readers explicit evidential standards, a clear line between institutional diagnosis and individual criminal guilt, and consistent application of both. These standards guard against two equally damaging errors, since requiring a captured institution to certify its own capture would make criticism impossible, and treating every allegation as a proven offence would turn accountability into punishment by political designation.

What Defeat Does Not Undo

Losing the government has still left SNS with a strong presence in the state, since it keeps 103 seats, the interim presidency until the new Assembly convenes and a chance in the presidential election, a victory in which would allow its president to appoint five of the fifteen judges of the Constitutional Court. Its appointees also remain throughout the judiciary, the prosecution service, the regulators and the public broadcaster, and pro-government outlets still dominate national media (OSW).

Vučić has promised a combative opposition, and if he wages it from these positions outside parliament, the danger is a government that wins elections and still cannot get institutions to act. The test for the students’ project is therefore whether judges, prosecutors, and nongovernmental actors can now act without political approval, regardless of which government is in office.

The students’ original demand – that institutions be allowed to do their jobs – remains the right measure of what follows. It is a demand to live and work without political permission: for a public employee, to refuse party work without losing their job; for a prosecutor, to investigate protected suspects; and for a university, to teach and criticise without retaliation. A change in government will matter only if it makes norms effective in these places, under duties that would also bind a Student List government. The SNS’s defeat has made that possibility real. Its realisation will show what institutions can do when the politically powerful want them to act otherwise.

item.title: France’s Ban on Fossil Fuel Advertising and Its European Implications
item.dc:creator: Marta Torre-Schaub
item.description:
The French Conseil d’État’s judgment of 2 October 2026 reaffirms the government’s obligation to give practical effect to environmental legislation by establishing a clear framework for fossil fuel advertising. Beyond strengthening legal certainty and transparency, it raises fundamental questions about the balance between climate protection, commercial freedom and the prevention of misleading environmental claims, while potentially informing future regulatory developments across Europe.

The post France’s Ban on Fossil Fuel Advertising and Its European Implications appeared first on Verfassungsblog.
item.content:encoded:
The regulation of fossil fuel advertising has become an increasingly important issue at the intersection of climate policy, commercial freedom and consumer protection. In France, the Total proceedings1) and the Volvic case2) have renewed attention to the legal boundaries of environmental advertising, corporate communication and potentially misleading sustainability claims. On 2 October 2026, the Conseil d’État (CE) addressed the issue from a different angle in its judgment Association Résistance à l’agression publicitaire3) and examined the government’s obligation to establish the regulatory framework necessary to implement the statutory prohibition on fossil fuel advertising.

Introduced by the Climate and Resilience Act of 22 August 2021, Article L. 229-61 of the French Environmental Code prohibits advertising relating to the sale or promotion of fossil fuels. However, the absence of the implementing decree left important questions concerning the prohibition’s practical scope and application unresolved. The Conseil d’État annulled the Prime Minister’s implicit refusal to adopt the decree and ordered its adoption within six months. The judgment thus reaffirms that the executive cannot indefinitely deprive legislation of practical effect through regulatory inaction.

The institutional significance of this decision is important when contrasted with the earlier civil proceedings. Whereas civil courts assess the legality of private actors’ communications and the potential liability of these operators, the Conseil addresses the government’s responsibility for establishing the rules against which such communications must be assessed. These forms of judicial scrutiny are complementary: litigation may resolve individual disputes, but it cannot fully compensate for uncertainty caused by the absence of regulations expressly required by Parliament.

The judgment is therefore significant in two respects. It strengthens the enforceability of environmental legislation while highlighting the need for legal certainty in a field where environmental objectives intersect with commercial freedom. Clearer rules may restrict certain forms of advertising, but they can also benefit businesses, advertising agencies, media operators and consumers by clarifying which communications are permitted. Greater transparency may, in turn, reduce ambiguity and help prevent avoidable civil and commercial disputes.

Beyond France, the decision raises a broader European question which is whether the regulation of climate-related advertising should remain primarily concerned with misleading claims or if it should also encompass restrictions on the promotion of particularly carbon-intensive products. This post examines the question under four different angles.

The Government’s Duty to Implement Environmental Legislation

The judgment confirms that implementing legislation is a legal obligation rather than a matter of unrestricted executive discretion. Article 21 of the French Constitution provides that the Prime Minister ensures the implementation of statutes and exercises regulatory power (Pt 2). Where legislation requires implementing measures, the government must adopt them within a reasonable period, unless a superior legal obligation prevents it.

This principle reflects established administrative jurisprudence. The executive cannot indefinitely suspend the practical application of legislation by failing to adopt measures necessary for its implementation. Although the government retains discretion over the technical content of regulations, that discretion does not include the power to disregard a statutory obligation to act. In this sense, Article L. 229-61 illustrates this distinction. It prohibits advertising relating to the sale or promotion of fossil fuels while requiring a decree in the Conseil d’État to specify the fuels concerned, determine the treatment of renewable components incorporated into fossil fuels and establish the practical arrangements governing the prohibition. The legislation also requires consideration of public access to price information and the existing obligations imposed on energy suppliers and distributors. The Conseil then considered the decree indispensable to the implementation of these provisions (Pt. 2). More than four years had elapsed since the adoption of the Climate and Resilience Act, making the delay incompatible with the requirement to act within a reasonable period. The judgment consequently distinguishes the formal existence of a statutory prohibition from its practical enforceability.

This distinction is important. Indeed, if the executive could determine whether legislation becomes operational simply by withholding the necessary regulations, Parliament’s legislative authority would be weakened. The effectiveness of environmental policy would depend not only on the law adopted but also on the government’s willingness to implement it.

The obligation to regulate is nevertheless not unlimited. It concerns measures necessary to implement the statute, rather than every administrative measure that might advance its broader policy objectives. The judgment is therefore best understood as enforcing an existing statutory duty, rather than expanding the government’s regulatory powers.

Judicial Intervention and the Need for Regulatory Clarity

The second contribution of the judgment lies in the Conseil d’État’s decision to go beyond the annulment of administrative paralysis (Pt. 3). Relying on Article L. 911-1 of the Code of Administrative Justice, the Conseil ordered the Prime Minister to adopt the implementing decree within six months of notification of the judgment. This injunction gives practical effect to judicial review. An annulment alone would establish the illegality of the refusal without necessarily ensuring that the missing regulatory framework would be completed promptly. By requiring affirmative action, the High Administrative jurisdiction connects its legal finding to a concrete obligation of implementation.

The distinction between the present administrative proceedings and the earlier Total and Volvic disputes is particularly instructive. Civil courts examine individual advertising campaigns, commercial practices and the potential liability of private companies. By contrast, the Conseil d’État determines whether the government has fulfilled its responsibility to establish the rules within which such conduct must be assessed. Its intervention is therefore structural rather than confined to the legality of a particular communication. In my view, these two forms of judicial scrutiny are complementary. Civil litigation may identify unlawful conduct and provide remedies in individual cases, but it cannot fully remedy uncertainty caused by the prolonged absence of regulations required by Parliament. Where the boundaries between prohibited fossil fuel promotion, corporate communication and environmental information remain unclear, companies may struggle to assess their obligations, while consumers may find it difficult to understand the legal significance of environmental advertising.

The government’s regulatory role is therefore important. By defining the applicable rules, it establishes the framework within which public and private operators must conduct their activities. Clearer provisions can reduce inconsistent interpretations, improve compliance and provide a more transparent basis for enforcement. Businesses gain greater predictability when assessing advertising campaigns, while regulators and courts gain a clearer standard against which to evaluate disputed practices.

This clarification may also help prevent future civil and commercial disputes. Where the law provides sufficiently precise definitions, fewer disagreements should arise solely from uncertainty about the scope of the prohibition. Nevertheless, litigation cannot be eliminated: questions of interpretation and application will remain, particularly in complex cases involving digital advertising, indirect promotion or cross-border communications.

The judgment also illustrates the limits of judicial intervention. The Conseil d’État does not draft the decree itself, nor does it determine every technical question concerning the prohibition. The executive retains responsibility for the regulatory choices required to implement the statute (Pts. 5 and 6). By compelling action without dictating the entire content of the resulting regulation, the Conseil preserves the distinction between judicial review and administrative rulemaking.

Environmental Protection, Commercial Freedom and Misleading Claims

The implementation of the advertising ban requires a careful reconciliation of environmental objectives with economic freedoms (see, for example, Google and others v. Russia). In the present case, the Conseil d’État rejected the argument that the statutory prohibition was inherently incompatible with France’s international commitments, including freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and European Union principles governing the free movement of goods and services (Pt. 7).

However, this should not be interpreted as an unconditional endorsement of every possible restriction on advertising. Commercial expression may fall within the protection of Article 10, while freedom to conduct a business and property rights remain relevant when assessing regulatory proportionality (see Barthold v. Germany; Markt intern Verlag v. Germany, and Google LLC & al. v. Russia cit.). The legality of specific provisions and enforcement measures may therefore depend on their clarity, scope and compatibility with superior legal norms (see Barthold v. Germany).

Returning to the central question of my commentary, the distinction between fossil fuel advertising and misleading environmental claims is equally important. An advertisement may be misleading because it exaggerates a product’s environmental benefits or gives consumers an unsubstantiated impression of a company’s climate performance. Conversely, an advertisement may fall within the statutory prohibition because of its promotional purpose, even if its individual factual statements are accurate.

The truthfulness of an advertising claim and the lawfulness of publishing the advertisement are separate legal questions. The implementing decree must therefore clarify which communications promote fossil fuels while preserving access to information that consumers are legally entitled to receive. This distinction is particularly relevant to corporate statements concerning renewable investments, decarbonisation strategies and climate commitments. Depending on their content and context, such statements may provide legitimate information or create a misleading impression by obscuring the continuing importance of fossil fuels to a company’s activities. Regulatory clarity can help resolve these difficulties by defining the scope of prohibited promotion and distinguishing it from mandatory consumer information or other communications protected by law. Such precision serves both environmental protection and commercial freedom: it prevents the statutory objective from being undermined while enabling businesses to understand the limits of permissible conduct. The judgment requires the government to establish the regulatory framework necessary for consistent application of the statute. Subsequent disputes will still need to be assessed under the relevant rules and considering their circumstances.

European Implications and the Future of Fossil Fuel Advertising Restrictions

The judgment may inform wider European debates on the regulation of climate-related advertising. Directive (EU) 2024/825 strengthens consumer protection against certain misleading environmental claims, including unsupported generic claims and misleading representations of future environmental performance. Member States were required to transpose the directive by 27 March 2026 and apply the relevant measures from 27 September 2026.

However, the directive does not establish a general European prohibition on fossil fuel advertising. Its primary objective is to improve the reliability of consumer information, whereas the French approach restricts the promotion of specified energy sources. The two frameworks are complementary but legally distinct: one targets misleading commercial practices, while the other restricts a category of advertising irrespective of whether each individual claim is deceptive.

France’s experience may encourage other Member States to consider whether existing greenwashing rules adequately address the environmental implications of promotional communication. Yet broader restrictions would raise important questions concerning proportionality, freedom of expression, internal market freedoms and the appropriate legal basis for European action. Indeed, cross-border advertising further complicates enforcement. Digital campaigns may reach consumers in several Member States through intermediaries established in different jurisdictions. Divergent national rules could then create uncertainty for businesses and media operators, while uneven enforcement might weaken the practical effect of domestic restrictions. This is why cooperation between national authorities may become increasingly important, mainly if additional countries adopt comparable measures.

Conclusion

The broader significance of the French judgment lies in demonstrating that environmental legislation requires effective administrative implementation. Other jurisdictions may draw lessons from the French approach when considering how to combine climate objectives, commercial freedoms and predictable regulatory standards.

In this context, the future of fossil fuel advertising restrictions will depend on the relationship between national initiatives and European harmonisation. A common European approach could provide greater consistency for businesses and consumers, but it would require careful consideration of the scope of prohibited communications, legitimate information needs and fundamental rights. Any such initiative would also need to address the practical distinction between direct promotion of fossil fuels and broader corporate communication about energy strategies.

For now, the judgment offers a more limited but significant lesson: governments must fulfil their obligation to implement environmental legislation, and regulatory uncertainty cannot be allowed to persist indefinitely where Parliament has expressly required further measures. Whether this principle contributes to broader European restrictions will depend on subsequent legislative choices, administrative practice and judicial decisions. The French judgment’s lasting importance will depend on whether the implementing framework provides sufficiently clear, transparent and proportionate rules.
